ranges.en: Mishna rules a virgin marries on Wednesday and a widow on Thursday, and ties the Wednesday rule to court sessions.
Rav Yosef transmits Shmuel's query: what is the reason the Sages set a virgin's wedding for Wednesday?
Answer: the Wednesday wedding is linked to a teaching about when the designated time arrives, which the Gemara cites.
Cites a mishna elsewhere about a postponed wedding and restates the Wednesday rule that it supports.
Rav Yosef, astonished, objects that Shmuel explains a taught halakha using a different teaching.
Asks which of the two cited teachings is taught and which is not, since both appear in tradition.
Answers that both teachings are transmitted in tradition, so both are valid sources.
Explains Shmuel's method: a halakha with a stated reason is made dependent on a later one without a stated reason.
Offers the alternate version of Shmuel's teaching and again asks the reason for the Wednesday rule.
Objects: if the reason is court-visit timing, a Sunday wedding would serve the same purpose.
Defends the mishna: the Sages set Wednesday so the groom spends three days preparing the feast.
Cites the later mishna about a postponed wedding to draw a conclusion from the feast-preparation rationale.
Concludes that a groom unable to marry before Wednesday because of preparations owes no sustenance until then.
Applies the same reasoning: if the groom or bride falls ill or she menstruates, no sustenance is owed before the wedding.
Raises a dilemma: is a groom's illness an unavoidable delay like the Wednesday ordinance, or does the duty still apply?
Asks whether a bride's illness counts as an unavoidable disaster, and whether the groom can say he stands ready.
Asks the ruling if the bride becomes menstruant and the wedding is postponed.
Replies that menstruation at her fixed time is predictable, so the question need not be raised.

2b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Clarifies the earlier dilemma: when menstruation falls at her set time she cannot claim inundation, since the delay was avoidable.
Asks the ruling when menstruation falls outside her set time, and whether varying cycles make the delay avoidable.
Rav Aḥai resolves the dilemmas by reading the wording of the mishna.
Quotes the mishna that a postponed wedding lets brides eat from the groom's food and teruma.
Explains the wording is passive, about brides not being married, rather than grooms not marrying.
Asks what 'not married' describes, and whether it must mean compulsion such as the bride's illness.
Rav Ashi replies that only groom-caused delay obligates support; the tanna's phrasing follows its earlier clause.
Rava holds that unavoidable circumstances do not count for bills of divorce, unlike the support obligation.
Asks what Rava's source is for this principle about divorce.
Cites a Gittin mishna on a conditional divorce that fails by death, inferring that illness would validate it.
Refutes the proof: illness may also void the divorce; death was cited only as an example of no posthumous divorce.
Asks why death is needed, since the first clause already states that a deathbed divorce is void.
Suggests the first clause excludes a ruling of 'our Rabbis' rather than the case of illness.
Quotes a baraita: the Rabbis permitted remarriage when the husband died within the stipulated twelve months.
Asks who the Rabbis mentioned in the baraita are.
Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel, identifies them as a court ruling, and the view follows Rabbi Yosei that a written date proves timing.
Cites the latter clause of the mishna: a conditional divorce takes effect if the husband dies or falls ill.
Rejects that proof: the divorce may take effect only at death, since the husband wants to avoid levirate marriage.
Cites a case where an agent arrived late because of a ferry; the condition is treated as met despite circumstances beyond control.
Shmuel rules that such an attempted return, prevented by circumstances, does not count as a return.
Rejects that proof: foreseeable circumstances differ, since the husband should have stipulated them and bears the failure himself.
Rava gives his own reasoning: circumstances beyond control are irrelevant to fulfilment, out of concern for virtuous and licentious women.

ranges.en: Rava's rationale for virtuous women: a husband who chose the delay may look compelled, leaving his wife unable to remarry.
Rava's concern for licentious women: a truly compelled husband may look willing, so she remarries, voiding the divorce and making children mamzerim.
Asks whether any matter is not a divorce under Torah law, yet the Sages permit a remarriage for the sake of women's welfare.
Answers that the Sages can annul a betrothal, since every betrothal is conditioned on their agreement.
Ravina objects: the answer works for money-betrothals, but what of a betrothal by intercourse?
Rav Ashi replies that the Sages rendered the intercourse licentious, so it does not validate a betrothal.
Others report Rava's view: unavoidable circumstances affect divorce just as they excuse the groom from providing support.
Objects with a Gittin mishna: a conditional divorce fails on death, implying illness would validate it, contrary to Rava.
Defends Rava: illness also voids the divorce; death is only an example showing that posthumous divorce is invalid.
Asks why the first clause needs to mention death, since it already teaches that a posthumous divorce is void.
Suggests the first clause mentions death to exclude the view of our Rabbis.
Cites the latter clause: a conditional divorce takes effect if the husband dies within twelve months, and asks whether illness is the same.
Rejects that proof: the divorce takes effect at death only because the husband avoids levirate marriage, not in general.
Cites the ferry story: a late agent prevented by the ferry is treated as having returned, implying unavoidable delay counts.
Shmuel rules that this attempted return does not count as a return.
Rejects that proof: foreseeable obstacles differ, since the husband should have stipulated them and so caused the failure.
Rav Shmuel bar Yitzḥak: the Wednesday rule applies only since Ezra's ordinance fixed court days on Monday and Thursday.
Asks what 'before Ezra's ordinance' means, since past practice has no halakhic effect.
Clarifies: if courts sit daily again, as before Ezra, a woman may marry on any day of the week.
Asks whether the Wednesday rule still needs the reason of the Sages' concern for the groom's feast preparations.

3b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks what 'the Sages were assiduous' means, and turns to a baraita explaining the Wednesday rule.
Baraita states the Wednesday rule: a bride marries then so that a groom with a virginity claim can go to court the next morning.
Baraita objects: if the court-timing reason holds, a Sunday wedding should be just as good.
Answers that the Sages were assiduous for brides' welfare, choosing Wednesday so the groom spends three days on the feast.
Baraita: the people adopted the custom of marrying on Tuesday, and the Sages did not object.
Baraita: no Monday marriage even in danger, but a marriage under coercion is permitted.
Baraita: the groom is separated from the bride before Shabbat evening, to avoid an act of wounding that is forbidden on Shabbat.
Asks what the danger is: if a decree threatens execution, why not abolish the Wednesday rule entirely?
Rabba: the baraita refers to a decree forcing the bride to submit first to the prefect, which is danger because virtuous women may die.
Asks why the Sages do not instruct women that submitting to violation under coercion is permitted.
Answers that licentious women would exploit such a ruling, and priests' wives would be forbidden even if raped.
Asks why the Sages do not abolish the Wednesday ordinance entirely and set a different day.
Answers that a rabbinic ordinance is not abolished because of a persecution decree that may soon be lifted.
Objects: if so, Tuesday is no better, since the prefect would come on Tuesday too.
Answers that the wedding date is uncertain, so the prefect will not uproot himself to pursue one bride.
Baraita continues: no Monday marriage in danger, but if due to coercion, the marriage is permitted.
Asks what coercion means, since the baraita's terms seem inconsistent with the earlier decree.
Rava: coercion means a general's army arriving on Wednesday to seize feast supplies; Monday is allowed because his entourage comes Tuesday.
Offers an alternative: 'coercion' refers to disruption of the feast preparations by a death in the family.
Cites a baraita: if the feast is ready and a parent of a party dies, the corpse is moved aside and the wedding proceeds.

4a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Baraita: the groom consummates, then observes seven feast days and seven mourning days; during both, the couple sleep apart and jewelry is not withheld.
Clarifies the baraita: this order applies only if the groom's father or bride's mother dies, since no one else would prepare the feast.
Rafram bar Pappa cites Rav Ḥisda: the wedding proceeds immediately only if water was already placed on the meat, since otherwise it would spoil.
Rava says meat sells in a city even with water added; Rav Pappa says in a village it does not sell without water.
Asks where a case matching Rav Ḥisda's ruling can actually be found.
Rav Ashi answers that such a case exists in an intermediate town, too small to be a city and too large to be a village.
Cites a baraita said to accord with Rav Ḥisda, where the wedding proceeds immediately once water was placed on the meat.
Baraita continues: the groom consummates, the corpse is buried, and the couple observe feast and mourning days apart.
Baraita adds: if the wife begins menstruating, the couple sleep apart, and jewelry is not withheld during the thirty days.
Baraita: regardless, the groom may not have intercourse with his bride on Shabbat evening or at Shabbat's conclusion.
The Gemara reads the baraita's separate sleeping arrangements as supporting Rabbi Yoḥanan's view.
Rabbi Yoḥanan: though mourning does not apply on festivals, private mourning practices continue during the feast days.
Rav Yosef bar Rava, citing Rava: separation applies only before intercourse; if already consummated, the wife may sleep with him.
Asks: here the baraita concerns a groom who already consummated, yet the tanna still requires separate sleeping.
Answers that the rule permitting shared sleep applies only to menstruation, which is not a mourning case.
Asks: doesn't the baraita say 'and likewise', equating the mourner's status with that of a husband whose wife menstruates?

ranges.en: Restates the tanna's point: a menstruating wife's husband sleeps apart before intercourse, while a mourner's couple sleep apart even after it.
Asks whether the mourning prohibition is more lenient than the menstruation prohibition, since seclusion is allowed with a menstruating wife but not in mourning.
Cites Rav Huna's list of services a menstruating wife may perform, and a baraita on mourning that permits some of the same services.
Resolves the conflict: the sleeping rule concerns the husband's mourning and the service rule the wife's, and mourning is less severe than menstruation.
Points out that the baraita names both the groom's father and the bride's mother, so it draws no distinction between the two mourners.
Explains that the no-distinction point refers to other mourning practices, not to the ban on seclusion.
Objects with a baraita on a father-in-law's death that distinguishes husband's and wife's mourning and states no seclusion ban.
Emends the baraita to refer only to the husband's mourning, so he sleeps apart from his wife and not the reverse.
Asks: doesn't the tanna teach 'and likewise', implying no difference between the two cases?
Answers that the no-difference point concerns only painting the eyes and rouging the face.
Asks whether 'with him' means together in bed, given the concern over intercourse.
Explains 'with him' means at home, citing Rav's instruction to his son about his wife's father's death.
Rav Ashi: the question rests on a false premise, since the leniency is specific to mourning immediately after a wedding.
Asks what leniency the Sages enacted, testing the options against the views of Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua on when mourning begins.
Answers that the leniency is allowing the groom to observe the feast days, which led the Sages to bar seclusion.
Quotes the baraita: the groom may not consummate on Shabbat evening or at the conclusion of Shabbat.
Asks: the Shabbat-evening ban is explained by the prohibition on inflicting a wound, but why ban intercourse at Shabbat's end?
Begins Rabbi Zeira's reply to that question; the reply continues beyond this span.

ranges.en: Proposes the reason for the Saturday-night wedding ban: calculating wedding arrangements on Shabbat, which is forbidden.
Abaye objects: calculations for a mitzva are permitted on Shabbat, citing Rav Ḥisda and Rav Hamnuna, so they cannot be the reason.
Cites sources permitting Shabbat activity for public needs, charity, saving lives, and matchmaking, showing mitzva-calculations are allowed.
Rabbi Zeira: the ban is a decree lest one slaughter a young fowl on Shabbat while preoccupied with the wedding feast.
Abaye objects by analogy: Yom Kippur eve falling on Shabbat would then be postponed for the same decree-based reason.
Defends Rabbi Zeira: on Yom Kippur eve the cook is not preoccupied and has time, unlike a wedding host.
Concludes that the ban on Shabbat-evening intercourse is likewise a decree against slaughtering a fowl, not intercourse itself.
Raises a dilemma: is the virgin's intercourse on Wednesday or Thursday, given that the groom's resolve might cool overnight?
Cites bar Kappara: a virgin has intercourse on Thursday, since the fish blessing was given on the fifth day of Creation.
Infers that the reason is the blessing, not concern that the groom's resolve would cool.
Objects: if so, a widow should also have intercourse on Thursday, the day the fish blessing was given.
Answers that postponing to the day of man's blessing is preferable, since that option is available.
Offers an alternative reason for the widow's Friday night: the Sages were assiduous for women's welfare.
Cites a baraita: intercourse on Friday keeps the groom from leaving early to work, ensuring three days of rejoicing.
Asks what practical difference lies between the blessing reason and the Sages' assiduousness reason.
Answers that the difference shows with an idle man, or with a Festival falling on Shabbat eve.
Bar Kappara teaches that the handiwork of the righteous exceeds the creation of heaven and earth.
Cites Isaiah's singular 'hand' for creation and Exodus's plural 'hands' for the Sanctuary, built by people.
Rabbi Ḥiyya the Babylonian challenges with Psalm 95:5, where dry land is formed by 'His hands' in the plural.
Asks: but is it not written 'formed' in the plural, which conflicts with the singular 'hand' reading?
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak: the plural refers to His fingers, citing Psalm 8:4 about the work of Your fingers.
Objects with Psalm 19:2, that the heavens were created by His hands, contrary to the righteous-handiwork claim.
Answers that the verse means the heavens attest to the righteous's handiwork, through rain brought by their prayers.
Bar Kappara's exegesis: reading 'azenekha' as 'your ear' teaches that one should not listen to improper matters.

ranges.en: The opening instruction that a person should place his finger in his ears.
Rabbi Elazar's teaching: why a person's fingers resemble pegs.
Asks what the underlying reason for the peg-like shape is.
Proposes that each finger is set apart and dedicated to its own sacred function.
Quotes the Master listing each finger's designated sacred measurement or use.
Rejects that explanation and asks for the real reason fingers are pointed.
Explains the pointed shape: fingers go in the ears to block hearing improper things.
Introduces a baraita from the school of Rabbi Yishmael as supporting evidence.
The baraita asks why the entire ear is hard while the earlobe is soft.
The ear is hard and the lobe soft so a person can fold the lobe in to seal the ear.
Baraita: one should avoid hearing idle talk because the ears burn first.
Dilemma: is intercourse with a virgin on Shabbat forbidden, depending on whether the blood is pooled or flows from a wound?
Follow-up dilemma: does the husband want the blood, or the opening the rupture creates?
Asks whether an unintended result is permitted per Rabbi Shimon or forbidden per Rabbi Yehuda.
Asks whether the act is destructive or constructive regarding the opening, under Rabbi Yehuda.
Notes that some authorities arrange the series of dilemmas differently.
Alternative series: does the husband want the act itself, making it forbidden, or just his pleasure?
If he wants only pleasure and the blood is incidental, which unintended-act view applies?
Under Rabbi Yehuda, is the act destructive or constructive in causing the wound?
If destructive, does Rabbi Yehuda exempt even intentional destructive Shabbat acts?

6a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon, who holds an intentional wound-causing act on Shabbat is liable.
Reports the rival Amoraic rulings of Rav and Shmuel on intercourse with a virgin on Shabbat, by locale.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzchak offers a mnemonic: each master is lenient only regarding his own locale.
Asks whether Rav permitted it, citing Rav's ruling that a barrel stopper may not be inserted on a Festival.
The barrel case differs: even Rabbi Shimon forbids an action with an inevitable consequence, like squeezing liquid.
Objects that Rav and Shmuel both ruled by Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon respectively, so how did Rav permit it?
Rav holds like Rabbi Yehuda; each version of the blood dispute makes the act destructive or permitted accordingly.
Rav Hisda raises an objection from a mishna.
The mishna on a young girl married before puberty: the Houses differ on how many nights blood is attributed to the wound.

6b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Proposes reading the prior ruling as referring to a case where intercourse on Shabbat is permitted.
Rava rejects that reading: the ruling refers to days other than Shabbat.
Abaye objects that the baraita counts four nights through the conclusion of Shabbat, so Shabbat is included.
Rava offers a new reading: the case is one where he already consummated the marriage before Shabbat.
Asks what the tanna then teaches, if the case is one of prior consummation.
Explains the ruling by analogy to Shmuel: entering a narrow opening on Shabbat is permitted despite falling pebbles.
Rav Yosef objects from a mishna on the groom exempt from Shema on Shabbat if he has not consummated.
Asks whether the exemption is due to preoccupation with the desire to consummate.
Abaye replies that the exemption is due to preoccupation with the consummation not yet done.
Rava challenges this: if preoccupation exempts, would someone whose ship sank at sea also be exempt?
Asks what follows if one were to accept that preoccupation is the reason.
Cites Rav's teaching that a mourner is obligated in all mitzvot except phylacteries, a verse proof.
Rava says the matter is a tannaitic dispute, as one baraita is taught differently.
Quotes two baraitot giving differing numbers of nights on which the groom is exempt from Shema.
Abaye resolves the baraitot as disputing preoccupation, not intercourse on Shabbat itself.
Quotes a baraita: a groom may not consummate a virgin marriage on Shabbat, and the Sages permit it.
Asks who the Sages are who permit it.
Rabba says it is Rabbi Shimon, who permits an unintended act on Shabbat.
Abaye objects that Rabbi Shimon concedes an inevitable consequence like the bleeding is forbidden.
Rabba replies that the Babylonians cannot divert, but some grooms are expert at diverting.
Asks why preoccupation would still exempt a groom if he is expert, and whether the Sages should spell it out.
Most men are experts, so the hymen is not an inevitable result and intercourse is permitted.
Rava bar Rav Hanan asks why groomsmen and a sheet are needed if intercourse without rupture is possible.
Abaye replies that the groom might see blood and intentionally destroy the hymen.
Rav Ami raises an objection from a mishna.
The mishna on draining an abscess on Shabbat: liability depends on whether the intent is to create a permanent opening.

7a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Distinguishes the abscess: there the pus is fully removed and nothing enduring is made, unlike the blood here.
Rav Ami permitted a man to consummate his virgin marriage for the first time on Shabbat.
The Sages object that her marriage contract is not yet written, so intercourse would be promiscuous.
Rav Ami replies that she should seize movables worth her contract as a deposit until it is written.
Rav Zevid permitted first intercourse on Shabbat, and some say he himself did so.
Rav Yehuda permitted first intercourse on a Festival; Rava's teaching is that the same applies to Shabbat.
Rav Pappa, in Rava's name, says Festival permission does not extend to Shabbat, which stays forbidden.
Rav Pappi asks whether the Festival permission for a wound extends to incense preparation by analogy.
Rav Pappa cites the verse on food preparation: incense is not universal need, while intercourse is universal.
Rav Aha asks whether a deer found on a Festival could then not be slaughtered, since it is not universal food.
Rav Ashi says deer meat is a universal need even if hard to get; incense is not universally used.
Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi reports that Rabbi Yohanan ruled in Tzaidan that first intercourse on Shabbat is forbidden.
Asks whether a ruling can be issued that establishes a prohibition at all.
Yes: a mishna shows Beit Hillel issued a stringent ruling extending Helene's nazirite vow.
A baraita on a severed spinal cord, with Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi ruling like Rabbi Yaakov's stringency.
Rav Huna says the halakha is not like Rabbi Yaakov, but like Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzchak gives an alternative version; Rav Abbahu reports Rabbi Yishmael ben Yaakov asking Rabbi Yohanan.
Rabbi Yishmael ben Yaakov asks whether first intercourse on Shabbat is permitted.
Rabbi Yohanan says it is prohibited.
The final halakha: first intercourse on Shabbat is permitted, and one need not fear causing a wound.
Rav's teaching: both a virgin and a widow who marry require the grooms' benediction.
Asks how Rav Huna could say so when he also taught that a widow does not require a benediction.
Resolves it: the two rulings concern a bachelor marrying a widow versus a widower marrying a widow.
Asks whether a widower marrying a widow also requires no benediction, given the ruling on it.
Rav Nachman reports Huna bar Natan's tradition on the source for the grooms' benediction.
Source for the benediction in a quorum of ten: Boaz took ten elders when marrying the widow Ruth.
A widow requires no benediction during the seven days of celebration, but does for one day.
A baraita: the Sages arranged the widow's wedding on Thursday so the groom rejoices with her three days.
Asks which case the baraita addresses, given seven or one day of celebration for those who marry.
Two resolutions: a widower has one benediction day and three celebration days, or a bachelor has seven and three.

7b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects from a baraita: seven days for a virgin, one day for a widow, so the bachelor-widow case seems omitted.
Asks whether a widow marrying a bachelor is also limited to one day, and why the baraita omits that case.
The baraita states categorical rules and omits details, since no virgin gets under seven days and no widow under one.
Rav Nachman cites a baraita deriving the groom's benediction from a quorum of ten via Ruth, and Rabbi Abbahu via Psalms.
Asks what Rav Nachman derives from the Psalms verse that Rabbi Abbahu uses.
Baraita of Rabbi Meir: even fetuses in the womb sang at the Red Sea, derived from the same Psalms verse.
Asks why the verse says source rather than belly, and what Rabbi Abbahu derives from Boaz's verse.
Boaz's ten elders teach that the Ammonite and Moabite prohibition applies only to males, implying a halakhic purpose.
Rav Nachman rejects that proof: if the purpose was halakhic, ten men would be unnecessary.
Ten men publicize a halakha; Shmuel's fetus-acquisition ruling and Boaz's assembly are cited as parallels.
Baraita: the groom's benediction is recited at the wedding canopy; Rabbi Yehuda adds the betrothal house.
Abaye explains Rabbi Yehuda's view as referring to Judea, where grooms secluded with their betrothed.
Baraita on the betrothal benediction, with Rav Yehuda's formula including the forbidden and permitted relatives.
Rav Aha son of Rava's variant concludes the betrothal blessing with the canopy and betrothal formula.
Explains the two formulae: concluding versus not concluding the blessing, like fruit blessings or kiddush.
Baraita: the groom's benediction is recited in a quorum of ten all seven days, per Rav Yehuda's qualification.
Asks which blessings are recited, and Rav Yehuda lists the seven blessings of the wedding.

8a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The first two wedding blessings: creation of all for His glory, and the Creator of mankind.
The third blessing: man made in God's image and a building formed from Him for eternity.
The fourth blessing: barren Jerusalem rejoices as her children are gathered within her.
The fifth blessing: bring great joy to loving friends as in Eden, blessing God who gladdens groom and bride.
The sixth blessing on joy and gladness, with a prayer for sounds of joy in Judea and Jerusalem.
Levi and Rav Asi recite five and six of the blessings at weddings in the houses of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rav Ashi.
Suggests the blessing dispute stems from whether man was created in one act or two.
Rejects that suggestion: everyone agrees man was created in one act of creation.
Explains the dispute differently: whether God's initial thought or the final action determines the outcome.
Rav Yehuda cites two verses, one saying God created man in His image and one saying male and female were created.
Asks how the apparent contradiction between the two verses is resolved.
God first intended to create two beings but ultimately created one, so the contradiction disappears.
Rav Ashi recites all seven blessings at a wedding, then only the zimmun form when no new guests come.
Guests from seven to thirty days after the wedding: the blessing In Whose dwelling is joy is said only if the hillula is mentioned.
Asks how long the blessing In Whose dwelling is joy continues when the groom states the wedding celebration.
Rav Pappi says twelve months after the wedding; Rav Pappa says the blessing starts at the preparation of barley for beer.
Asks whether Rav Pappa's practice of starting from betrothal for his son's wedding conflicts with that.
Rav Pappa was different: his wedding preparations were already in place, so the celebration started at betrothal.
Ravina recites from betrothal but the wedding is canceled; Rav Tahlifa's long blessings are rejected in favor of the Sages' formula.
Rav Haviva recites the In Whose dwelling is joy blessing at a circumcision, but the halakha is not like him because the baby is in pain.
Rav Nachman, quoting Rav: grooms count toward the quorum of ten for the wedding blessings, but mourners do not.
Objects from a baraita that grooms and mourners both count toward the quorum.
Rav was a tanna and could disagree with a baraita, as Rabbi Yitzchak reports from Rabbi Yochanan.
Rabbi Yitzchak, quoting Rabbi Yochanan: grooms count in the quorum, but mourners do not.
Objects again from the baraita that grooms and mourners are both counted in the quorum.

8b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Reconciles the baraita on grace with Rabbi Yohanan by limiting his ruling about mourners to the comfort line
Objection: Rabbi Yitzhak's report of Yohanan implies a blessing in the line, so his ruling must concern the square
Asks whether blessings are recited in the square throughout the seven days when the comfort meal happens only once
Introduces the precedent of Rav Hiyya bar Abba whose child died while Reish Lakish delayed coming to comfort him
Reish Lakish sends his disseminator the next day and instructs him to speak words of comfort, which are accepted
The disseminator begins his comforting speech
Cites Deuteronomy 32:19 to explain the child's death as punishment for ancestral provocation of God
Alternative account: the child was a youth, and the disseminator cited a verse to him accordingly
Quotes Isaiah 9:16 on God withholding compassion from youths and orphans, with His hand still outstretched
Asks what the phrase about God's hand still being outstretched means
Rav Hanan bar Rav's gloss: avoid speaking of the bridal canopy, since reckless speech can overturn a favorable decree
Asks how Reish Lakish could send someone to comfort Rav Hiyya and instead upset him
Explains the intent was to say Rav Hiyya is significant enough to suffer for a sinful generation's sins
Reish Lakish instructs the disseminator to praise God's greatness
The praise text itself, ending with the blessing about God who revives the dead
Reish Lakish instructs the disseminator to speak words of comfort to mourners
The mourners' comforting text, ending with the blessing about God who comforts mourners
Abaye criticizes the wording, objecting to phrasing that speaks of drinks yet to come as a dire prediction
Supports Abaye's correction by citing Reish Lakish and a teaching in the name of Rabbi Yosei against tempting misfortune
Rav Yosef introduces a further point about the wording
Asks which verse is the source for that point
Quotes Isaiah 1:9 about being like Sodom and Gomorrah
Asks how the prophet responded to that statement
Quotes Isaiah 1:10, the prophet's reply calling them rulers of Sodom, showing the words came true
Reish Lakish instructs the disseminator to speak words for those who comfort mourners
Begins the speech praising those who perform kindness, descendants of kindness-doers, bound to Abraham's covenant
Cites Genesis 18:19 on God knowing Abraham so he will command his children to do righteousness
Concludes the speech with the blessing that God pays the just reward
Reish Lakish instructs the disseminator to speak a statement on behalf of the entire Jewish people
The prayer for the people of Israel asking for redemption from calamities, ending with the blessing about halting plague
Ulla attributes a baraita: the attribution introduces the rule on the ten cups of wine for a mourner
The baraita's rule: ten cups to be drunk in a mourner's house, three before the meal, three during, four after
Later Sages added four more blessings, but people got drunk, so the number was restored to ten cups
Asks what Rabban Gamliel has to do with the practice of mourners' houses
Baraita: funerals grew opulent until Rabban Gamliel had himself buried in plain linen, and the people followed his example
Rav Pappa notes that today everyone is buried in plain garments, even inexpensive cloth worth one zuz
Rabbi Elazar's statement, introduced at the end of the daf

9a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A groom's claim that he found his bride not a virgin is credible enough to render her forbidden to him
Asks why his claim is credible, since the case looks like compound uncertainty that should be resolved leniently
The ruling is needed for a priest's wife, or for an Israelite's wife betrothed as a girl under three, leaving one uncertainty
Asks what new point this case teaches, since it seems to follow from a known law
Cites the mishnah on a man claiming betrothal against a woman's denial, where he alone is restricted

Rav Hisda tells the claimant to bring witnesses that he is the brother.
The claimant replies he has witnesses but fears Mari, which suggests he is indeed the brother.
Rav Hisda tells Mari to bring witnesses that the claimant is not his brother.
Mari objects that the burden of proof rests on the claimant, so the claimant must bring evidence.
Rav Hisda replies that he places the burden on Mari and his violent fellows, since they intimidate witnesses.
Apparently one is not suspected of two dishonesties, since requiring Mari's witnesses accomplishes nothing?
The amoraic dispute about a maidservant's testimony may follow a dispute between tanna'im: a baraita allows the father, mother, siblings and children.
A second baraita allows everyone to testify about a captive woman except her and her husband.
Rav Pappi and Rav Ashi hold that the maidservant is credible, contrary to the first baraita.
Does Rav Pappa's view depend on the tannaitic dispute, or can both baraitot be read consistently?
Rav Pappa could answer that the baraita refers to an incidental remark in an unrelated conversation, not direct testimony.
Rav Dimi relates that Rav Hanan of Carthage, or Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, reported an incident about an incidental remark.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi accepted a man's incidental remark about his mother's captivity, so a son's remark about his mother is allowed in this case.
Mishna: Rabbi Zekharya ben HaKatzav swore his wife was never defiled, but the Sages ruled he cannot testify about himself or his wife.
Tosefta: the Sages forbade the wife, but he did not divorce her, and they avoided seclusion by walking out and in with the sons.
Abaye asks whether a priest divorcing his wife may arrange a house in the courtyard with the children, as he did with his captive wife.
A baraita rules that a divorced woman may not marry and live in the courtyard of her former husband.

ranges.en: A priest may not share an alleyway with his divorcee; in a small village, the village counts as one neighborhood, as an incident there showed.
When they cannot share a courtyard or alleyway, which of them must be ousted?
Baraita: she is ousted in his favor, but if the courtyard is hers, he is ousted in her favor.
What is the rule if the courtyard belongs to both of them?
Attempted proof from the baraita that she is ousted in his favor, and asking what circumstances it describes.
If the baraita concerns his courtyard, the point is obvious, and if hers, it contradicts the other baraita, so it must concern a jointly owned courtyard.
The proof is rejected: the baraita may concern a courtyard he rented, in which case she is still ousted.
What halakhic conclusion was reached on this matter?
Rav cites Isaiah 22:17 to show a man is more distressed by being dislocated than a woman, so the woman is ousted.
Baraita: a priest who borrowed from his wife's inherited property is repaid only through a third party, to prevent business dealings between them.
Rav Sheshet: if such dealings come before a court, the court does not attend to them, since they were a transgression.
Rav Pappa: they are excommunicated for violating that prohibition.
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua: they are also flogged.
Rav Naḥman, citing Evel Rabbati: after divorce from betrothal, she is repaid directly, since they were never intimate.
An incident with a divorced betrothed couple before Rava, where Rava placed an intermediary between them.
Rav Adda bar Mattana objects, citing Rav Naḥman that after betrothal divorce she is paid directly.
Rava replies that the ruling applies only where the couple is not accustomed to each other, which these are.
Some say Rava did not place an intermediary between them.
Rav Adda asks Rava to place an intermediary, and Rava asks why, given Rav Naḥman's ruling.
Rav Adda replies that the ruling applies only where the couple is not accustomed, and these people are.
Mishna: witnesses may testify about what they saw as minors, including their father's, teacher's and brother's handwriting.
Mishna continues: a witness may testify about a wedding with a hinnuma, about a priest who immersed for teruma, and about the Shabbat boundary.
A person may not testify that someone had a path or a ceremonial burial plot on a property, since full testimony is needed to remove property from its owner.
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua: testimony about handwriting seen as a minor requires a witness who saw it as an adult.
Each of the cases in the mishna is needed, since none could be derived from the others.
Since document ratification is by rabbinic law as well as Torah law, the Sages accepted testimony from a minor's perspective, including about a brother's handwriting.
Mishna: a witness may testify about a wedding where the bride went out with a hinnuma or uncovered hair.
What is the reason he is deemed credible?
Most women marry as virgins, so the presumption is already there; his testimony only reveals a matter presumed true.
Mishna: a witness may testify that a man left school to immerse for teruma, which establishes that he is a priest.
Perhaps he is a priest's slave, who may also eat teruma?
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi holds it is forbidden to teach one's slave Torah, so the testimony that he was in school shows he is not a slave.
But is one not permitted to teach his slave Torah, given a baraita about a master who borrowed from or made his slave free?

ranges.en: Mishna: a slave who wore phylacteries before his master or read three verses in synagogue does not thereby go free.
The baraita is no proof, since the slave acted on his own initiative; the mishna's proof applies where he is raised like a child.
Mishna: a witness may testify that as a minor he saw people immerse to eat teruma, and that a man shared teruma with them at the threshing floor.
Perhaps the man is a priest's slave?
The mishna follows the view that teruma may be given to a slave only if his master is with him.
Baraita on a priest's wife's son and a priest's maidservant's son, with the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei.
Rabbi Yosei: each may say, if I am a priest give it to me for my own sake, and if a slave, give it for my master's sake.
The dispute depends on the place: where teruma led to lineage, the slave was barred, and where it did not, direct distribution was allowed.
Baraita: Rabbi Elazar son of Rabbi Yosei said he once testified and a slave was elevated to priesthood on his word.
Does it enter your mind that a slave was actually elevated?
A kal vachomer: God does not cause a pitfall through the righteous or their animals, so certainly not through the righteous themselves.
Rather, they sought to elevate the slave but did not, because Rabbi Elazar testified in Rabbi Yehuda's place, where teruma led to lineage.
Mishna: a witness may testify that this place is a beit haperas, which the witness saw as a minor.
What is the reason the witness is believed about what he saw as a minor?
Beit haperas impurity is rabbinic, so a trodden path is pure, and rabbinic matters can be established by testimony of this kind.
Mishna: a witness may testify that until here they would come on Shabbat.
The Shabbat boundary is rabbinic, so the witness is believed in that matter.
Mishna: a person is not believed to say that a path or a eulogy place existed on a property.
What is the reason?
One does not remove money from its presumptive owner on testimony about a matter witnessed as a minor.
Baraita: a child may testify that his father told him a family is pure or impure.
Does it enter your mind that the father meant ritual purity and impurity for a family?
Rather, the father meant unflawed or flawed lineage.
Baraita continues: testimony about ketzatza and about bringing ḥalla and gifts to a priest; Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka says such witnesses are credible.
Which clause is Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka disputing, since the last clause removes money from its owner?
Restating the clause: a witness who was a gentile or slave is not believed after conversion or liberation, and Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka disagrees.
What principle do they disagree about?
The first tanna holds a gentile was not exacting about the matter; Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka holds one who intended to convert was exacting.
What is a ketzatza?
Baraita on ketzatza: family members break a barrel of fruit in a public square to publicize a brother's unsuitable marriage; a child who witnessed it is believed.
Chapter closing formula: the Hadran marking the end of the chapter that begins with the widow.

ranges.en: Mishna lists young women whose rapist pays a fine, starting with mamzeret, Gibeonite and Samaritan cases and the converts, captives and freed maidservants.
Mishna continues with relatives and a menstruating woman: a fine is paid though karet applies, since no court-imposed death penalty exists.
Gemara asks whether only flawed-lineage young women carry a fine, implying unflawed young women do not.
Gemara explains the tanna is not giving a complete list, only the flawed-lineage cases where a fine is paid.
Gemara infers from the wording that a minor has no fine, and asks which tanna holds this view.
Rav Yehuda, quoting Rav, identifies Rabbi Meir as the tanna who holds that a minor has no fine.
A baraita supports this: a minor up to two pubic hairs has sale but no fine, and from two hairs until maturity a fine but no sale, attributed to Rabbi Meir.
Rabbi Meir's principle supports the attribution: wherever there is a sale there is no fine, and wherever there is a fine there is no sale.
The Rabbis hold that a minor from three years and a day until maturity has a fine.
Gemara challenges whether this means a fine but no sale, and then proposes emending the text.

29b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Gemara restates that a fine is paid even where sale is also possible, since the minor can be sold and still receives the fine.
Gemara questions whether these flawed-lineage young women are entitled to a fine at all, and why they are so named.
Gemara cites the rapist verse about a wife to show that only a wife suitable for him receives the fine.
Reish Lakish derives from three mentions of young woman that fines apply generally, and extend to prohibition violators and karet cases.
Rav Pappa derives the same extensions from the seducer law's three mentions of virgin, with the same inclusions.
Gemara asks why Rav Pappa did not follow Reish Lakish's derivation.
Rav Pappa needs his three-mention derivation for Abaye's separate teaching.
Abaye's teaching is cited: if the young woman dies before trial the rapist is exempt, since the verse names the young woman's father.
Gemara asks why Reish Lakish did not follow Rav Pappa's derivation.
Reish Lakish needs the three-mention derivation for a verbal analogy, as a baraita teaches.
A baraita links the seducer's fine to the virgin dowry through a verbal analogy using the word weigh.
Gemara objects that each scholar also needs the other's derivation, so the verbal analogy cannot settle the disagreement.
Six verses are used together: two pairs cover the basic halakhot, and the remaining mentions cover prohibition violators and karet cases.
Gemara notes the mishna's wording excludes the view of a tanna whose position is then cited in a baraita.
Baraita: Shimon HaTimni holds the wife must be one for whom betrothal takes effect, Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya that she is suitable to keep.
Gemara asks what practical difference separates the two tannaim's views.
Rabbi Zeira explains the difference concerns a mamzeret or Gibeonite, for whom betrothal takes effect but who cannot be sustained.
Gemara asks what difference arises under Rabbi Akiva, for whom betrothal does not take effect even with a mamzeret.
The difference lies in a widow raped by a High Priest, following the view of Rabbi Simai.
Baraita: Rabbi Simai holds Rabbi Akiva deems all illicit children mamzerim except a child from a widow and High Priest, derived from the ban on profanation.
Rabbi Yeshevav holds that a child from any relations without a permitted option in Israel is a mamzer, even a widow with a High Priest.
Gemara asks what difference remains between the two opinions on whether a fine is owed.

30a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Gemara restates the example of women liable for violating a positive mitzva, namely Egyptian and Edomite converts.
Gemara asks whether Rabbi Yeshevav's ruling makes sense if it merely rejects Rabbi Simai's reasoning.
If Rabbi Yeshevav states his own view, he holds that any child lacking permitted relations among Jews is a mamzer.
Gemara asks what difference remains between the two tannaim if even positive-mitzva violators are included.
The difference arises in the case of a non-virgin raped by a High Priest.
Gemara objects that this too involves a positive mitzva violation, so why is it different?
It is a positive mitzva not binding equally on all: it is positive and applies only to the High Priest.
Rav Ḥisda holds everyone agrees a fine is paid for rape of a menstruating woman, since she qualifies under both criteria.
The mishna's ruling on relations with a sister is said to exclude Rabbi Neḥunya ben HaKana's view, cited in a baraita.
Baraita: Rabbi Neḥunya ben HaKana treats Yom Kippur like Shabbat, so one who desecrates it is exempt from damage payments.
Gemara asks for the reasoning behind Rabbi Neḥunya ben HaKana's position.
Abaye's reasoning: the verses use harm for man and for Heaven, so as with man-caused harm, heaven-caused harm also exempts from payment.
Rav Adda bar Ahava objects that Jacob's warning may concern lions and thieves, which are human-caused, not cold and heat.
Refutes the objection: Jacob warned about every potential harm, so the verse cannot be restricted to one kind of catastrophe.
Gemara challenges whether cold and heat truly belong to Heaven's hand, given a conflicting baraita.
Baraita: all is in Heaven's hands except cold and heat, which man can avoid, while lions and thieves are human-caused.
Rav Yosef and Rabbi Ḥiyya teach that after the Temple's destruction the four death penalties remained though the Sanhedrin was abolished.
Gemara asks whether the four death penalties were in fact abolished, since no capital punishment exists today.

ranges.en: Gemara concludes that the four death penalties were not abolished, despite the Sanhedrin's abolition.
A list illustrates how each of the four death penalties can happen in practice, such as a fall from a roof for stoning.
Gemara proposes reversing the earlier assignment: lions and thieves are from Heaven, while cold and heat are from man.
Rava gives a different source for Rabbi Neḥunya ben HaKana's rationale, drawn from a verse in Leviticus.
Leviticus 20 juxtaposes karet with the death penalty, teaching that karet exempts from payment just as capital punishment does.
Gemara asks what practical difference lies between Rava and Abaye's rationales for Rabbi Neḥunya ben HaKana.
The difference appears with a non-priest who eats teruma: Abaye exempts him from payment, while Rava holds him liable.
Gemara objects, citing Rav Ḥisda: Rabbi Neḥunya concedes payment for stealing and eating forbidden fat, challenging Abaye's exemption for teruma.
Gemara asks with what case we are dealing, in order to reconcile the objection.
The case is one where another person inserted the teruma into his mouth, so acquisition and death liability coincide.
Gemara objects that once he chews the teruma he acquires it and owes payment before swallowing creates death liability.
Another person inserted it into the pharynx, so payment and death liability both arise when he swallows.
Gemara asks, if the teruma could be retrieved, why he is liable; and if not, why he is liable at all since he did nothing.
The case is needed only where retrieval is possible, but only with great difficulty and duress.
Rav Pappa: another inserted teruma liquids into his mouth, where they are ruined on entry, so acquisition and enjoyment coincide.
Rav Ashi: refers to a non-priest eating his own teruma, inherited or acquired from a priest, so no payment but death liability.

ranges.en: Restates the case: during a single Shabbat act he also tore another person's silk.
Rav Ḥisda's ruling: Rabbi Neḥunya ben HaKana concedes payment for one who steals and eats forbidden fat, since the theft preceded the prohibition.
Gemara suggests Rav Ḥisda's view contradicts Rabbi Avin's ruling.
Rabbi Avin's ruling: an arrow that tears silk during a Shabbat act is exempt, since lifting is a prerequisite for placement.
Gemara applies the same logic to eating: lifting is a prerequisite for eating, so the fat-eater should be exempt too.
Refutes the parallel: an arrow cannot be placed without lifting, but eating is possible without lifting, and the fat can be replaced.
Gemara asks what practical difference lies between the two formulations of Rabbi Avin's criterion.
Applying the formulations to a knife carrier: under one the act is unified and exempt; under the other he can retract it, so he is liable.
Rabbi Avin's ruling is restated: the arrow case is exempt because lifting is a prerequisite for placement.
Rav Beivai bar Abaye raises an objection from a baraita.
Baraita: one who lifts a purse on Shabbat is liable for theft before the Shabbat violation, while one who drags it out is exempt.
Rav Beivai objects: lifting should be a prerequisite for carrying out, so the theft falls within the Shabbat labor and he should be exempt.
The case is one where he lifted the pouch to conceal it, then changed his plan and carried it out, so he is liable.
Gemara asks whether one is liable in such a case of changed intention when carrying out on Shabbat.
Rav Simon, quoting Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Yoḥanan, rules that one who moves objects within a house and changes plan is exempt, as lifting was not for carrying out.
Gemara emends: he lifted it to carry out, but the thief stopped in the courtyard, so the initial lifting was only theft, not the start of labor.
Gemara asks why he stopped: adjusting a load on the shoulder is ordinary motion, so what is the halakha if he stopped only for that?

ranges.en: Gemara recalls the baraita's ruling that one who drags and exits on Shabbat is exempt from payment.
Gemara objects that the tanna should have distinguished within the carrying case itself, namely a person who stopped to rest.
The Gemara identifies the view as that of ben Azzai, the author of the pause principle.
Ben Azzai's principle: one who walks is like one who stands, since each step pauses between lifting and placement.
Gemara asks what the halakha is for one who throws an object from one domain to another.
Gemara answers that the thrower is exempt, and argues the tanna should have taught this inside the walking case instead.
The dragging case was needed because it is an unusual manner of carrying out, and the tanna teaches that it still counts.
Gemara asks which size of purse is meant: large ones are typically dragged, small ones never, so intermediate size is the case.
Gemara asks where he carried the pouch: into the public domain violates Shabbat but not theft, and into a private domain the reverse.
The ruling is needed only where he carried it to the sides of the public domain, marked off by small pegs.
Gemara asks whose view this is: Rabbi Eliezer treats the sides as public domain, while the Rabbis do not.
Rabbi Eliezer's view applies only to Shabbat liability, since crowds occasionally enter, but acquisition occurs there because crowds rarely gather.
Rav Ashi explains the exemption: he passed the purse hand to hand below three handbreadths, and a hand counts as a personal domain per Rava.
Ravina: he acquires the stolen item by removing it from the owner's domain, even without moving it into his own domain.
Mishna on a stolen animal: if it dies in the owner's domain after being dragged out, the thief is exempt; if lifted or taken out, he is liable.
Ravina infers from the mishna's first clause that taking an animal out of the owner's domain is acquisition, so he is liable.
Rav Aḥa infers from the latter clause that taking out is like lifting, so removal from the owner's domain is acquisition.
Gemara notes the first clause is difficult for Rav Aḥa, while the latter clause is difficult for Ravina.
Resolution: for Rav Aḥa the first clause works since the owner's domain persists until the animal enters another's; Ravina rejects taking-out as lifting.
The mishna repeats its list of relations incurring a fine, beginning with a sister and a father's sister.
Gemara raises a contradiction from a mishna listing the same relations for which offenders are flogged, which suggests no fine.

32a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objection: the principle that one is not both flogged and fined conflicts with the mishna's case of relations with a sister.
Ulla rejects the difficulty as unfounded.
Resolution: the mishna concerns a young sister, where a fine is owed, versus a grown sister where no fine is owed.
Objection: a grown sister also yields no fine, yet humiliation compensation exists, so lashes should not apply.
Resolution: the mishna concerns an imbecile sister, who suffers no humiliation beyond her status.
Counter: pain payment would still apply to raping an imbecile.
Resolution: the case is a seduced woman, who receives no pain payment since she consented.
Restatement: even a young sister works, since she is an orphan and seduced, so the seducer owes no fine.
Inference that Ulla holds: wherever both money and lashes apply, one pays money and is not flogged.
Asks what source Ulla has for this principle.
Source offered: the law of one who injures another.
The injury case: money is owed and lashes are not, supporting the general rule.
Generalization: in every case of both money and lashes, one pays money and is not flogged.
Asks why the injury case can serve as a paradigm, given its particular stringency.
Reply: injury also has a lenient aspect, since it is permitted selectively in court.
Alternative source: conspiring witnesses, who owe money and are not flogged.
Generalization restated from the witnesses case.
Asks why conspiring witnesses can serve as a paradigm, given they need no forewarning.
Reply: conspiring witnesses are lenient, since they performed no action, only speech.
Derivation from the common features of both cases: money and lashes, with money paid and no flogging.
General rule: in any case with both liabilities, one pays money and is not flogged.
Asks why the common ground can serve, given the stringent features in both cases.
Reply: both cases carry a lenient feature absent elsewhere, so they cannot ground the general rule.

32b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Ulla derives the rule that one pays money and is not flogged through a verbal analogy.
Verbal analogy: the word taḥat in the rape verse matches taḥat in the injury verse, where money replaces lashes.
Generalization: wherever both money and lashes apply, one pays money and is not flogged.
Rabbi Yohanan resolves it: if witnesses forewarned him he is flogged, otherwise he pays, since lashes need forewarning.
Inference that Rabbi Yohanan holds: with liability for both, a forewarned offender is flogged and does not pay.
Asks what source Rabbi Yohanan has for this principle.
Source: a verse limits punishment for one wrong, and the forty-lashes verse follows, so lashes prevail over payment.
Objection: the injury case pays money without lashes even when forewarned, which undermines Rabbi Yohanan's principle.
Possible reply: the rule applies only without forewarning; with forewarning, lashes apply and payment does not.
Objection: a teaching of Rabbi Yohanan requires lashes for a blow, which seems to contradict the proposed reply.
The cited teaching: a blow that does not cause damage worth a peruta is punished with lashes.
Asks what case this is, since without forewarning lashes cannot apply, so why flogging?
Reply: obviously he was forewarned, and the reason is that the damage has no monetary value worth a peruta.
Inference: if the damage is worth a peruta, one pays money and is not flogged even when forewarned.
Rabbi Ile'a's principle: the Torah explicitly extends the witness and injury cases to payment.
Asks where Rabbi Ile'a said this.
Reply: it was said concerning a mishna about conspiring witnesses.
Mishna: conspiring witnesses who falsely claimed a debt are flogged and pay, each liability having its own source; the Rabbis disagree.
Objection: perhaps the reverse holds, that whoever is flogged does not pay.
Rabbi Ile'a replies that the Torah explicitly extended conspiring witnesses to payment, not to lashes.
Asks where the Torah extended the case of conspiring witnesses.
Derivation: the phrase hand for hand seems superfluous unless it refers to an item passed from hand to hand.
That item is money, and the same reasoning applies to the one who injures another.
Parallel derivation from the injury verse: the repeated so shall be done implies an item that is given.
That item is money.
Asks why Rabbi Yohanan did not state Ulla's rule that one pays and is not flogged.
Reply: otherwise the prohibition of relations with a sister would carry no lashes, rendering it moot.
Supporting verse: the nakedness of your sister you shall not uncover.

33a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objection: the same reasoning applies to injury, so if he pays and is not flogged, the lashes verse is nullified.
Cited verse: he shall not exceed, lest he add more, so lashes are a required penalty.
Objection: the same reasoning applies to conspiring witnesses, so the verse on flogging the wicked is nullified.
Cited verse: if the wicked man deserves flogging, which the objection says must apply to conspiring witnesses.
Reply: the verse can apply to witnesses who testify that a priest is the son of a divorcee or halutza, where no fine is due.
Reply: for injury, the verse applies where the blow causes no damage worth a peruta.
Reply: for a sister, the verse applies to a grown sister, where no fine is due, so lashes are required.
Rabbi Yohanan replies that the tormented her verse is needed for Abaye's derivation, not for Ulla's analogy.
Abaye's verse: the words because he tormented her show the fifty is payment for the act.
Inference: the verse implies compensation for humiliation and degradation beyond the fine.
Asks from where Ulla derives Abaye's halakha, since he uses the verse for a verbal analogy.
Rava's verse: the phrase who lay with her teaches that fifty shekels are paid for the pleasure of lying with her.
Inference: beyond the fine, there is compensation for humiliation and degradation.
Rabbi Eliezer holds conspiring witnesses pay money and are not flogged, because they cannot be forewarned.
Rava's support: forewarning is impractical before, during, or after testimony, so forewarning is impossible.
Abaye objects: they can be forewarned in the brief interval after they finish speaking, while testimony is open.
Rav Aha objects: forewarn them first, and gesture during testimony to remind them, so they cannot claim forgetting.
Abaye's reductio: if forewarning were required, conspiring witnesses could not be put to death, contradicting the as he conspired verse.
Verse: you shall do to him as he conspired to do to his brother, requiring equal punishment, without forewarning.
Rav Samma objects: witnesses who falsely call a priest illegitimate fall under false witness, not as he conspired, so they should need forewarning.
Reply: the verse one law for all of you demands equal law, so exceptional cases also need no forewarning.
Rav Sheisha holds the injurer pays and is not flogged, derived from the pregnant woman verse rather than verbal analogy.
Verse: if men quarrel and hurt a pregnant woman, the penalty is set by her husband, showing payment without lashes.
Rabbi Elazar explains the verse concerns a quarrel involving death, where they sought to kill each other.
Verse: if harm follows, then you shall give a soul for a soul, showing a context of death.
Asks the circumstances: without forewarning, why is one killed, so the case must involve forewarning.
Reply: obviously he was forewarned, and forewarning about murder means forewarning about a lesser injury.
Principle: one forewarned about a severe matter is forewarned about a lesser one, so an injurer is forewarned.
Verse: if no harm follows, he shall surely be punished, indicating a monetary penalty rather than lashes.
Rav Ashi objects: forewarning for a lesser matter is not proven, and death may not be a more severe punishment than lashes.

33b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Proposal: perhaps lashes are more severe than death, since Rav said Hananiah's group would have bowed had they been flogged.
Rav's example: had Hananiah, Mishael and Azariah been flogged rather than thrown into the furnace, they would have worshipped the idol.
Objection from Rav Samma: there is a difference between limited Torah lashes and unlimited coercive lashes, which are more severe.
Objection from Rav Yaakov: the verse works only on the Rabbis' view that a soul means life, not on Rabbi's view of money alone.
Reply upholding the view: Rava's derivation is the source that one pays and is not flogged.
Verse: if he rises and walks outside with his staff, he who struck him is absolved.
Reductio: it cannot be that the victim walks in the marketplace while the aggressor is executed as a murderer.
Explanation: the verse teaches imprisoning the aggressor; if the victim dies he is killed, otherwise he pays for loss and healing.
Asks the circumstances: without forewarning, why is the offender killed if the victim dies?
Reply: obviously he was forewarned, and that makes him forewarned about the lesser matter of injury.
Principle: one forewarned about a severe matter is forewarned about a lesser matter, such as injury.
Verse: he shall give his loss of livelihood and cause him to be thoroughly healed, showing payment without flogging.
Rav Ashi objects: forewarning for the lesser matter is unproven, and lashes may be more severe than death.
Rav's statement repeated: flogging Hananiah's group would have induced idol worship, showing lashes are harsher.
Rav Samma repeats his objection: limited Torah lashes and unlimited coercive lashes differ in severity.
Rav Mari objects: the verse may refer to unintentional striking, where he is absolved of exile, so no proof follows.
Reish Lakish: the mishna follows Rabbi Meir, who holds that one is flogged and pays.
Objection: if so, even one who raped his daughter should pay, but the mishna lists only prohibition and karet cases.
Reply: Rabbi Meir may hold one is flogged and pays, but not that one who is executed also pays.
Objection: isn't Rabbi Meir of the view that one who is executed also pays?
Baraita: a thief who slaughters on Shabbat or for idolatry pays fourfold or fivefold per Rabbi Meir, while the Rabbis exempt him.
Explanation from Rabbi Yohanan: the baraita concerns one who slaughters through an agent, so the thief pays.
Objection: is the agent sinning while the thief pays, violating the rule that there is no agent for transgression?
Rava's verse: slaughter or sell, so just as sale can be done by an agent, slaughter can too, by Torah decree.
Two schools' sources: the word or and the word for both include an agent in slaughter liability.
Objection from Mar Zutra: is there a case where one performing it himself is exempt but through an agent he is liable?
Reply: he is exempt not for lack of slaughter liability, but because he receives the greater death penalty for Shabbat desecration.
Asks the reason the Rabbis exempt him from payment if the thief merely slaughters through an agent.
