ranges.en: Rabbi Shimon's view: slaughter that does not render the meat fit for eating does not count as slaughter.
Objection: this works for idolatry and the stoned ox, but Shabbat slaughter is a valid slaughter.
Mishna: one who slaughters on Shabbat or Yom Kippur is liable to death, yet his slaughter is valid.
Reply: the baraita follows Rabbi Yohanan HaSandlar's view on who may eat food prepared by desecrating Shabbat.
Baraita on Shabbat cooking: an unwitting cook may eat after Shabbat, an intentional cook never, and Rabbi Yohanan HaSandlar forbids others too.
Asks the rationale for Rabbi Yohanan HaSandlar's view.
Reply: Rabbi Hiyya's teaching given at the entrance to the Nasi's house.
Verse: keep Shabbat, for it is sacred; as sacred items may not be eaten, so Shabbat products may not be eaten.
Asks whether the analogy should extend to forbidding benefit from Shabbat products, as with sacred items.
Reply: the phrase to you indicates that the product is yours, so benefit from it is permitted.
Asks whether unwitting desecration should also yield forbidden food, by the same analogy.
Reply: the verse shall be put to death limits the analogy to intentional desecration, which carries execution.
Rav Aha and Ravina dispute whether products of Shabbat desecration are forbidden by Torah law or rabbinic law.
Verse for the rabbinic view: it is sacred, but the product of its actions is not sacred, so it may be eaten.
Asks the rationale of the Rabbis who exempt the thief from payment for an agent's Shabbat slaughter, given it is valid.
Reply: the exemption applies to the other cases, idolatry and the stoned ox, not to Shabbat.
Asks how Rabbi Meir can require payment for idolatry slaughter, when the animal is partly forbidden as it is slaughtered.
Rava: the case is one who declares idolatry only at the completion of the slaughter, so the prohibition arises only then.
Asks why Rabbi Meir holds one liable for slaughtering a stoned ox that is no longer the owner's.
Rabba: the case is an ox entrusted to a bailee, injured and sentenced in his house, then stolen and slaughtered.
Explanation: Rabbi Meir follows Rabbi Yaakov, who lets a returned ox revert, and Rabbi Shimon, that loss of money counts as money.
Rabba's alternative: the case is one who slaughters the animal himself, against Rabbi Yohanan's reading of the baraita.

34b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Meir holds one is flogged and pays, but does not hold that one who is executed also pays.
Explanation: the rape case is a novel Torah element, a fine that is paid even though the offender is put to death.
Rabba: one who slaughters a previously stolen kid on Shabbat pays, but one who steals and slaughters on Shabbat is exempt.
Rabba on burglary: a previously stolen kid slaughtered during burglary is paid for, while one who steals and slaughters it during burglary is exempt.
Both cases were needed: Shabbat is an eternal prohibition, while burglary carries its own forewarning, so each differs.
Rav Pappa: a previously stolen cow slaughtered on Shabbat is paid for, while a borrowed cow slaughtered on Shabbat is exempt.
Rav Aha asks Rav Ashi whether Rav Pappa is teaching anything new about a cow, since the principle is the same.
Rav Ashi: the borrowed cow teaching is that liability for accidents arises only when they occur, so a Shabbat accident is exempt.
Rava: heirs using a borrowed cow are not liable for accidents and pay only for the meat, unless a lien on the father's property secures it.
Explanation: each teacher reads a different clause of the ruling, and each reading matches or differs from Rav Pappa's view.
Asks why Reish Lakish did not adopt Rabbi Yohanan's reading of the mishna.
Reply: if forewarned he is exempt from payment, so when not forewarned he is exempt too.
Rav Dimi reports the dispute: for unwitting sins carrying death or lashes that also involve payment, Rabbi Yohanan holds liable and Reish Lakish exempt.
Rationales: Rabbi Yohanan says not forewarned means unwitting, so liable; Reish Lakish says forewarned exempts from payment, so unforewarned does too.
Reish Lakish objects to Rabbi Yohanan from the pregnant woman verse, which prescribes payment without lashes.

35a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether the verse refers to actual harm, meaning the woman's death, so that he is exempt if she dies.
Reply: the verse means no sentence of harm, so he pays unless the court actually executes him.
Variant: Rabbi Yohanan objects to Reish Lakish from the same verse, asking whether it refers to a sentence of harm.
Variant reply: the verse means actual harm, not a court sentence.
Rava's objection: no one holds that those liable to death for unwitting sins also pay; a baraita contrasts animal and human smiting.
Argument: the animal case is unconditionally liable for payment, so the human case is unconditionally exempt, regardless of execution.
Ravin: all agree those liable to death for unwitting sins are exempt; the disagreement concerns unwitting sins liable to lashes.
Rabbi Yohanan: death-liable cases are juxtaposed to payment and lashes-liable ones are not, so they pay. Reish Lakish: the Torah explicitly equates lashes-liable with death-liable, exempting them.
Asks where the Torah included those liable to be flogged.
Abaye's verbal analogy: the word wicked in the murder verse and the word wicked in the flogging verse.
Rava's verbal analogy: the word smites appears in two verses.
Rav Pappa asks Rava which smites he means, since the death verse concerns murder.
Rav Pappa rejects the first verse, which is written about killing, and points instead to the blemish verse.
Verse: he who smites an animal shall pay, a life for a life, juxtaposed to the blemish verse, likening lashes to payment.
Objection: the second verse concerns a blemish, not smiting, and injury there is for payment, undermining the analogy.
Reply: apply the analogy to smiting that causes less than a peruta of damage, where no payment is due, so lashes apply.

35b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks how exemption without actual flogging can be derived, if a blow worth less than a peruta is flogged and not paid for.
Reply: the juxtaposition is needed only where he struck and tore clothing at once, so the exemption holds without flogging.
Rav Hiyya asks the tanna of Hizkiyya's school how he knows the verse refers to a weekday rather than Shabbat.
Reply: the verse must refer to a weekday, since a Shabbat killer is executed and so would be exempt from the animal payment.
Rav Pappa asks Abaye to consider Rabba's position and how Rabba then establishes the mishna.
Rabba: the Torah innovated a fine, so one who is executed still pays the fine.
Asks which opinion establishes the mishna: Rabbi Meir, Rabbi Nehunya ben HaKana, or Rabbi Yitzhak, each of which raises a difficulty.
Reply: this works if Rabba holds like Rabbi Yohanan, who explains the mishna as requiring payment absent forewarning.
Asks how Reish Lakish's view could explain the mishna, since Reish Lakish exempts those liable to lashes.
Reply: one must say that Rabbi Yohanan's view is the one held here.
Rav Mattana asks Abaye which tanna disagrees with Rabbi Nehunya ben HaKana if Reish Lakish exempts lashes-liable offenders from payment.
Reply: the dissenter is either Rabbi Meir, who obligates a fine for lashes-liable offenders, or Rabbi Yitzhak.
Baraita: forbidden relatives, a wife who refuses her husband, an underdeveloped woman, and one who leaves over bad reputation get neither rape nor seduction fine.
Asks what forbidden relatives and secondary forbidden relatives mean in the baraita, starting with forbidden relatives.

36a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks why secondary-relative rapists get no fine, since those relations are Rabbinic and not forbidden by Torah law.
Explains the categories: death-penalty and karet relatives get no fine; only regular-prohibition violators receive one.
Asks whose opinion the attribution to Shimon HaTimni reflects.
Some say the categories are defined differently, following Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya, who denies a fine even when betrothal is valid.
Baraita: a girl who refuses to remain married receives neither a rape fine nor a seduction fine.
Gemara infers that an ordinary minor does receive a fine, which seems to conflict with the baraita as stated.
Asks in whose opinion the Rabbis hold that a minor has a fine for rape.
The Rabbis hold that a minor girl does have a fine for rape.
Objects that the latter clause would then belong to Rabbi Meir, so the whole baraita cannot follow one view.
Baraita: an ailonit receives neither a rape fine nor a seduction fine.
Resolves that the first clause follows the Rabbis and the latter follows Rabbi Meir, since she matures from minor to grown woman.
Proposes that the whole baraita follows Rabbi Meir, while on refusal he adopts Rabbi Yehuda's view.
Asks whether Rabbi Meir really holds that view.
Baraita shows Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda disagree on when a girl's refusal of marriage ends, refuting the proposal.
Suggests the baraita follows Rabbi Yehuda, and on minors it follows Rabbi Meir.
The proposal: according to Rabbi Meir a minor has no rape fine, as the baraita's ailonit ruling implies.
Asks whether Rabbi Yehuda really holds that minors have no fine.
Cites Rav's teaching that the mishna on fathers selling daughters is Rabbi Meir's alone.
Argues that if Yehuda agreed, Rav should have attributed the view to both Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda.
Concludes this tanna agrees with Rabbi Meir on one point and disagrees with him on another.
Rafram: the whole baraita follows Rabbi Meir, and refusal applies only to a minor fit to refuse.
Objects that the tanna should simply teach the minor case directly; the Gemara calls this difficult.
Baraita: an ailonit receives neither a rape fine nor a seduction fine.
Raises a contradiction from a baraita stating that deaf-mutes, imbeciles and ailonits receive rape fines and virginity claims.
Asks what the apparent contradiction is, since the resolution seems obvious.
Resolves that the two baraitot follow Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis respectively, so there is no real contradiction.
Asks why the objector raised the contradiction at all, given the known dispute.
Explains the objector had another baraita to cite, making the same contradiction on virginity claims.
Baraita: deaf-mutes, imbeciles, grown women and torn-hymen women have no virginity claim, but blind women and ailonits do.
Sumakhos, in Rabbi Meir's name: a blind woman has no virginity claim, conflicting with the earlier baraita.
Rav Sheshet resolves that one baraita follows Rabban Gamliel, who accepts a post-betrothal rape claim, and the other Rabbi Yehoshua.
Challenges whether Gamliel accepts claims only when the woman makes them, and whether a mute can be believed.
Rav Sheshet replies that Gamliel believes the court can make the claim for a mute, citing Proverbs 31:8.
Baraita: a grown woman has no virginity claim, since her hymen changes as her body matures.
Objects that Rav held a grown woman's hymen remains intact after first-night relations, implying she can have a claim.

36b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Resolves that a claim of no blood after consummation is effective, while the baraita refers to a claim of an open entrance.
Continuing the baraita: Sumakhos, in Rabbi Meir's name, holds that a blind woman has no virginity claim.
Asks what the rationale for Sumakhos's view is.
Rav Zeira explains that a blind woman falls and injures her hymen, so her husband should have anticipated this.
Objects that all girls fall too, so blindness alone cannot be the distinguishing reason.
Sighted girls see the bleeding and show their mothers, while a blind girl cannot see it and so cannot report it.
Continuing the baraita: one who leaves her husband over a bad reputation gets neither a rape nor a seduction fine.
Objects that one leaving over a bad reputation faces stoning as an adulteress, so the initial reading cannot be right.
Rav Sheshet explains the baraita refers to a woman with a bad reputation from her youth, presumed no longer a virgin.
Rav Pappa infers that a tainted document with a compromised reputation should not be used to collect a debt.
Asks what the circumstances of the tainted-document analogy are, and what makes a rumor about it comparable to a woman's reputation.
Objects that Rava held a rumor of promiscuity about a woman in town is disregarded, which undermines the analogy.
Suggests the case is two witnesses who testify she propositioned them, parallel to witnesses reporting a request to forge.
Describes the scenario in which a man asks others to forge a document for him.
Asks why suspicion should attach to the document, since not all Jews are presumed forgers.
Replies that since he actively sought a forgery, suspicion attaches to the document he wrote, making the cases comparable.
Mishna: no rape or seduction fine for relations with a convert, captive or freed maidservant past age three and a day.
Rabbi Yehuda dissents: a redeemed captive woman remains in her sanctity even as an adult, since intercourse cannot be assumed.
Mishna lists relatives such as a daughter or granddaughter for whom no fine is paid, since such offenders face court death penalty.
Cites Exodus 21:22 to show that one liable to the death penalty is exempt from paying money.
Rabbi Yochanan says Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Dosa agree on captive women, with Yehuda in the Mishna and Dosa in a baraita.
Baraita of Rabbi Dosa: a redeemed captive priest's daughter may eat teruma, since a captor's squeezing does not disqualify her.
Rabba objects that perhaps the two sages differ rather than agree, so Rabbi Yochanan's claim may be wrong.
Rabba distinguishes: Yehuda's fine ruling prevents the sinner profiting, while Dosa's teruma ruling is rabbinic and lenient, unlike the Rabbis.
Abaye objects that Yehuda's rationale of not letting the sinner profit cannot apply here, so the distinction fails.
Cites a baraita: Rabbi Yehuda says a captive woman remains sanctified even at age ten, with a two hundred dinar marriage contract.
Gemara answers that Yehuda's ruling on the marriage contract has a different rationale, so men will not avoid marrying her.
Objects that Yehuda holds she remains sanctified, but a baraita says one who testifies she was not violated may not marry her.
Asks whether the baraita is internally inconsistent about marrying a redeemed captive.
Resolves that one who redeems her and testifies she was not violated may marry her, while testimony alone does not permit it.
Notes the baraita is still difficult for Yehuda, who elsewhere says a captive loses her virgin presumption.
Rav Pappa proposes emending the text so that Yehuda permits marriage in both cases.
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua keeps the text, saying Yehuda spoke according to the Rabbis, and the halakha follows the other opinion.
Asks how the Rabbis explain their ruling.
Rabbis explain that a redeemer who paid ransom must know she is a virgin, while testimony alone may be self-serving.
Rav Pappa bar Shmuel raises a contradiction against a ruling of Rav Yosef.

37a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects that a baraita on converts and menstruation suggests Rabbi Yehuda does not maintain that captives keep their sanctity.
Cites baraitot on converts: Yehuda's menstrual-impurity ruling, then a three-month wait before marriage, while Yosei permits immediate marriage.
Rav Yosef objects that a convert, unlike a captive who guards herself, does not avoid prior relations, so the cases differ.
Rav Pappa bar Shmuel cites a baraita on redeemed captives, converts and maidservants that seems to contradict Yehuda's view on waiting.
Rav Yosef, unable to answer, asks whether Rav Pappa has heard any explanation of the matter.
Rav Pappa reports Rav Sheshet's explanation: Yehuda's ruling applies to a captive seen engaging in intercourse.
Asks Yosei's rationale for permitting immediate marriage, since pregnancy concern should still apply.
Rabba explains Yosei holds that a promiscuous woman uses an absorbent insert before relations to prevent pregnancy.
Asks whether planned precautions can explain converts, captives and maidservants, but not a maidservant freed suddenly.
Objects that the view cannot cover unplanned events, since a baraita says Yosei permits raped and seduced women to marry immediately.
Rabba: Yosei holds a promiscuous woman turns over after intercourse to avoid pregnancy, so unplanned relations are covered; Yehuda worries she did not turn properly.
Cites Exodus 21:22 for the principle that one liable to death is exempt from paying money.
Asks whether the exemption principle derives from Exodus 21:22, then notes it actually derives from Deuteronomy 25:2.
Deuteronomy 25:2, according to his iniquity, teaches one act yields one liability, not two punishments.
Both verses are needed, since death-with-money and lashes-with-money cases each need their own source to rule out a misreading.
Asks why two derivations are needed, given Rabbi Meir's view that one is flogged and pays in such cases.

37b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains both verses are needed: otherwise death with money or with lashes could be misread about whether two punishments apply.
Asks why the verse on ransom for a murderer is needed, since the principle was already derived elsewhere.
The verse teaches that money may not be taken to free a murderer from the death penalty.
Asks why the verse on ransom for a fugitive to a city of refuge is needed, if the principle is already known.
The verse teaches that money may not be taken to free him from exile.
Asks why two verses are needed for the same principle.
One verse covers unwitting killers and the other intentional ones, since severity and loss of life differ between them.
Asks why another verse is needed to show that money cannot atone for bloodshed on the land.
Baraita on the beheaded calf: a murderer found after the calf ritual is not exempted by its atonement.
Asks why the verse on putting away innocent blood is needed, since it seems to teach the same point.
Baraita: murderers are executed by sword at the neck, since the calf verse likens all bloodshedders to the beheaded calf.
Asks whether, just as the calf is beheaded with a cleaver at the nape, murderers should be executed the same way.
Rav Naḥman, citing Rabba bar Avuh, derives from love your neighbor as yourself that the death should be agreeable, so no cleaver.
Asks why the herem verse is needed, as it seems to teach the same halakha as before.
Introduces a baraita asking from where it follows that a valuation vow made on a man already taken for execution is not binding.
Cites Leviticus 27:29 read as of men, not all men: a condemned man's valuation cannot be redeemed, while a living man's is binding.
Asks, following Rabbi Hananya ben Akavya, what the herem verse teaches, since he deems valuation of a condemned man binding.
Rabbi Yishmael's baraita: those killed by Heaven pay ransom and are atoned, so the verse excludes ransom for those executed by men.
Reasons that the herem verse must extend the no-ransom rule to lesser court-executed prohibitions that have atonement, not only severe ones.
Asks why the herem phrase is needed, since the no-ransom principle was already derived from another verse.
Rami bar Hama answers that the phrase is needed, lest one assume the ruling applies differently in another case.

38a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Limits the no-payment rule to upward-motion killing, where no atonement applies; downward killing would allow paying money.
Proposes that the downward-motion killer might pay money and go free, asking why a further herem phrase would then be needed.
Rava replies that the principle comes from a baraita of the Hizkiyya school.
The baraita juxtaposes smiting a person with smiting an animal, as its textual basis.
Argues a fortiori from smiting an animal, where all distinctions are ignored, that smiting a person likewise exempts from payment in every case.
Rami bar Hama replies that herem is needed, since the exemption might be thought to cover only a blow that both blinds and kills.
Proposes that exemption applies only if one blinds and kills with the same blow; a different blow would require paying for the eye.
Rava replies that this case too is derived from another Hizkiyya-school teaching.
Cites Exodus 21:24, an eye for an eye, which excludes owing both an eye and a life.
Rav Ashi replies that herem is needed, since the fine might be thought payable even by one who is killed.
Argues the fine is a novel Torah decree payable even by one who is executed; the herem phrase excludes that.
Asks, on Rabba's view that the fine is paid even when one is killed, what the herem phrase then teaches.
Rabba follows the first tanna, who disagrees with Rabbi Hananya ben Akavya, holding that a vow to ransom a condemned person does not bind.
Mishna: Rabbi Yosei HaGelili holds that a betrothed and divorced girl who is raped gets no fine.
Rabbi Akiva holds that she receives the fine, and it is paid to her, not to her father.
Asks the basis for Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's position.
Derives it from Deuteronomy 22:28, 'who was not betrothed', inferring that a betrothed woman has no fine.
Rabbi Akiva reads the same verse: if not betrothed the fine goes to the father, so a betrothed woman keeps it herself.
Objects that the same logic would apply to grown women and non-virgins, wrongly exempting the rapist in those cases.
Defends Akiva: the verse is needed for a separate halakha, so the inference drawn from it need not extend to all cases.
Cites a baraita: the phrase excludes a betrothed and divorced girl from the fine, per Rabbi Yosei HaGelili.
The baraita gives Rabbi Akiva's view: she receives the fine, paid to her father, contrary to the mishna's attribution.
Argues the fine follows betrothal money: as betrothal money goes to the father despite divorce, so does the fine.
Asks why the verse 'who was not betrothed' is written if logic already yields the result.
Answers that the verse is superfluous in its own context, so it is used to form a verbal analogy.
Gezera shava: 'who was not betrothed' appears both here and in Exodus 22:15, linking the two cases.
Applies the analogy: as here the payment is fifty, so there; as there the payment is in shekels, so here.
Asks Rabbi Akiva what led him to read 'not betrothed' as an analogy and 'virgin' as excluding a non-virgin.

38b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Proposes an alternative reading: 'virgin' serves a verbal analogy, and 'who was not betrothed' excludes the betrothed-and-divorced girl.
Replies that 'who was not betrothed' serves the analogy, since even after divorce she still counts as a virgin.
Objects: let 'virgin' serve the analogy instead, since 'not betrothed' would still apply to a woman who is not a virgin.
Replies that 'virgin' excludes the non-virgin, because intercourse changes her body whereas divorce does not, so her fine status stays the same.
Asks where Rabbi Yosei HaGelili derives this, namely the fine amount and the currency for seduction and rape.
A baraita: 'like the dowry of the virgins' (Exodus 22:16) makes the seduction fine equal the rape dowry of fifty silver, and vice versa.
Notes a contradiction: Akiva rules the fine goes to the woman in the mishna but to her father in the baraita.
Defends the mishna's Akiva: a verbal analogy would not override the plain meaning of the verse, so that view is reasonable.
Objects that for the baraita's Akiva the analogy overrides the plain meaning, erasing any difference between betrothed and unbetrothed girls.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak reads 'who is not betrothed' as referring to her current status, not a past betrothal.
Objects that the verse is unnecessary, since raping a betrothed girl is already punishable by stoning and so exempts the fine.
Answers that the verse is needed, lest one think a novel fine decree is paid even by one who is killed.
Asks, on Rabba's view that the fine is paid even when killed, what the verse then excludes.
Rabba follows Rabbi Akiva of the mishna, reading the verse as referring to one who was betrothed and divorced.
A baraita: the fine for a raped young woman goes to her father, though some say to her.
Asks why the fine would go to her, given that the verse says it goes to the father.
Rav Ḥisda answers that the case is a betrothed and divorced girl, and the tanna'im dispute the two rulings of Akiva.
Abaye rules: if the rapist had intercourse and she died before sentencing, he is exempt from the fine.
Derives it from Deuteronomy 22:29, which says the fine goes to the father of the young woman, not of one who died.
Notes that what was obvious to Abaye was raised by Rava as a dilemma.
Rava's dilemma: does a girl reach adulthood in the grave, so the fine goes to her heir, or does it remain her father's?

39a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether a minor can conceive at all, since a baraita lets her take precautions.
Cites a baraita: three women may use a contraceptive, a minor, a pregnant woman and a nursing woman, each for a stated risk.
Rabbi Meir defines a minor as aged eleven years and a day to twelve years and a day; outside that range she may proceed normally.
The Sages hold that all these women proceed normally, with heaven ensuring their protection.
Support: 'The Lord preserves the simple' (Psalms 116:6), so providence guards them.
Objects that a young woman bearing a child before adulthood would require birth within six months of conception, which seems impossible.
Cites Shmuel: the gap between young woman and grown woman status is only six months.
Proposes that Shmuel meant the gap is under six months; rejects this, since his word 'only' means exactly six.
Restates Rava's dilemma: does achieving grown-woman status in the grave end the father's right to the fine, or not?
Mar bar Rav Ashi raises the same dilemma: does death itself effect grown-woman status?
No resolution is found; the dilemma stands unresolved.
Rava asks Abaye: if one forcibly had intercourse with a young woman who was later betrothed, what is the halakha?
Abaye replies that the verse refers to betrothal before the rape, not to the status at the time of payment.
Rava counters with a baraita on later marriage, asking whether the same reading applies to it.
Presses that the marriage verse likewise does not address the moment of payment, so the cases are parallel.
Abaye distinguishes: grown-woman status and marriage both end the father's authority, which justifies the reading.
Betrothal does not fully remove her from her father's authority, so its halakha cannot be derived from that of grown-woman status.
Proof from a mishna: a betrothed young woman's vows may be annulled by her father and husband together, so betrothal does not free her.
Mishna: the seducer gives the father three payments, the rapist four, the rapist adding payment for pain.
Asks what distinguishes the rapist from the seducer.
Lists differences: the rapist pays for pain and immediately and must marry her; the seducer pays neither for pain nor immediately.
The seducer may release her if he wishes.
Asks how the rapist 'drinks from his vessel', meaning he marries her.
Answers he must marry her even if lame, blind or covered in boils, but not if she is unfit, like an adulteress or mamzeret.
Proof from Deuteronomy 22:29, 'And to him she shall be a wife', implying she must be suitable for him.
Asks what pain the rapist must pay for.
Shmuel's father: the pain of being slammed onto the ground while raped.
Rabbi Zeira objects: by that logic, slamming her onto silk should exempt him from paying for pain.
A baraita reports Rabbi Shimon that a rapist does not pay for pain, supporting the objection.

39b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether the rape victim's pain is the same as the pain she later suffers with her husband.
Answers that rape is not comparable to willing intercourse, so the pain is directly caused by the forced act.
Rabba bar Avuh explains the pain as that of spreading the legs during intercourse.
Cites Ezekiel 16:25, 'you opened your legs to every passerby', as a verse describing spreading the legs for intercourse.
Asks: if so, the seduced woman should also owe payment for that pain.
Gives a parable: a man tells another to tear his silk and thereby waive payment, as a seduced woman waives the pain.
Alternatively, the clever women say a seduced woman feels no pain, since she participates willingly.
Objects that even a married woman feels pain at first intercourse, so willingness does not remove pain.
Cites three women's testimonies describing first-intercourse pain, to show it is real even within marriage.
Mishna: the rapist pays immediately, while the seducer pays when he releases her.
Asks how the mishna can speak of release, since she is not yet his wife.
Abaye suggests reading it as when he declines to marry her, in which case he pays.
A baraita confirms: the seducer pays when he declines to marry, while humiliation and degradation are paid at once; both parties may block marriage.
Asks: for the seduced woman, the verse 'if her father refuses' gives the father a veto; from where does she have one?
The double verb maen yemaen shows that marriage may be blocked in any case, so she too may block it.
For the rapist, asks how the verse 'shall be a wife' gives her a say, but from where does the father get a veto?
Abaye: no verse is needed; the father must be able to block, so that a sinner does not profit.
Rava's a fortiori: both may block a seducer, who defied only the father, so all the more both may block a rapist.
Rejects Abaye's reasoning as applied by Rava, since the rapist pays a fine and so does not profit from sin.
Abaye rejects Rava's view: where the seducer can block the marriage the father can too, and where the rapist cannot, neither can the father.
A baraita: though the rapist pays immediately, she has no claim when she leaves; if he dies, her fine money counts toward her marriage contract.
Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda: even a raped woman receives a marriage contract of one hundred dinars.
Asks what principle underlies the dispute between the Rabbis and Rabbi Yosei ben Rabbi Yehuda.
The Rabbis reason that the marriage contract deters easy divorce, since divorcing costs money.
This rape victim cannot be released under Torah law, so the contract serves no deterrent purpose.
Rabbi Yosei ben Rabbi Yehuda: he can torment her until she seeks divorce, so the contract is still needed.
Mishna: the rapist drinks from his vessel, i.e., must marry her, while the seducer need not.
Challenges Rav Ashi: since the rapist and seducer rules are derived from each other, their rulings should be consistent.

40a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Continues the proposal that the seducer and rapist rules be derived from each other regarding marriage against her will.
Rav Ashi cites Exodus 22:15: 'to him' means by his will, so the seducer's marriage requires his consent.
Mishna: how does the rapist drink from his vessel? He must marry her despite physical flaws, unless marriage is forbidden.
Rav Kahana reports asking Rav Zevid whether a positive mitzva overrides a prohibition against marrying a forbidden woman.
Rav Zevid answers: a mitzva overrides a prohibition only when the mitzva cannot otherwise be fulfilled; here she may refuse, so it does not.
Mishna: for an orphan betrothed and divorced, Rabbi Elazar says the rapist pays the fine, while the seducer is exempt.
Rabbi Yoḥanan: Rabbi Elazar follows his teacher Rabbi Akiva, who holds that she is entitled to the fine and it is paid to her.
The mishna's wording on an orphan shows Rabbi Elazar's view matches Akiva's, since the rapist pays there.
Asks: an orphan's case is obvious, so why does the mishna teach it?
Answers that the mishna teaches a betrothed and divorced girl, even with a living father, is like an orphan, receiving the fine herself.
Transmitters report Rav's ruling that the halakha follows Rabbi Elazar, whom Rav praised as the happiest of Sages.
Mishna: humiliation depends on both parties, and degradation is assessed by valuing her as a maidservant before and after the act.
The fine is a fixed sum equal for all people, since Torah-fixed payments do not vary by lineage or status.
Asks whether the Merciful One may have set fifty sela as the single payment for all these components.
Rabbi Zeira objects: it would follow that raping a king's daughter and a commoner's daughter cost the same, which is unreasonable.
Abaye replies the objection is not decisive: a slave's fixed thirty-sela value, despite differing skills, shows fixed sums are possible.

40b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects by analogy to a slave of common needlework skill, whose fixed thirty-sela value suggests fixed sums regardless of status.
Rabbi Zeira offers a second proof: a fixed fifty for an untainted virgin, and the same fifty for a tainted one, shows the rest varies.
Abaye replies this is no proof: a slave gored by an ox is fixed at thirty sela whether healthy or afflicted with boils.
Abaye cites Deuteronomy 22:29, 'because he tormented her', implying humiliation and degradation payments beyond the fifty.
Rava's proof: fifty for the pleasure of lying with her implies extra payments for humiliation and degradation beyond the fine.
Asks whether these additional payments might instead go to her.
Answers from Numbers 30:17: all profits of her young womanhood in her father's house go to her father.
Asks the source for the rule that a daughter's handiwork goes to her father, as Rav Huna cited from Rav.
Derives it from Exodus 21:7: as a sold maidservant's handiwork goes to her master, a daughter's goes to her father.
Asks why not derive it directly from 'in her young womanhood, in her father's house'.
That verse concerns the father's authority to nullify vows, so it does not address monetary rights.
Proposes deriving monetary matters from vows or from fines; both are rejected, since monetary rights do not follow ritual or penal rules.
Reasonable that humiliation and degradation payments go to the father, since he can marry her to a repulsive or afflicted man.
Mishna: degradation is assessed by viewing her as a maidservant sold in the market, valued before and after.
Asks how her value is assessed.
Shmuel's father: estimate the gap between what a buyer pays for a virgin maidservant and for a non-virgin maidservant.
Asks what difference virginity makes to a master who buys a maidservant for service, or for marrying to his slave.
Answers: a virgin is sought for a slave the master favors, so the price gap reflects the degradation payment.
Mishna: a minor may be sold and has no fine; a young woman has a fine but no sale; a grown woman has neither.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav: this is Rabbi Meir's view; the Rabbis hold a fine is payable even where sale applies.
Baraita gives Rabbi Meir's ranges: sale until two pubic hairs, then fine without sale until adulthood, never both.
The Rabbis: from age three years and a day until adulthood, a girl is entitled to a fine and is not sold.
Objects that this makes the Rabbis deny sale, so the text should be emended to allow a fine even where sale applies.
Rav Ḥisda asks the rationale for Rabbi Meir's view.
Cites Deuteronomy 22:19, 'and to him she shall be a wife', which speaks of one competent to marry herself, a young woman.
The Rabbis' rationale per Reish Lakish: the word na'ara, though written with a heh, includes minors by its sense.
Rav Pappa son of Rav Ḥanan brings this ruling from Bei Keloḥit to Rav Shimi bar Ashi.
Rav Shimi objects: you teach it on that matter, while our tradition applies it to slander against a minor.
Reish Lakish rules: one who slanders a minor girl is exempt from the fine.
Cites Deuteronomy 22:19, 'they shall give to the father of the young woman', as the source.
The verse spells na'ara in full, limiting the slander fine to a young woman, not a minor.
Rav Adda bar Ahava objects: the spelling cannot be the reason, since minors are excluded from the capital case.
Cites Deuteronomy 22:20, the capital case of a young woman, to show that a minor is not subject to punishment.
Concludes: where the text says na'ara with a heh a minor is excluded, and wherever na'ar appears even a minor is included.

41a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: one who admits 'I seduced' pays humiliation and degradation on his own word, but not the fine.
Mishna: one who admits 'I stole' pays the principal on his own word, but not the double or fourfold and fivefold payments.
Mishna: one who admits his ox killed a person or another's ox pays on his own word.
Mishna: one who admits his ox killed a slave pays nothing on his own word, since that payment is a fine.
The principle: whoever pays more than the damage he caused does not pay on his own word, only on others' testimony.
Asks why the mishna cites seduction and not rape, which the tanna could have listed.
Answers that rape admission is obviously payable, while seduction needed teaching, since admitting it tarnishes her reputation.
Objects that the mishna does not follow this tanna, since a baraita says otherwise.
Baraita: Rabbi Shimon holds even humiliation and degradation are not paid on one's own word, as no one may tarnish another's daughter by confession.
Rav Pappa asks Abaye: if she herself accepts his account, is he still exempt?
Abaye: perhaps her father would not accept the tarnishing of his daughter's reputation, so the admission is not relied on.
Rav Pappa asks: if her father also accepts the claim, what is the law?
Abaye: even if all local relatives accept, some relative overseas would surely not, so the admission is never effective.
Mishna: one who admits 'I stole' pays the principal, but not the double payment and fourfold and fivefold payments.
Amoraim dispute whether half the damage an innocuous ox pays is money (Rav Pappa) or a fine (Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua).
Pappa's reasoning: standard oxen are presumed dangerous, so the owner would owe all, but the Merciful One limits him to half.
Huna's view and reasoning: standard oxen are presumed safe, so the owner owes nothing, and God penalizes him to guard his ox.
A mnemonic for the proofs in this dispute: damaged, what, killed, principle.
The mishna teaches that the damaged and damager share the payments when an innocuous ox kills another ox.
Objects: on Huna's view the injured party has no entitlement, so how can he be said to share in the payments?
Answers that the mishna addresses only the carcass's degradation, which the injured owner bears, so sharing is meant in that sense.
Explains that both innocuous and forewarned oxen must be taught, so the mishna proves nothing about money versus fine.
Baraita: the innocuous owner pays half from the ox's body, while the forewarned owner pays from his property, suggesting half is money.
Refutes the proof: the baraita omits other differences, so its silence on one point is not evidence of the rule.

41b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Identifies the baraita as Rabbi Yosei HaGelili's view: the innocuous ox owner pays half the ransom.
Proposes a proof: admitting an ox killed another's ox pays on one's word, which shows half is money if the ox was innocuous.
Asks why the mishna does not instead teach the distinction within this very case.
Rejects: the whole mishna concerns forewarned oxen, so it settles nothing about the innocuous ox.
Another proof: one who pays more than the damage does not pay on his word, implying one who pays less does.
Rejects that inference; the rule should instead read that one who pays exactly the damage pays on his word.
Asks what the halakha is for one who pays less than the damage, and why the tanna does not state the general rule.
The general formula would imply both less and more, a conclusive refutation of Rav Huna's view that half is a fine.
Concludes that the halakha is that half the damage is a fine, contrary to the other view.
Asks whether the refutation is conclusive and the halakha therefore follows Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua.
Answers that the tanna omitted the general formula because the pebble damage is monetary by tradition, so it is not a clean rule.
Consequence: a dog eating lambs or a cat eating large roosters is unusual damage, a fine uncollectable in Babylonia; small roosters are collected.
Fines are not enforced in Babylonia, so seized fines are not repossessed; a party refusing to go to Eretz Yisrael for judgment is excommunicated.
Either way, one who keeps a cause of damage is excommunicated, following Rabbi Natan's principle to remove the hazard.
Baraita of Rabbi Natan: one may not keep a vicious dog or unsteady ladder at home, derived from Deuteronomy 22:8.
Closing formula marking the end of the chapter, 'These are the young women'.
Mishna: if the seduced girl's case was tried before the father died, the payments belong to him and pass to the brothers at his death.
If she did not stand trial before the father died, the payments belong to her, since she is now independent.
If she stood trial while a minor, the payments are the father's, then the brothers' if he dies, even after she comes of age.
If she did not stand trial before coming of age, the money is hers.
Rabbi Shimon: if she did not manage to collect before the father died, the money is hers, not the brothers'.

42a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna's ruling: earnings and found objects not yet collected go to her brothers if the father died, as his property.
Asks what the mishna is teaching, since this was already learned.
Restates the mishna: the seducer pays three items, the rapist four, with the payments going to the father.
Answers that the mishna must teach that the money is given to her father.
Asks: it is obvious the money goes to the father, since a seducer who acted with her consent would not pay her.
The mishna addresses a case where she stood trial before the father died, the dispute between Rabbi Shimon and the Rabbis.
Mishna in Shevuot: one who falsely denies raping or seducing, then admits, owes the payments plus one-fifth and an offering.
Rabbi Shimon exempts him, since the fine is not paid on admission, so he did not deny a monetary claim.
The Rabbis reply: although the fine is not paid on admission, humiliation and degradation are, so he denied a monetary claim.
Abaye raises a dilemma before Rabba about a denier who stood trial and was found liable.
Sets out the case: after a court found liability, the defendant swore falsely and later admitted; under Rabbi Shimon, is an offering owed?
Abaye explains the two sides: is the court-ordered payment a regular monetary claim, or is it in essence a fine?
Rabba: since he already stood trial, it is a regular monetary payment, so the oath offering is owed.
Abaye objects with a baraita of Rabbi Shimon, which first suggests an offering is owed for such fines, against Rabba.
The verse (Leviticus 5:21-22) lists monetary items, so the rule covers only monetary claims, excluding fines like rape or seduction.

42b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether the baraita really concerns a defendant who stood trial, contrary to the suggested reading.
Abaye objects: if the first clause concerns one who stood trial, the latter clause must too.
Baraita: the offering covers principal payments, and asks from where the double, fourfold, rapist, seducer and defamer payments are included.
The doubled word 'trespass' (Leviticus 5:21) amplifies the rule to include these payments.
Asks: if he never stood trial, is a double payment owed? So it must concern one who stood trial.
Abaye summarizes: the first clause concerns one who stood trial, so the latter does too, yet Rabbi Shimon exempts the offering.
Rabba's answer: the whole baraita concerns one who stood trial, the first clause following the Rabbis and the latter Rabbi Shimon.
Rabba concedes the offering is exempt here, clarifying that after conviction the payment is inheritable like money.
Abaye objects from a Rabbi Shimon baraita: if the money is inheritable after trial, why does the daughter, not the brothers, collect it?
Rav Yosef's resolution: the rape payment goes to the father only upon receipt, so the daughter, not his sons, inherits it.
Rabba's rule about inheritable fines applies to other fines, not to rape or seduction payments.
Asks: by this logic, the thirty-shekel payment for a slave killed by an ox would also be owed only upon payment.
Asks why the baraita cites 'and deal falsely' rather than 'shall give', which would show the fine persists after trial.
Rava: the 'and deal falsely' proof is needed where she reached majority, the case was tried, and she died before payment.
Asks: then the baraita's 'excluding these, as they are fines' is inaccurate, since they are regular monetary payments.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak: 'excluding these, as they are originally fines', and only after the court orders payment are they monetary.
Abaye objects: if Rabbi Shimon exempts non-tried admitters, a tried one who denies should owe an offering, contradicting the explanation.
Rabbi Shimon argues on the Rabbis' terms: after trial the offering is exempt by verse; concede that an untried claim is a fine.

43a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Principle: one who admits a fine is exempt; the Rabbis hold the father's claim concerns humiliation and degradation, not the fine.
Asks what the tanna'im disagree about, if that explanation holds.
Rav Pappa: Rabbi Shimon holds one does not forgo a fixed fine for an unfixed claim; the Rabbis hold the opposite.
Rabbi Avina asks Rav Sheshet: whose are a sustained daughter's earnings, when her brothers feed her from the father's estate?
Sets out the dilemma's sides: the brothers may stand in the father's place, or the case differs because she is sustained from the estate.
Rav Sheshet cites a mishna: a widow is sustained from orphans' property, and her earnings belong to them.
Refutes the analogy: a widow's husband need not want her comfortable, but a father wants his daughter comfortable.
Asks: is his daughter's welfare more important to him than his widow's, given Rabbi Yosei's ruling on small estates?
Distinguishes: for degradation the widow is preferred, while for comfort the daughter is preferred.
Rav Yosef objects from the mishna that earnings go to the brothers after the father's death, and asks whether this covers a sustained daughter.
Asks why teach a case of a non-sustained daughter, which is obvious by analogy to a Canaanite slave.
A Hebrew slave is fed under 'with you', so a fortiori the brothers must sustain a daughter whose earnings they take.
Rabba bar Ulla: the mishna concerns only the surplus beyond her sustenance, which belongs to her.
Rava says Rav Yosef, a great scholar, would not raise an objection while ignorant of the surplus explanation.
Rava's alternative: the mishna itself challenges Rav Sheshet, which led Rav Yosef to his conclusion.
Rava notes the mishna's word 'collect' is inappropriate for found items, showing the wording concerns the earnings themselves.
Her earnings, like found items, are the father's in life and hers after death, even if she is sustained by the estate.
Rav Yehuda, citing Rav: a daughter sustained by her brothers keeps her own earnings.
Rav Kahana cites Leviticus 25:46: a man bequeaths rights over slaves to his sons, not over his daughters, so personal rights do not pass.
Rabba objects that the verse may instead address fines and injury payments for a seduced or raped daughter, which Rav Ḥanina also taught.
Objects that injury payments compensate her own pain and so should not belong to the father, making their listing puzzling.

ranges.en: Context: he injured her face, so he pays the lost value, which belongs to her father.
Rav's ruling, transmitted by Rav Zeira and Rav Mattana: a daughter sustained by brothers keeps her earnings.
Cites Leviticus 25:46 as proof that a man cannot bequeath his rights over his daughter to his son.
Avimi bar Pappi attributes this halakha to Shakud.
Asks who Shakud is, and why not attribute it to Rav directly.
Answers that Shakud also agreed with Rav's ruling.
Mar bar Amemar reports that the Neharde'ans rule like Rav Sheshet, that brothers sustaining a sister take her earnings.
Rav Ashi rules that the halakha follows Rav, so her earnings belong to her.
Mishna: if her father merely betrothed his daughter, the marriage payment is his; if he married her off, it is hers.
Explains the reason: a woman widowed twice is deemed dangerous, following Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi that two occurrences establish a presumption.
Mishna's ruling: Rabbi Yehuda holds the first marriage payment belongs to the father.
Asks the reason for Rabbi Yehuda's view.
Rabba and Rav Yosef: the father gains the right at betrothal, while she was under his authority, so the payment is his.
Rava objects from a baraita: by that reasoning, Rabbi Yehuda should give the father the payment even when she married after majority.
Rabba and Rav Yosef restate: the contract is drafted under the father's authority, so he is entitled to the money.
Asks from when a husband's property is liened to secure the marriage payment.
Rav Huna: the basic sums are liened from betrothal, while additions from marriage; Rav Asi says both from marriage.
Objects with Rav Huna's two-contract case, then argues that his view implies she could collect the full five hundred.
Rather, the second contract does not add to the first, so she may collect two hundred or three hundred depending on the date.

44a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Explains: the second contract does not cancel the first; she forgave her earlier lien to accept the new document.
Asks whether Rav Huna disagrees with Rav Naḥman, whose rule holds that a later of two documents cancels the earlier.
Refutes the suggestion: Rav Naḥman concedes that adding even a palm tree in the second document shows an addition, not cancellation.
Analyzes Rav Naḥman's rule: a later gift after a sale does not cancel it, as the gift improves the recipient's neighbor-based rights.
A fortiori, a gift followed by a sale also does not cancel, since the sale is written out of a creditor's concern.
Rav Naḥman meant: if both documents are sales, or both gifts, the later one nullifies the earlier.
Asks the reason for this halakha.
Rafram: the recipient admitted the first was invalid; Rav Aḥa: the recipient forgave his lien from the first date.
Asks the practical differences between these two explanations, and where the marriage-contract question stands.
Baraita: Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon says the basic sum is liened from betrothal; the Sages say both from marriage, which is the halakha.
Mishna: a convert's daughter who converted with her and committed adultery is strangled, lacking the father's-house execution and the hundred-sela penalty.
If conceived before conversion but born after, she is stoned and lacks those penalties; if conceived and born after conversion, she is fully Jewish.
A betrothed young woman who commits adultery is stoned even if the father lacks a house entrance or is deceased.
The house-entrance requirement in Deuteronomy 22:21 is stated only as a mitzva, not as an indispensable requirement.

ranges.en: Asks the source for the rule that a daughter conceived outside sanctity but born within it is stoned.
Reish Lakish: the superfluous 'that she die' (Deuteronomy 22:21) includes such a daughter for execution.
Asks: if she equals a Jewish woman, should the husband also be flogged and pay the hundred sela?
Answers that 'that she die' includes her only for death, not for the fine.
Asks whether the verse includes only a girl conceived and born in sanctity, and answers that she is a full Jewess.
Asks from the opposite side: may the verse include one conceived and born outside sanctity as well?
Answers: then 'in Israel' would be pointless, so the halakha applies only to one born Jewish.
Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina: the defamer of an orphan is exempt, since 'give to the father' excludes one without a father.
Objects from a baraita: 'ma'en yima'en' includes an orphan for the fine, per Rabbi Yosei HaGelili.
Resolves: the baraita concerns one seduced while she had a father, who was orphaned afterward.
Rava: the defamer of an orphan pays, since 'virgin of Israel' excludes only converts.
Rava infers: if a Jewish-born orphan were exempt, excluding converts would be superfluous, so the Jewish-born orphan must pay.
Reish Lakish: the defamer of a minor is exempt; 'na'ara' written in full limits it to a young woman.
Rav Aḥa bar Abba objects: the full spelling cannot be the reason, since otherwise minors would be included.
Cites Deuteronomy 22:20-21, the capital case, which clearly concerns a young woman, since a minor is not punishable.
Concludes: 'na'ara' with a heh indicates a young woman; without it even a minor is included, excluding only adult women.
Sheila's baraita: three situations concern a defamed young woman, such as witnesses testifying to adultery in her father's house.

ranges.en: Baraita: a sinner from betrothal stoned at the city gate, but one who matured after the sin is strangled as a grown woman.
Asks: does the method of execution change whenever her body changed after the sin?
Raises a contradiction from a baraita: a defamed woman who matured is stoned with her conspiring witnesses, despite the change.
Rejects the baraita's wording: she and her conspiring witnesses cannot both be executed, so the text should read either/or.
Rava: a defamer's case is novel, since the method follows the time of the sin, despite her status changing.
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua: the novelty may apply only where her body has not changed, not when she matured.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak: this is a tanna'itic dispute, as in the mishna of the High Priest or king who sinned before appointment.
Rabbi Shimon: if the sin was known before appointment they are liable; if known after, they are exempt, as status change retroactively applies.

ranges.en: Questions the comparison: Rabbi Shimon may follow the time of awareness, so the offering case proves nothing about the time of sin.
Answers the issue is disputed: Rabbi Ile'a grounds stoning in 'the young woman' as she was at the time of sin.
Rabbi Ḥanina objects: if status follows the time of sin, the defamer should be flogged and pay the hundred sela too.
Rabbi Ile'a replies that Rabbi Ḥanina's reasoning is illogical, and each side calls the other's opinion baseless.
Asks the reason she is a young woman for stoning but a grown woman for the fine.
Rabbi Yitzḥak bar Avin: her act caused her punishment, while the husband's lip-twisting caused his, timed to the moment of defaming.
Baraita: a betrothed sinner is stoned at her father's gate, or at the city gate; in mostly gentile cities at the court's gate; likewise for idolaters.
Asks the source that an idolater is stoned at the gate where he worshipped, rather than at the court's gate.
Verbal analogy: 'your gates' above (where he worshipped) applies equally to 'your gates' below for execution.
Alternatively, 'your gates' excludes gentile gates and indicates Jewish-populated city gates, yielding two rulings.
Asks: we have a source for the idolater's gate; from where for the betrothed woman at the city gate?
Rabbi Abbahu: a chain of verbal analogies links 'entrance' to 'gate' to 'your gates', so the betrothed woman is stoned at the city gate.
Baraita: a defamer is flogged and pays a hundred sela; Rabbi Yehuda says flogging applies always, but the fine only if he had intercourse.
The first tanna follows the Rabbis, who require payment whether or not intercourse occurred, while Rabbi Yehuda follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov.
Rabbi Yehuda's position: flogging always, the fine only after intercourse, matching Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov.
Some say the whole baraita follows Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov, with flogging applying always per Rabbi Yehuda.
Objects: a baraita says Rabbi Yehuda flogs only if he had intercourse, contradicting flogging always.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak: the flogging for defaming without intercourse is rabbinic rebelliousness lashes, not Torah law.

ranges.en: Asks whether the baraita's 'flogged only after intercourse' refers to the fine, and whether money can be called flogging.
Baraita: one who vows half his valuation gives half, but Rabbi Yosei ben Rabbi Yehuda says he is flogged and gives full valuation.
Rav Pappa: the flogging is a rabbinic decree, since half a valuation is treated as a limb on which life depends, so full valuation applies.
Baraita: 'and they shall fine him' refers to money, and 'chastise him' refers to flogging.
Asks how we know that 'chastise' means flogging, given that 'fine' clearly refers to money.
Rabbi Abbahu derives 'chastise' by verbal analogy with the rebellious son passage, linking 'son' to the flogging of Deuteronomy 25:2.
Asks the source of the warning (prohibition) underlying the defamer's flogging.
Rabbi Elazar derives it from 'no talebearing' (Leviticus 19:16); Rabbi Natan from 'keep from every evil thing' (Deuteronomy 23:10).
Asks why Rabbi Elazar does not use Rabbi Natan's verse.
That verse is needed for Rabbi Pinhas ben Yair's teaching against impure thoughts by day that lead to night emission.
Asks the reverse: why Rabbi Natan does not use Rabbi Elazar's verse.
Rabbi Natan reads 'talebearer' as a warning to courts not to favor one litigant over the other.
If witnesses testify for the husband unasked and prove false, the husband is not flogged or fined, as he did not harm her.
Asks: may both she and her conspiring witnesses be stoned? Rather, either she or the witnesses.
Infers that the husband is exempt only if he did not tell witnesses to testify; Rabbi Yehuda says he is liable only if he hired them.
Asks the reason for Rabbi Yehuda's view, since the Torah nowhere says the husband hired false witnesses.
Rabbi Abbahu: verbal analogy with 'placing' in the interest prohibition (Exodus 22:24) shows money is paid, so he paid the witnesses.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak: Rav Yosef Tzidoni taught the same analogy in the school of Rabbi Shimon ben Yoḥai.
Rabbi Yirmeya's dilemma: if the husband hired witnesses with land, or with less than a peruta, what is the halakha?
Rav Ashi's dilemma: does defaming concern a prior marriage, or a levirate marriage to his brother?
Rabbi Yona's teaching: 'I gave my daughter to this man' excludes a yavam, so defamation about a prior marriage to his brother is not covered.
Asks the opinions of the Rabbis and Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov on the matter, as taught in a baraita.
Baraita: a husband says he found no virginity; if witnesses show adultery under him, the wife has a hundred-dinar contract.
The Gemara is surprised: is she stoned yet still owed a hundred-dinar contract?
The tanna means: if she sinned under him she is stoned; if she sinned before betrothal, she has the non-virgin's contract.
If the accusation proves false, the husband is flogged and pays the father one hundred sela, whether or not intercourse occurred.
Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov: these rules apply only if he had intercourse with her before defaming her.
Asks: for Rabbi Eliezer, 'go in unto her' means intercourse; but for the Rabbis, what does it mean?
The Rabbis: 'go in unto her' refers to wanton charges, and 'came near to her' means near with words, not intercourse.
Asks the same about 'I did not find tokens of virginity' on the Rabbis' reading.
The Rabbis: it means I did not find for your daughter the fitness of virginity, i.e., she was unfaithful.
Asks the Rabbis' meaning of 'these are the tokens of my daughter's virginity' spoken by the father.
The Rabbis: the father means these are proofs of the fitness of her virginity, such as witnesses or other evidence.
Asks the Rabbis' meaning of 'and they shall spread the garment' when intercourse is not required.
Rabbi Abbahu: 'spread' means examine what was placed against her, cross-examining the witnesses; Rabbi Eliezer: an actual cloth.
Rabbi Yoḥanan: the Torah distinguishes typical and atypical intercourse only for the defamer, whose fine requires either kind.
Asks whose opinion Rabbi Yoḥanan's ruling follows: the Rabbis, or Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov.

46b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Kahana, citing Rabbi Yoḥanan: liability requires typical intercourse, and defamation about typical intercourse, per Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya'akov.
Mishna: a father controls his daughter's betrothal, earnings, found items and vows; after marriage the husband takes over support, redemption and burial.
