ranges.en: Asks whether a daughter of a penalized mother has sustenance; the dilemma is left unresolved.
Rava asks whether a daughter of a betrothed woman, who has a contract, has sustenance; left unresolved.
Rav Pappa asks about the daughter of a raped woman, with a Yosei-based consideration; the dilemma stands.
Asks whether the rabbis' view, that the fine replaces the contract, leaves the daughter with sustenance; unresolved.
The Mishna's stipulation: a widow may sit in her husband's house and be sustained from his property.
Rav Yosef's teaching limits this to 'my house, not my hovel'; Mar bar Rav Ashi's dissent is rejected in practice.
Rav Naḥman reports Shmuel's rule that a widow who agreed to a new suitor loses her sustenance, while a refusal keeps it.
Rav Anan clarifies Shmuel's rule: a refusal for her late husband's sake keeps sustenance, a refusal due to unsuitable men does not.
Rav Ḥisda and Rav Yosef rule that a widow's immorality or cosmetic remarriage signals she forfeits sustenance.
Explains the two rulings' scope: immorality by force of temptation does not forfeit sustenance, so the rulings are not uniform.
The halakha follows Shmuel via Rav Yehuda: claiming the contract in court forfeits sustenance.
Asks whether a widow who sells or pledges her contract loses sustenance, citing a baraita.
Infers from the baraita that forfeiture applies whether or not the action is taken in court, only for claims made in court.
Mishna on local customs for widows' residence; Rav and Shmuel hold opposing halakhot for Judea and the Galilee.
Babylonia follows Rav, Neharde'a follows Shmuel, and their surrounding areas follow the same practice.
A woman from Meḥoza marrying from Neharde'a: Rav Naḥman applies the custom by region, with its boundary set by measures.
Rav and Shmuel dispute whether a widow's clothing is appraised and deducted from her contract payment.
Rav Kahana's version, with a mnemonic, shows Rav holds garments are appraised for both widow and hired worker.
Rav Naḥman cites a Mishna on consecrated property to show the halakha follows Rav, despite its apparent agreement with Shmuel.
Rava asks why the halakha follows Rav when the Mishna appears to agree with Shmuel.
Explains the Mishna reads as Shmuel's view only superficially; the husband bought the clothes for her to wear while living with him.
Relates a case where a daughter-in-law claimed her contract from orphans, and the response about her attire and the ruling.

54b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Yosef rules that when wine bought with the orphans' girl's money gains value, the surplus goes to the male orphans.
Relatives of Rabbi Yoḥanan ask how to handle their father's wife's wasteful spending; he advises assigning her a plot of land.
Reish Lakish rules that the heirs must still support her according to her accustomed standard, with the land as supplement.
The relatives object that Rabbi Yoḥanan never said that, and Reish Lakish threatens them to comply anyway.
Rabbi Yoḥanan replies that he cannot impose his view, since an equal of his disagrees with him.
Rabbi Abbahu explains that the husband's wording determines whether the land is a supplement or the only source of support.
Closing marker for the chapter, beginning the Mishna of the chapter on the marriage contract.
The Mishna rules that a husband may add to the contract sum, and the wife collects all of it upon divorce or widowhood.
Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya limits the full collection to marriage, not betrothal, since the addition was written only to marry her.
Rabbi Yehuda permits a husband to write a larger sum that the wife may waive by writing a receipt for part of it.
Rabbi Meir forbids any reduction of the contract's minimum sums, calling such a marriage licentious.
Asks why the Mishna needs to say a husband may add, since that seems obvious.
Notes the Mishna's wording 'add' rather than 'write', which supports Rabbi Aivu's view that additions are part of the contract.
Rabbi Aivu reports Rabbi Yannai's principle that stipulations and additions are treated like the marriage contract itself.
Lists the practical effects: sale, waiver, rebellion, claiming, vitiation, and forfeiture all apply to the additional sum too.

55a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Lists further effects of the additional marriage contract sum: increased land value, oath, and the Sabbatical Year.
The Pumbedita Sages hold the male-children stipulation is not seized from liened property sold by the father, per the 'they inherit' wording.
The Mata Meḥasya residents hold it is seized from sold property, reading the wording as 'they take'; the halakha follows Pumbedita.
On movable property set aside for the contract, Pumbedita and Mata Meḥasya dispute the oath; the halakha is no oath.
On land demarcated on one border or all four, the halakha is that the widow takes it without an oath.
Witnesses given a gift deed: the Pumbedita and Mata Meḥasya Sages dispute whether consultation is needed; the halakha is yes.
Rav and Rabbi Natan dispute whether the halakha follows Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's view that additions are collected after marriage.
Concludes Rabbi Natan held that view, since he assesses intention, as shown in his view on a dying husband's divorce bill.

55b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Natan's ruling on teruma of demai also follows the principle of assessing intention, as Rabbi Shimon Shezuri holds.
Objects that Rav does not follow intention, since Rav and Shmuel disagreed about a deathbed gift that was also acquired formally.
Reports Rav's school: the gift was 'ridden on two horses,' secured by two legal grounds.
Explains the two horses: the gift is like a healthy person's gift, which cannot be retracted, and like a deathbed gift, transferring a debt orally.
Shmuel's view: he does not know; the formal acquisition may show intent to transfer only by a bill of sale, which is void after death.

56a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Concludes that Rav also follows intention, so Rabbi Natan is not uniquely the one; both explain the debate differently.
Rav Ḥanina says the halakha follows Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, but Rabbi Yannai rebukes him: it does not.
Traditions in the names of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, Shmuel and Rav Naḥman give conflicting rulings on Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya.
Rav Naḥman's conflicting statements, and his curse on judges who follow Rabbi Elazar, lead to the practical halakha that it does apply.
Ravin asks whether a woman who entered the canopy but was not intimate gets the additional sum.
A baraita by Rav Yosef on affection of the first night is cited to show the wedding itself effects the marriage.
Objects that 'first night' may refer to the wedding, but a wedding need not occur only at night.
Rava's rule shows intercourse is generally at night, so the baraita is not a proof either way.
Rav Ashi asks about a bride who menstruated after the canopy; the Mishna of Rabbi Yehuda on receipts is then questioned.
Rabbi Yirmeya and Abaye explain that Rabbi Yehuda permits the receipt when written within the contract, since no loss of the note is feared.
Asks why Rabbi Yirmeya does not follow Abaye's reasoning and why the receipt must be written inside the contract.
The receipt must be written in the contract, due to a decree against typical receipts, and a verbal waiver is not effective.
A Tosefta on verbal conditions in betrothal, where Rabbi Yehuda says monetary stipulations stand, is cited as support.
Rabbi Yehuda holds the contract is rabbinic, so its waivers must be written, unlike Torah obligations like food and clothing.
Challenges that the husband's rabbinic claim to produce is not reinforced either, contrary to that answer.

56b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Gemara asks what the word writes means in the stipulation.
Writes is explained to mean says, so an oral waiver before witnesses suffices.
Abaye holds the Sages enforced written stipulations only for common matters like marriage contracts, not for produce.
Objection: donkey drivers are a common matter, yet the Sages did not reinforce their rulings there.
A mishna on donkey drivers, where Rabbi Yehuda deems verbal claims credible, is brought as support.
Abaye replies that certain rabbinic matters were reinforced while doubtful ones were not, which covers donkey drivers.
Rava explains the donkey drivers case was lenient because demai is itself a stringency.
Rabbi Meir's mishna: reducing the marriage contract below the set amount makes the union licentious.
The Gemara infers from the mishna's wording that Rabbi Meir holds such a stipulation void even if she agreed.
Objection: Rabbi Meir says any stipulation against the Torah is void, which implies rabbinic stipulations stand.
Reply: Rabbi Meir treats the marriage contract as a Torah requirement, so reducing it is void.
Baraita: Rabbi Meir says reducing the contract below the set amount makes the union licentious.
Rabbi Yosei permits reducing the amount through a verbal stipulation if the wife agrees.
Rabbi Yehuda permits written documents in which the wife's receipt records the lower amount paid.
Does Rabbi Yosei really hold that the reduction is permitted?
Contradiction: a baraita rules that the contract cannot be collected from movables, for the betterment of the world.
Rabbi Yosei asks what betterment this serves, since the value of movables is not fixed and may fall.
The first tanna's ban applies only when no guarantee was given; with a guarantee, the arrangement is valid.
Rabbi Yosei holds that even with a guarantee, the arrangement should be rejected because values are not fixed.
If movables may lose value, is it not all the more so objectionable when the loss is certain?
The cases differ: she did not know there, but here she knew the loss and waived her claim.
The sister of Rami bar Ḥama was married to Rav Avya.

57a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A couple whose marriage contract was lost comes to Rav Yosef asking what to do.
Rav Yosef cites Shmuel, via Rav Yehuda, that reducing the contract voids the marriage, as Rabbi Meir holds.
The Rabbis hold a husband may maintain his wife two or three years without a new written contract.
Abaye objects that Shmuel ruled the halakha follows Rabbi Meir in all his decrees, which should apply here.
Rav Yosef concedes that if so, the husband must write her a new contract.
Rav Dimi reports a dispute about verbal waivers that applies only to the beginning, while at the end all agree.
Rabbi Yohanan holds the dispute applies in both cases, beginning and end.
Rabbi Abbahu reports Rabbi Yohanan's clarification that he and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi do not disagree.
The Gemara asks what Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi means by the beginning.
The beginning is the start of the wedding and the end is the start of intercourse, so both sides agree at the wedding stage.
Ravin reports the same tradition differently: the dispute concerns the end, while at the beginning all agree she may waive verbally.
Rabbi Yohanan again holds that the dispute applies in both cases.
Rabbi Abbahu repeats that Rabbi Yohanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi do not actually disagree.
The Gemara asks what Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi means by the end.
The end is the end of the wedding ceremony.
The Gemara asks what the beginning means.
The beginning is the start of the wedding, and the dispute concerns the beginning and end of intercourse.
Rav Pappa says that without Rabbi Abbahu's clarification he would read the sources as an actual disagreement between Rabbi Yohanan and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi.
Rav Pappa's alternative reading: Ravin's end is the end of the wedding and Rav Dimi's beginning is the start of intercourse.
What is Rav Pappa teaching us, if he accepts Rabbi Abbahu's account?
He teaches that two Amoraim disagreeing over reasons is more plausible than two Amoraim transmitting differing traditions.
Mishna: a virgin gets twelve months to prepare after betrothal, a widow thirty days, and a betrothed priest's bride may eat teruma once the time arrives.
Rabbi Tarfon says the priest may provide all of her sustenance from teruma, selling it during her impurity if needed.
Rabbi Akiva says half of her sustenance must come from non-sacred food and half may be teruma.
A yavam does not enable his yevama to eat teruma, even if she waited six months under the husband and six under him.
Even if all the waiting was under the husband except for a single day under the yavam, or the reverse, she may not eat teruma.
These rulings are the initial mishna, and a later court said otherwise in a later generation.

57b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A woman may not eat teruma until she has actually entered the wedding canopy.
The Gemara asks what the source is for the twelve-month preparation period for a virgin.
Rav Hisda derives it from the verse about Rebecca's family asking she stay for days or ten.
The Gemara asks what the word days means in that verse.
Objection: reading days as two days and ten as ten days is implausible, since no one would speak that way.
The Gemara asks what days means if not two days.
Days refers to a year, as in the verse on redeeming a house in a walled city within a year.
The Gemara asks whether days might instead mean a month, based on another verse.
One derives an undefined days from another undefined days meaning a year, not from a passage that specifies a month.
Rabbi Zeira cites a Tosefta: a minor girl's wedding may be delayed by her or by her father.
Why should the father have a say if the girl herself may delay, and what does it matter to him?
The father worries she will consent now without understanding, then regret it and become his burden.
Rabbi Abba bar Levi: one may not betroth a minor to marry her while a minor, but may do so for marriage once she is an adult.
The Gemara asks why this is needed, since it seems obvious.
The ruling is needed in case one fears the minor's early planning would weaken her resolve when she grows up.
Rav Huna holds that a girl betrothed after reaching majority, even one day, gets thirty days like a widow.
Objection from a baraita: a grown woman is like a virgin who was asked in marriage and so gets twelve months.
Counter-proof from a mishna: a grown woman who waited twelve months is still subject to her husband's authority over vows.
Reply: the mishna should be emended to say a grown woman who waited thirty days, which supports Rav Huna.
Another baraita refutes Rav Huna: a grown woman who was betrothed on her majority day gets twelve months from betrothal.
The Gemara asks what it means that a woman already betrothed at majority gets thirty days.
Rav Pappa explains: a woman grown for twelve months and then betrothed gets thirty days, like a widow.
Mishna: if the appointed wedding time arrives and they did not marry, she may eat teruma.
Ulla holds that by Torah law a betrothed daughter of an Israelite may eat teruma immediately.
Ulla supports this from the verse that a priest's purchased person may eat of his money.
The Gemara asks what the rabbinic reason is for prohibiting her from eating teruma.
The concern is that she might give teruma wine to her non-priest brother or sister while still in her father's house.
If so, the same concern should apply after the wedding time has arrived.
After the time arrives, the husband designates a specific place for her to eat, which removes the concern.
If so, a priest working as a gleaner for an Israelite should also be barred, lest the household eat his teruma.
Household members would not eat from the priest's food, so there is no concern.
Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yehuda: the decree is due to possible cancellation of the betrothal because of a defect.
If so, a woman who entered the canopy but has not had intercourse should also be barred.
There, the husband first investigates her through female relatives before entering the canopy, so there is no concern.
If so, a priest's slave bought from an Israelite should also be barred, due to possible cancellation.
Slaves have no cancellation risk, since external defects are seen at the sale and internal ones matter less for labor.

58a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A buyer cannot annul a sale because the seller has caught him in a binding transaction.
The Gemara asks whether the rule holds if the slave is an armed bandit or is sentenced by the king.
Such serious defects become public, so the buyer is presumed to have known and accepted the defect.
The Gemara asks what difference there is between Ulla and Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yehuda if both bar her from teruma.
The difference appears when the husband accepted her blemishes, or when the father transferred her to the husband's agents.
Mishna: Rabbi Tarfon says the priest may give her all her sustenance in teruma, while Rabbi Akiva requires half non-sacred food.
Abaye limits the dispute to a priest's daughter married to a priest and to a betrothed woman, not to a wife or an Israelite betrothed.
A baraita repeats the Tarfon and Akiva dispute and confirms the same limits on the cases where it applies.
Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira says the husband gives two parts teruma and one part non-sacred food.
Rabbi Yehuda says all may be teruma, but the amount must be enough for her to buy food by selling it while impure.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says where teruma is mentioned he gives double, since teruma is hard to sell.
The Gemara asks what the practical difference is between Rabbi Yehuda and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.
The difference concerns effort: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel adds extra teruma so she need not work hard to sell it.
Mishna: a yavam does not enable his yevama to eat teruma.
The Gemara asks what the reason is for that ruling.
The verse says a priest's purchased person may eat, but this woman is her brother's acquisition, not the yavam's.
Mishna: if she spent six months under the husband and six under the yavam, she may not eat teruma.
If the mishna says she is barred even when mostly under the husband, why repeat the case of mostly under the yavam?
The tanna lists cases from the less obvious to the more obvious, so the second part is needed for the style.
Mishna: according to the later version, she may not eat teruma until she actually enters the wedding canopy.
The Gemara asks the reason for this later ruling.
Ulla, or some say Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda, holds it is due to concern for abrogation of the marriage.
Ulla's earlier concern is about teruma wine in her father's house, and the later ruling is about abrogation, so two reasons apply.

58b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: According to Rav Shmuel bar Yehuda, both the initial ruling and the later ruling are due to concern about abrogation.
The Gemara asks what the practical difference is between the two reasons.
The difference lies in whether a superficial investigation by her female relatives counts as a valid check for blemishes.
Mishna: if one consecrates his wife's earnings she may keep working for herself, but Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yohanan the Cobbler dispute the surplus.
Rav Huna, citing Rav, holds a wife may waive her right to sustenance and so her earnings belong to her, since the arrangement is for her benefit.
Objection from a baraita: the husband's duty to sustain her is granted in exchange for her earnings, which contradicts Rav Huna.
Objection: the mishna about consecrating earnings supports Rav Huna only if the husband does sustain her, which the Gemara rejects.
If the mishna concerns a wife who is not sustained, why state that he cannot consecrate her earnings, even for a slave who is not sustained?
The latter clause was needed because it adds a novelty about the surplus, on which Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yohanan the Cobbler disagree.
Reish Lakish explains Rabbi Meir's reason: he has a legal claim to her earnings, so it is as if he said her hands are consecrated.
The Gemara asks that the husband did not say this to her, only that he consecrated her earnings.
Rabbi Meir holds a person does not say things for naught, so the words are read as if he said the consecration of her hands.
The Gemara asks whether Rabbi Meir holds that one cannot consecrate what is not yet in existence, citing a baraita that seems to say he does.
The baraita shows Rabbi Meir's view, but Reish Lakish means the mishna alone does not prove it, since another reading is available.
Mishna: according to Rabbi Meir, the surplus of her earnings is consecrated property.
The Gemara asks when the surplus becomes consecrated.
Rav and Shmuel hold it is consecrated only after her death, while Rav Adda bar Ahava holds it is consecrated during her life.
Rav Pappa asks what they dispute, testing each assumption about whether the husband provides sustenance and a ma'a for her needs.
The dispute concerns a husband who provides sustenance but not the ma'a for her needs, and Rav and Shmuel differ on the enactment.

59a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Adda bar Ahava holds the husband's sustenance is exchanged for the surplus and the ma'a for her earnings, so the surplus is his.
The Gemara asks what the two Sages actually disagree about.
One Sage treats common for common, the other treats fixed amount for fixed amount, explaining the two positions.
Objection from a baraita: sustenance is granted in exchange for her earnings, not for the surplus.
A mishna is brought as support: if he does not give her a ma'a, her earnings belong to her.
Objection: the emendation conflicts with the continuation, which gives a fixed quota of five sela in Judea.
The mishna gives the fixed quota so one can tell what counts as surplus.
Shmuel rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Yohanan the Cobbler: a husband cannot consecrate her earnings.
The Gemara asks whether Shmuel really said this, citing a mishna on a wife's konam vow that the husband need not nullify.
Shmuel also rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri.
Shmuel's ruling for Rabbi Yohanan ben Nuri applies only to the surplus.
The Gemara asks why Shmuel did not state the ruling more clearly for the surplus.
Rav Yosef explains that konamot are special, since a person can prohibit another's produce to himself.
Abaye objects that a person cannot prohibit another's future produce to a third party, so the konam analogy fails.
Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua explains the mishna is about her saying her hands are consecrated, which exist already.
The Gemara asks how she can consecrate what is not hers, since she is subjugated to her husband.
The Gemara asks whether anything consecrated later could not be consecrated now.
Rabbi Elai says a field sold with a future consecration clause is consecrated later, so the same may hold here.
Rabbi Yirmeya objects that the field comparison fails, since the seller owns the field but she cannot divorce herself.
A proper analogy is a field already sold, which is not consecrated later, since it was not in his possession.
Rav Pappa objects that the field and its produce are in the buyer's possession, while her body is in her own possession.

59b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A field mortgaged to another, to be consecrated when the owner redeems it, is consecrated because the land itself was not transferred.
Rav Sheisha son of Rav Idi objects: the mortgage case is not comparable, since she cannot divorce herself as the mortgagor can redeem.
The proper comparison is a field mortgaged for ten years, which is consecrated on redemption, so the wife's earnings may be too.
Rav Ashi objects that after ten years the owner can always redeem, while a wife can never free herself from her husband.
Rav Ashi resolves it: konamot are inherent sanctity that can take effect on property subject to a lien, as Rava held.
The Gemara asks why her earnings would not then be consecrated already, before the divorce.
The Sages reinforced the husband's lien so that her earnings are not consecrated now, but only after she leaves him.
Mishna: a list of household tasks a wife must do, reduced according to how many maidservants she brings.
Rabbi Eliezer holds he may compel her to spin wool even if she brought a hundred maidservants, since idleness leads to licentiousness.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that one who forbids his wife any work must divorce her, since idleness leads to foolishness.
The Gemara asks how the mishna can say she grinds wheat, since grinding is done by a mill.
She supervises the grinding, or alternatively she grinds with a hand mill.
The mishna does not follow Rabbi Hiyya, who holds a wife is for beauty and children, not household tasks.
Suggestion: the mishna's nursing duty may not follow Beit Shammai, who let a woman vowing not to nurse be exempt.
Even if the mishna follows Beit Shammai, here the husband ratified the vow, and responsibility lies with him.
The Gemara asks why the dispute is framed as nursing rather than a marriage-contract payment, and concludes the mishna is not Beit Shammai.
The Gemara recalls a baraita: if the child recognized her, the husband may compel her to nurse after divorce, paying her for it.

60a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Gemara asks how old a child must be before he recognizes his mother.
Rav says three months, Shmuel says thirty days, and Rabbi Yohanan says fifty days; the halakha follows Rabbi Yohanan.
The Gemara asks whether the views of Rav and Rabbi Yohanan can be reconciled, and whether Shmuel's view has any real case.
Rami bar Yehezkel reports Shmuel's ruling: there is no fixed age, and each baby must be checked for recognizing its mother.
A divorcee who would not nurse was tested by Rav Dimi bar Yosef, and the child's reaction showed he knew her, supporting Shmuel's approach.
The Gemara asks how a blind baby can recognize his mother.
Rav Ashi says the blind baby recognizes her by smell and the taste of her milk.
Baraita: a child may nurse until twenty-four months, and after that nursing is like nursing from an impure animal, per Rabbi Eliezer; Rabbi Yehoshua allows four or five years.
Objection from a baraita: milk of humans should be impure like that of an animal, by a fortiori reasoning.
A verse about the camel's impurity is cited to show human milk and blood are not impure, and the Torah excludes them.
Rav Sheshet holds there is not even a rabbinic prohibition on consuming human milk.
The permission refers to milk removed from the body, while nursing directly is prohibited by rabbinic law.
A baraita on blood: blood removed from bread must be scraped off, while blood between teeth may be sucked, supporting the distinction.
Objection: a different baraita says Rabbi Yehoshua allows nursing even if the child can carry his bundle, which seems to conflict.
The two baraitot give the same measure, and Rav Yosef rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehoshua.
Baraita: Rabbi Marinos allows sucking milk from an animal on Shabbat when coughing from illness.
The Gemara asks the reason for this leniency.
Sucking is an unusual way of extracting, so it is prohibited only by rabbinic law, which does not apply when there is pain.
Rav Yosef rules that the halakha follows Rabbi Marinos.
Baraita: Nahum of Galia allows crushing a blocked drainage pipe with the foot on Shabbat in private.
The Gemara asks the reason for Nahum's leniency.
Repairing in an unusual manner is prohibited only by rabbinic decree, which does not apply when financial loss is at stake.
Rav Yosef rules that the halakha follows Nahum of Galia.
If the child stopped nursing after twenty-four months and then resumed, he is like one who nurses from an impure animal.
The Gemara asks how long the child must stop nursing to count as weaned.
Rav Yehuda bar Haviva says Shmuel holds three days.
Some say the three-day ruling was a baraita that Rav Yehuda bar Haviva taught before Shmuel, not a ruling of Shmuel.
Baraita: a nursing woman whose husband died within twenty-four months after the birth may not become betrothed or remarried.

60b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabbi Meir says twenty-four months; Rabbi Yehuda permits after eighteen months, which mirrors the Shammai and Hillel dispute.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel decides that the nursing woman may marry at twenty-one months, or fifteen on the lower view.
Ulla holds the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda, and Mar Ukva reports Rabbi Hanina permitted marrying after fifteen months.
Abaye's tenant farmer asks Abaye whether he may betroth a nursing woman after fifteen months.
Abaye gives reasons: the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda and Beit Hillel, so betrothal is all the more permitted.
Rav Yosef tells Abaye that Rav and Shmuel require twenty-four months even for betrothal; Abaye runs to stop his tenant but fails.
Abaye's lesson: one should not rule even on a simple matter in his teacher's presence, since he may not state it correctly.
Baraita: if the child was given to a wet nurse, weaned, or died, the mother may marry at once; an old woman reports Rav Nahman prohibited this to her.
The Gemara asks whether Rav Nahman did not permit this for the Exilarch's household.
The Exilarch's household is different, since its employees do not renege out of fear.
Rav Pappi objects with a baraita requiring a three-month wait for many women, per Rabbi Meir.
Rabbi Yosei permits them to marry at once, and Rav Nahman says Shmuel held the halakha follows Rabbi Meir in all his decrees.
They answer that the matter had not been in mind, and the halakha is then stated.
The halakha: if the child died the mother may remarry at once, but if weaned she may not; Mar bar Rav Ashi says even if the child died she is barred.
The concern that a mother might kill her child is not a practical risk; the incident involved an insane woman.
Baraita: a wet nurse paid to nurse may not nurse another child with the paid child, and must eat enough and avoid foods bad for milk.
The Gemara asks why the baraita needs to say she may not nurse another woman's child, since that seems obvious.
Without the rule, one might think the concern applies only to her own child, so the baraita forbids both.
The Gemara asks where she gets the extra food if the allowance is small.
Rav Sheshet says from her own funds, since she accepted the obligation to nurse.
The Gemara asks what foods are harmful to milk.
Rav Kahana, Abaye, Rav Pappa, and Rav Ashi each list foods that dry or spoil milk.
The Gemara lists how a mother's behavior during pregnancy, such as intercourse in a mill or eating certain foods, affects her children.

61a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: A list of prenatal diet effects on children, followed by a story about the daughter of King Shapur and her fragrance.
Rav Huna bar Hinnana poses a case: if the husband and wife disagree on nursing, whose custom or whose wishes control?
The question is answered from a statement: she ascends with her husband's status but does not descend with it.
Rav Huna asks what verse the principle is derived from.
The verse on his wife's ascent is read to show she rises with her husband but does not descend with him.
Rabbi Elazar derives the same principle from a verse that she was given to live, not to suffer, with him.
Mishna: if she brought one maidservant she need not grind, bake, or wash clothes.
Objection: the wife could argue she brought a maidservant to replace her, so she should be exempt from all tasks.

Objection: with two maidservants she could argue she brought one to serve both, so she needs to do nothing.

Mishna: students may travel for thirty days, laborers for a week, and the frequency of conjugal duty varies by occupation, per Rabbi Eliezer.

Beit Shammai derive the two weeks from a mother of a girl, while Beit Hillel derive a week from a mother of a boy.

Beit Hillel derived it from the menstruating woman, who is barred seven days by Torah law.

Beit Hillel derive a common matter from a common matter, while Beit Shammai derive a self-caused matter from another self-caused matter.

ranges.en: The Gemara asks what the acceptable amount of time is that a husband may spend away from home for study.

Building the Temple could be done by others, but Torah study cannot, so the temple proof does not apply.

David gained profit from working for the king, so his wife would waive more, but a wife generally wants her husband home for Torah study.
Rav holds groaning breaks half the body, citing Ezekiel; Rabbi Yohanan holds it breaks the whole body.
The Gemara asks why Rabbi Yohanan does not also say half the body, given the verse about the loins.
The verse means that the sigh begins from the loins, not that it reaches only that far.

The news of the Temple's destruction is uniquely crushing, while an ordinary sigh breaks only half the body.
A Jew walking with a gentile who reminds him of the Temple sighs but is not affected, because he is used to such tragedy.
Mishna: men of leisure must have conjugal relations every day.
The Gemara asks what is meant by men of leisure.
Rava says they are students of Torah who review their lectures daily and return home each evening.

Rabbi Abbahu and Rabbi Yohanan show the strength of Eretz Yisrael inhabitants, surviving collapses that would have injured others.
Mishna: laborers must have conjugal relations twice a week.
Objection: a baraita says laborers only once a week.
Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Hanina: the baraita refers to laborers working in another city, and the mishna to their own city.
A Tosefta gives the same distinction: twice a week in their own city, once a week in another city.

Rabba bar Rav Hanan challenges Abaye: why does the mishna bother to teach the halakha of men of leisure and laborers only.

ranges.en: The Gemara asks why a week's vow would require divorce if sailors may abstain for six months.
One who has bread in his basket suffers less than one who lacks it, so a vowed wife suffers more when waiting.
Rabba bar Rav Hanan asks whether a married donkey driver may become a camel driver, reducing conjugal relations.
A woman prefers modest means with conjugal relations over plenty with abstinence, so he needs her permission to change.
Mishna: sailors have conjugal relations once every six months, per Rabbi Eliezer.
Rav Berona and Rav Adda bar Ahava report Rav's ruling for Rabbi Eliezer, and the Rabbis allow students to leave for two or three years.
Rava says the Sages relied on Rabbi Adda bar Ahava's opinion and acted on it, with some fatal results.
Rav Rehumi, who studied in Mehoza, died when a roof collapsed after he caused his wife anguish by staying away on Yom Kippur eve.

Rav Yehuda, Shmuel, and others hold the proper time is from Shabbat eve to Shabbat eve.
Yehuda son of Rabbi Hiyya missed Shabbat eve while studying, and his father-in-law wrongly declared him dead, and he died.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi arranges a marriage for his son, but the girl dies; the families' ancestry is examined and a disqualification is ruled out.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi arranges a match with the household of Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra, and the groom's desire leads him to marry before studying.
The Torah's Sinai verses show God brought forward an intended later Temple, which the father uses to justify his son's haste.
The groom studies twelve years, and his wife becomes infertile; Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says God is asked to show mercy and she is cured.
Rabbi Hananya ben Hakhinai goes to study at the end of Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai's wedding and returns after twelve years, unable to find his way home.
Rabbi Hananya's wife dies from the shock of seeing him, and Rabbi Hama bar Bisa, having learned from that, returns home unannounced and meets his son.
Rabbi Hama stands for his son, whom he takes for a Torah scholar, and Rami bar Hama applies the three-stranded cord verse to Rabbi Oshaya.
Rabbi Akiva, a shepherd for ben Kalba Savua, is betrothed to the daughter on condition he studies, and returns with twelve thousand students after twelve years.

ranges.en: Rabbi Akiva's wife tells him to go study, and he returns with twenty-four thousand students; she meets him and is embraced by his attendants.
Ben Kalba Savua seeks Rabbi Akiva's help to annul his vow, and his daughter does the same with ben Azzai, giving the folk saying about the ewe and her lamb.
Rav Yosef son of Rava is sent to study, leaves early for Yom Kippur to see his wife, and his father confronts him.
Mishna: a rebellious wife's marriage contract is reduced seven dinars a week, per Rabbi Yehuda; Rabbi Yosei says it continues without end, and a husband's rebellion adds to her contract.
The Gemara asks what the nature of the wife's rebellion is.

Yes: the mishna concerns a husband who says he will not sustain or support his wife.

Objection from a baraita: the same rule applies to a betrothed, a married, a menstruating, or an ill woman, or one awaiting yavam.
The Gemara asks whether a menstruating woman's refusal can be a rebellion, since she is not fit for relations.
The reply: a man who has had relations suffers more from her refusal even when she is menstruating or ill, and the ill-woman case fits this view.

ranges.en: The Gemara asks how the view that rebellion means refusing tasks can apply to an ill woman, who has no duty of tasks.
Everyone agrees refusing relations is rebellion; the dispute is whether refusing tasks counts, with Rav Huna saying no and Rabbi Yosei saying yes.
Mishna and the later Sages' enactment: a rebellious wife's contract is reduced, replaced by four Shabbat announcements and a warning from the court.
Rabbi Hiyya bar Yosef asks Shmuel whether a menstruating woman is fit for relations.
Shmuel replies: one who has bread in his basket is not comparable to one who lacks bread, since he expects relations after her impurity ends.
Rami bar Hama holds announcements are made only in synagogues and study halls, not in the street.
Rava supports Rami bar Hama from the baraita's wording on four consecutive Shabbatot, when people are in synagogues.
Rami bar Hama adds the court sends people to speak with her twice, before and after the announcement.
Rav Naḥman bar Rav Hisda holds the halakha follows the Sages' decision.
Rava calls this ruling an absurdity.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak defends the ruling as stated in the name of Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Hanina.
The Gemara asks whose opinion Rava follows.
Rava follows Rav Sheshet's ruling that she is consulted and deductions are made meanwhile, while Rav Huna bar Yehuda reports a different version.
The Gemara asks what circumstances make a woman rebellious.
Ameimar says the case is one of wanting to provoke him; if she is disgusted by him, she is not compelled, while Mar Zutra compels her.
An incident where Mar Zutra compelled a woman to stay, and a son of that couple became Rabbi Hanina of Sura.
The Gemara concludes that this should not be a precedent, since the good outcome came from heavenly assistance.
The daughter-in-law of Rav Zevid rebels, and Ameimar, Mar Zutra, Rav Ashi and Rav Gamda debate whether she forfeits her worn clothes.

64a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objection: one should not twist the ruling against Rav Zevid, since Rava left Rav Kahana's dilemma unresolved.
Since the matter was never settled either way, the worn clothes stay with her if she seized them and are not given to her if she did not.
A rebellious wife's bill of divorce is delayed twelve months, and during that time she receives no sustenance from her husband.
Shmuel holds the court writes a rebellion letter for a betrothed woman, but not for a yavam's widow who refuses levirate marriage.
Objection from a baraita: the rebellion rule applies equally to betrothed women, married women, menstruating or ill women, and yavam widows.
The baraita refers to a case where he asked to marry her, while Shmuel's ruling covers where she asked and he refused.

Rather, a letter is issued only where a woman comes with a claim for children to support her in old age and bury her.
The Gemara asks why the court should not hear a yavam's widow who comes with the same claim.
The cases differ by who asks: the yavam asking for halitza is answered, while one asking for levirate marriage is not.
The Gemara asks why refusing levirate marriage is not rebellion, since the yavam could simply marry another woman.
The reason is that he says she is attached to him and no one else will marry him until halitza, which is a valid claim.
The Gemara asks why the court does not write a letter when she refuses levirate marriage under the same claim.
Both statements concern a request for levirate marriage, and they follow different versions of the mishna.
A mishna in Bekhorot: levirate marriage precedes halitza while people intended the mitzva, but later halitza precedes it.
Mishna: how far does the husband reduce her contract, with the amounts counted in terapa'ikin per Rabbi Yehuda.
The Gemara asks what terapa'ikin are.
Rav Sheshet says an asteira, a small coin worth half a dinar.
A baraita: Rabbi Yehuda's three terapa'ikin equal nine ma'as, a ma'a and a half a day for six days.

ranges.en: The prior discussion concludes the payment in question appears to be wages for Shabbat.

Mishna: a husband feeding his wife through a trustee must give at least two kav wheat or four kav barley weekly.

Clothing worth fifty dinars yearly, suited to the season; she uses worn garments in summer and keeps them.

If the mishna follows Rabbi Yohanan ben Beroka there are eight meals, and Rabbi Shimon gives eighteen. Which is it?

If eating means intercourse, what follows? Even without Shabbat evening there are still thirteen meals needed.

Rav Hisda's two statements seem to contradict each other.
No contradiction: one place pays extra for wood, the other does not, so the markup differs.
Sixteen meals exceed the need, so who is the author of the mishna?

The mishna further teaches that half a kav of legumes is given to her.
The mishna omits wine, which supports Rabbi Elazar's position as he stated it.

Rav Pappa addresses Abaye with a challenge; the exchange continues beyond this daf, so only its opening is drafted.

ranges.en: This tanna seems to leave the wife barefoot-clothed yet giving her shoes three times a year, which is odd.

Chapter-ending formula, closing the previous chapter before the next mishna begins.

It was needed to state the dispute between Rabbi Yehuda ben Beteira and the Rabbis over ownership of the compensation.

Rava calls the baraita puzzling: if the surplus of her earnings beyond the required sum belongs to the husband, then...

ranges.en: Rabbi Akiva holds that surplus from a wife's handiwork belongs to her, not to her husband.

Rav Pappa says a found object is like surplus gained through extraordinary effort, so it falls under the same dispute.
Rav Pappa and Ravina ask the status of earnings from two or three simultaneous tasks; the dilemma stays unresolved.

Rav Ashi replies that a wife is considered his own self, so the husband is humiliated, unlike distant relatives.
Mishna on a father-in-law's dowry pledge to a son-in-law who dies, and the appraisal and sums a wife brings.

66b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna's rule: the second son-in-law pledges one-fifth less, matching the real value of the dowry.

Are the examples in the mishna's first clause not the same case, so why repeat them?
The tanna gives large and small appraisals to show no halakhic difference, and both the husband's and wife's appraisals are covered.

What is this account?
Rav Ashi says it is for perfumes and cosmetics, and it applies only to women in Jerusalem.
Rav Ashi asks whether the ten dinars apply per hundred appraised or per hundred accepted, and how often; unresolved.
Rav Yehuda cites Nakdimon ben Guryon's daughter, whose four hundred gold coins were set aside for perfumes, and the Sages agreed.

Rabban Yohanan asks where the money of her father's household went.

Rabban Yohanan weeps and teaches that Israel rules when it does God's will, and is subject to animals of lowly nations when it does not.

ranges.en: Nakdimon ben Guryon's garments were spread under him for the poor to gather, showing abundant charity.

A second baraita, read by Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, seems to contradict the first tanna on the dinar case, so the objection stands.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's words apply to gold dinars where exchange is rare, so the baraita is read differently.
The difficulty remains: why does the baraita say like utensils rather than like its own gold utensils?
Read it as smashed gold fragments or granules, which are like ordinary utensils and not like gold dinars.
Rabbinic rulings on whether commodities like spices, camels, robes, sacks and pouches count as money for a wife's collection of her settlement.

Abaye infers from the mishna's final clause that the fifty dinars are provincial dinars.
What is the kis, the fund, in the mishna's phrase?

ranges.en: The orphan girl is married off before the orphan boy, since a woman's humiliation at remaining unmarried is greater.
A baraita on an orphan groom: the charity rents a house, furnishes it, and then provides a wife, derived from verses in Deuteronomy and Genesis.
A baraita: one must support the poor according to what they lack, even a horse and a runner, as Hillel did for a noble pauper.
A baraita reports that the Upper Galilee people bought a noble pauper a litra of meat every day.
If a litra of meat was the usual ration, what is novel about the incident?
Rav Huna says it was poultry or meat bought for a litra of coins, and Rav Ashi says it was a small village that slaughtered daily.
A pauper who dined on fatty meat and aged wine was given lentils by Rabbi Nehemya and died; Nehemya lamented.
Should Nehemya not have said woe to him who killed this one, rather than woe to this one?
The pauper was to blame, since his excessive indulgence left him unable to digest simple food.
Another pauper asked Rava what he normally ate, and he said a fattened hen and aged wine.
Rava asks whether he should burden the community; the pauper says he eats from the support of the Merciful One.
A verse in Psalms: God gives each person sustenance in its time, so the community is only God's agent.
Rava's sister brings him a fattened hen and aged wine, a providential reply to his claim, so he eats.
A baraita: a poor person who refuses charity is given a loan as a gift, and Rabbi Meir and the Sages differ on the order.
But does he not take the gift, so why give it?
Rava says the Sages begin by offering it as a gift, and if he refuses, it is given as a loan treated as a gift.
If a person has means but refuses support, they give it as a gift and then collect the debt from him.
But how can the fund collect, since he would not take the support knowing he would have to repay?
Rav Pappa says they collect from his estate only after his death.
Rabbi Shimon disagrees: the community need not help a wealthy refuser, and a poor refuser must give collateral so he feels he takes no handout.
The verse on ha'avet is read as one who lacks means and refuses charity: a loan first, then a gift.
The verse on ta'avitenu is read as one who has means: a gift, collected from his estate after death, per Rabbi Yehuda.
The Rabbis say a wealthy refuser is not engaged with at all.
How then does one uphold the double expression of the verse?
The Torah speaks in human language, so the double form carries no halakhic weight.
Mar Ukva secretly placed four dinars daily for a pauper, until one day the pauper came out to see his benefactors.
Mar Ukva and his wife fled into a furnace; his wife was spared burns because she gives food directly, which is more useful.
Why did they go to such extreme lengths to avoid being discovered?
Rav, Rav Huna bar Bizna and Rabbi Yohanan say one should deliver oneself into a furnace rather than embarrass a friend in public.
The conduct of Tamar, who sent the evidence rather than shame Judah publicly, supports the principle.
Mar Ukva's story continues: he gave away his wealth, distributing seven thousand dinars from the charity ledger to poor people.
Rabbi Ilai's teaching: a person should not give more than a fifth of his property, which contradicts the lavish giving.
Rabbi Abba slipped coins into a cloth and placed them behind his back to give to the poor without being seen.
Rabbi Hanina gave a pauper four dinars each eve of Shabbat, and the pauper's wife asked what he was doing; the passage is cut off.

ranges.en: Are the tablecloths silver or gold, so that the claimant is clearly not entitled to charity?
Rabbi Elazar says to appreciate the swindlers, since otherwise we would sin daily by not supporting the needy, as Deuteronomy 15:9 warns.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korha equates averting one's eyes from charity with idolatry, deriving it from the shared word beliyaal.
A baraita: one who falsely feigns blindness, bloating, or a crushed leg for charity will end up suffering that very ailment.
A mishna teaches that one is not required to sell his house and household utensils before receiving charity.
A baraita says one who used gold vessels should use silver, and silver should become copper, which seems to require selling possessions.
Rav Zevid: the sources differ, since one speaks of bed and table and the other of cups and plates.
Why are cups and plates exempt, and does the same reasoning not exempt a bed and table?
Rava son of Rabba: there is no difference, and only decorative luxuries, like a silver comb, must be sold.
Rav Pappa: the source requiring a sale refers to a person who has more than two hundred dinars and nonetheless collects charity.
A mishna: a minor orphan girl married off by her mother or brothers may claim a proper dowry, a tenth of the estate, upon majority.
Rabbi Yehuda says the second daughter gets what the first got, while the Rabbis say the court appraises the estate.
Shmuel says the court estimates the father's support for a daughter's dowry based on the father's standing.
A baraita says daughters are sustained from their father's property without speculating on what he would have given, which contradicts Shmuel.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak: the baraita refers to her own support, not to a dowry for the husband.
The baraita uses two terms, sustained and supported, which seems to mean two separate allowances, one for dowry.
Both refer to her own support: sustained is food and drink, supported is clothing and covering.
The mishna's Rabbis say that a poor or wealthy father may become otherwise, so the court appraises the estate.
What do poor and wealthy mean here, and does that imply a fixed dowry even if the father lost his wealth?
Poor and wealthy may mean in mindset, which still shows the court does not assess the father's intention.
This refutes Shmuel, but Shmuel holds the view of Rabbi Yehuda, who does assess the father's inclinations.
Why did Shmuel not simply say the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda?
Had he said so, one might limit it to a married daughter; stating only his acceptance teaches the reason, and the Rabbis dissent on assessment.
Rava tells Rav Hisda that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda, and Rav Hisda accepts the attribution.
Did Rava really say this, when a baraita has Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi giving a tenth, and Rava ruled accordingly?
Rava follows Rabbi Yehuda where the father can be assessed, and a tenth where he cannot.
Rav Adda bar Ahava's report of a twelfth given by Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi shows the ruling depends on assessing the father.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi rules that an orphan daughter takes a tenth, with the first taking a tenth, the second the remainder, and then all share equally.

68b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Why should the daughters divide the portions equally, since each takes her own dowry?
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi means: if they all marry together they divide equally; if at different times, each takes her share at marriage.
This supports Rav Mattana, who said that if all marry together they take one tenth, shared uniformly, then redistributed.
A baraita: daughters who mature or marry before maturity lose support, per Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar, and hire husbands to collect.
Rav Nahman reports from Rav Huna that the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.
Rava objects that a mishna on a married orphan girl suggests she forfeits the balance if she matured without protest.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi distinguishes a bride who protests from one who does not.
The resolution is reasonable, as a Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi view on the orphan's tenth follows the same logic.
If this is so, one statement of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi contradicts another, since it seems she loses her tenth at majority.
Ravina reports Rav Adda bar Ahava's view: maturity or marriage alone requires no protest, but both together require one.
Did Rava really say this, when earlier he objected to Rav Nahman's ruling that protest is needed?
Where she is still sustained by them, she is embarrassed to protest; where not, she has no reason to stay silent.
Rav Huna says that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi holds support is not like a marriage contract stipulation.
In what sense is support not like a marriage contract stipulation, and what is being taught?
Daily cases show the court seizes liened property for support but not for maintenance, so no special teaching is needed.
Support may be collected from movable estate property, while a marriage contract stipulation may be collected only from real estate.
A baraita has Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi allowing collection from both real estate and movables, so the explanation fails.
What then does the statement that support is not like a stipulation actually mean?
Its implication: a father cannot abrogate his daughters' support by will, since support is an ordinance on the father or heirs.

69a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav's letter asks whether brothers' mortgaged or sold property can be seized for the daughters' dowries.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi says the court seizes property for dowry support, whether sold or pledged, but not for sustenance.
Why did Rav use an ambiguous term rather than specifying sold or pledged?
Rav was uncertain about both cases, so he wrote in a way that yields a full answer either way.
Rabbi Yohanan rules that neither sold nor assigned property is seized for support or sustenance.
Did Rabbi Yohanan not hear Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's ruling, or did he hear and reject it?
A dispute among amoraim about a second daughter who did not collect her tenth before the son died is brought as proof.
Rabbi Yohanan says the second daughter forfeited her tenth; Rabbi Hanina says liened property is seized for support, not sustenance.
If Rabbi Yohanan never heard the ruling, why did he not object to Rabbi Hanina?
He may not have heard it, and there the abundance in the house makes her indifferent to the tenth.
If she has a found object or independent wealth, why should she not also get her full dowry?
Abundance from the estate's own property matters; independent wealth outside the estate does not diminish her share.
Ameimar holds that a daughter is considered an inheritor with respect to her dowry support.
Rav Ashi challenges Ameimar: can an heir be removed by money, or does she insist on property in kind?
Rav Ashi holds that a daughter is legally a creditor of the inheritance, not an heir.
Rav Minyumi reports Ameimar retracted, since he did not object when the brothers offered money as a creditor's repayment.
Is the daughter a creditor of the father or of the brothers, and what practical difference does that make?
The difference concerns collecting intermediate land without an oath versus inferior land with an oath.
Ravina's division of the estate for Rav Ashi's daughter shows she was treated as the creditor of the sons, not of the father.
A series of incidents: Rav Nehemya's letter to Rabba bar Rav Huna, Rav Ashi's practice on rental income, and Rav Anan's letter to Rav Huna.
Rav Sheshet relays Rav Huna's sharp reply to Rav Anan, which Rav Sheshet is reluctant to repeat.
Rav Anan consults Mar Ukva about the offensive wording and the meaning of marzeiha; the passage continues onto the next daf.

69b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mar Ukva rebukes Rav Anan: Rav Huna was justly offended by a letter that presumes familiarity with him.
Jeremiah 16:5 explains that a marzeiha is a house of mourning.
Rabbi Abbahu derives from Job 29:25 that a mourner sits at the head.
The verse's word yenahem seems to mean comforting others, not the mourner.
Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak reads the unvocalized word as yinnahem, the mourner being comforted.
Mar Zutra derives the same from Amos 6:7, reading mirzah as bitter and flustered, so the mourner rules the visitors.
Rava rules that one collects from inheritors' real estate, not movables, for sustenance, marriage contract, or dowry support.
Mishna: a father's money placed with a third party for his daughter's field; Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei dispute her authority.
A Tosefta gives the same dispute, distinguishing when the appeal occurs, from betrothal or from marriage, and by adult or minor.
What is the practical difference between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yosei, given the Tosefta's cases?
The latter clause cannot be Rabbi Yosei's, since his view on sale is already stated in the first clause.
Rather, the latter clause is Rabbi Meir's, and the mishna is incomplete; the dispute concerns an adult woman between betrothal and marriage.
Rav Yehuda, citing Shmuel, rules like Rabbi Yosei, while Rava, citing Rav Nahman, rules like Rabbi Meir.
Ilfa, passed over for the yeshiva head, hangs himself from a ship's mast, vowing to resolve any baraita from Rabbi Hiyya's school by a mishna.
A Tosefta: a deathbed instruction to give a son a shekel weekly is applied by the court within the father's intent, and inheritance intact.
In accordance with whose opinion is this baraita?

70a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Ilfa's answer: the mishna follows Rabbi Meir, who holds it is a mitzva to fulfill the instructions of the dead.
Rav Hisda cites Mar Ukva: the court gives sons all they need, whether the father said give a shekel or not more than a shekel.
How can the father's words be disregarded, given Rabbi Meir's principle that the dead's wishes must be fulfilled?
That principle applies to other matters; here the father's limit was meant to encourage thrift, and his children's welfare is preferred.
A mishna in Gittin: children's acquisitions and sales are valid for movables but not for real estate.
Rafram limits this to cases without a guardian; where a guardian exists, even movable transactions are void.
From where does one know this, and perhaps the rule applies only where a third party is present?
Had that been meant, the mishna would say so; hence a minor cannot transact even real estate generally.
Chapter-ending formula, followed by the next mishna on a husband's vow prohibiting his wife from benefit.
Mishna: a husband's vows against his wife's benefit require support by a trustee up to thirty days, otherwise divorce, with Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei giving differing periods.
If he is already obligated to support her under the marriage contract, how can he vow to remove that obligation?
A mishna on a wife's konam vow shows one cannot remove a prior obligation by vow, so the husband likewise cannot.
Rather, he can tell her to support herself from her own earnings, so the vow is effective within that framework.

70b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If the wife can say she will neither be supported nor work, why does a konam vow not require nullification by him?
Rather, the mishna concerns a husband who explicitly tells her to spend her own earnings on her support.
If he supports her by letting her use her earnings, why does she need a trustee at all?
Rav Ashi: her earnings cover major needs but not minor ones, so a trustee supplies the balance.
What are the minor needs, and if she is accustomed to them, why would she need a trustee?
She was used to such provisions at her father's house, accepted a lower standard, and now that he vowed she wants her old standard back.
What is different about the thirty-day period in the mishna?
Up to thirty days people do not hear of her, so the arrangement is not demeaning; longer, it becomes known and demeaning.
Alternatively, the vow was made while she was betrothed and the marriage time had arrived, so she may eat from his property.
If so, what is the difference between thirty days and longer?
Within thirty days the trustee acts effectively; longer, he neglects her until she can no longer bear it.
Alternatively, she was betrothed when he vowed and later married him, after which she may still be entitled to ask for divorce.
Is the rule for blemishes, where either party may demand divorce, applicable to sustenance too?
Rather, the case is as first answered: he told her to support herself, or the vow was taken during betrothal.
Mishna: if the vow lasts up to thirty days he must appoint a trustee to support his wife.
Does a trustee not perform the husband's agency, so that the vow forbidding benefit would apply to the trustee's support?
Rav Huna: the trustee is not an appointed agent; the husband only said whoever supports my wife will not lose out.
When a husband says this, is the one who responds not performing the husband's agency?
A mishna on a man in a pit who asked that whoever hears his voice write a divorce shows those who hear act as his agents.
The comparison fails: there he commanded that a bill be written, here he merely said whoever supports her will not lose out.
Rabbi Ami: on Shabbat fire, one may say whoever extinguishes it will not lose out, which seems to contradict the distinction.
The fire case serves only to exclude other Shabbat prohibitions, not to create an agency.
Rabba cites a mishna: a man vowed off from benefit may use a storekeeper's hint, but not say whoever sustains him will not lose out, which would appoint an agent.
The tanna speaks in the style of it is not necessary, and the storekeeper is not an agent, since no explicit command was given.
The mishna's case restated: one under a benefit vow may use a storekeeper, a worker, or a gift or ownerless objects; Rabbi Yosei prohibits the last.
What is the reason for Rabbi Yosei's ruling, and is it a rabbinic decree?

Rav Minyumi son of Rav Naḥumi replies the halakha follows Abaye, but asks for Rav Yosef's reasoning.
Rav Yosef searched the mishnayot and found a baraita supporting his view.
A baraita says a yavam who borrowed from his brother must have the debt appropriated and buy land for the widow's contract.
Abaye suggests the baraita only gives good advice, since they did what was good for him.
Rav Yosef replies that the wording 'one appropriates' shows a binding obligation, not advice.
Rav Minyumi reports Rav Yosef's view and Rav Naḥman's ruling that the baraita is not a mishnah and carries no authority.
Why is the baraita rejected? Perhaps it follows Rabbi Meir, who holds that movable property is mortgaged to a marriage contract.
The real reason is that the husband tells the yevama she is not his litigant, so she cannot claim the debt.

ranges.en: Perhaps the baraita reflects Rabbi Natan's view rather than being corrupt.
A baraita of Rabbi Natan derives from a verse that the borrower pays the lender of his creditor, which may explain Rav Yosef's baraita.
No tanna holds both stringencies for a marriage contract, so the baraita must follow Rabbi Meir or Rabbi Natan and is rejected.
Rava explains that this is what Abaye meant when he called the baraita not a mishnah, though he initially did not know why.
A similar case: a yavam's brother wants a bill of divorce, and the man offers to share the property, fearing it will be retracted.
Rav Dimi reports Rabbi Yoḥanan's rule that a cow sold for pulling after thirty days is acquired by the pulling, and Mar bar Rav Ashi distinguishes.
Mar bar Rav Ashi explains the difference: the seller controls the cow now, but the yavam cannot yet divide property that is not his.
If Ravin reports Rabbi Yoḥanan holds the cow is not acquired, how does this fit his ruling?
The cases differ: the cow sale is valid only if he said to acquire it from now, so the acquisition takes effect retroactively.
What is the halakha if the yavam performs levirate marriage and afterward divides the property, as asked of Ulla?
Ulla replies that he has done nothing.
What is the halakha if he divides the property and afterward performs levirate marriage?
Ulla again replies that he has done nothing.
Rav Sheshet objects that the first answer already implies the second is of no consequence, so the question need not be asked.
The Gemara answers that the two questions were asked on separate occasions, so Ulla answered each one.
Reish Lakish's ruling, conveyed by Ravin, is that in either order he has done nothing, and that is the practical halakha.
The Rabbis say attached produce is the yavam's, as the mishnah states.
Why is attached produce his, when all his property guarantees her marriage contract?
Reish Lakish says the text should be emended to teach that attached produce is hers.
The mishnah teaches that once he marries her she is like his other wife.
With regard to what halakha was this stated?
Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina says it teaches that he divorces her by a bill and may remarry her afterward.
This is obvious, so what could be the point of this clarification?
It is needed lest one think that the first levirate bond requires ḥalitza too, so the tanna teaches a bill of divorce suffices.
It is obvious that he may remarry her if they both choose to do so.

ranges.en: Lest one think the prohibition on a brother's wife returns after the levirate act, the tanna teaches it no longer applies at all.

The mishnah teaches that after levirate marriage she is his wife in all respects, except that her contract is on the first husband's property.
What is the reason for this rule?
Heaven gave her to him, so he relies on his brother's contract, and if none exists he still owes her one so she is not cheap in his eyes.
The yavam may not tell her here is your contract; all his property is mortgaged for it, as the mishnah rules.
What is the point of the phrase 'and similarly' if the halakha is identical in both cases?
It is needed lest one think the full lien applies only to a yevama, not a wife whose contract already relied on his property.
If he divorced her, she has only her marriage contract and no lien remains on the property.
The mishnah's wording implies that without divorce the property stays liable, following Rabbi Abba's view.
If he remarried her, she is like all women and has only her marriage contract.
Why emphasize remarriage on the first contract for a yevama, since the same rule is already taught elsewhere?
The yevama's contract was written by his brother, so the case is needed to show no new contract is required on remarriage.
Rav Yehuda says contracts used to be large sums that men could not pay, until Shimon ben Shataḥ made the property liable instead.
A baraita describes the earlier practice and later ordinances: the sum was placed in her father's house, then her husband's house.
Wealthy women fashioned their contract money into silver and gold vessels, while poor women made do with a small vessel.
Shimon ben Shataḥ instituted that the husband writes that all his property is liable, so he must think carefully before divorcing.
This marks the end of the chapter, which begins with the woman.

ranges.en: A husband who disclaims rights to his wife's property in her lifetime may still eat its produce, and he inherits if she dies first.
If he disclaims rights to the property and its produce, he may not eat the produce, but still inherits from her.
Rabbi Yehuda holds he always eats the produce of the produce until he disclaims that forever as well.
If he disclaims the property, its produce, and its produce's produce for life and death, he neither eats nor inherits.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says he inherits, since a stipulation against the Torah's law is void.
Rabbi Ḥiyya's baraita teaches that the disclaimer applies when said verbally to one's wife, not only in writing.
Why is the disclaimer effective at all, given a baraita holding that a verbal waiver of rights to shared property has no effect?
The mishnah refers to a betrothed wife, since he could waive a future inheritance; Rava holds one may waive a Sages' ordinance for his own benefit.
What is meant by such as this one?
Rav Huna quotes Rav that a wife may opt out of maintenance in exchange for her earnings, a Sages' ordinance for her benefit.
If Rava allows waiving a Sages' ordinance, why did Rabbi Yannai need to limit the rule to a betrothed woman?
Abaye says the husband's rights equal the wife's in a married woman's property; Rava says his rights exceed hers, which matters for a yavam.
A dilemma: if a husband disclaims rights and then the property is formally acquired from him, is the acquisition effective?
Rav Yosef holds only the promise was acquired, Rav Naḥman holds the land itself was acquired, and Abaye finds Rav Yosef's view reasonable.

83b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: When one waits before objecting, the other has acquired the land itself, since he cannot retract at that late stage.
Ameimar rules that the acquisition of the land itself applies.
Rav Ashi asks Ameimar whether he means the immediate objector or the one who waits.
Ameimar replies he has not heard Abaye's explanation of Rav Yosef and does not distinguish the two cases.
If the husband retains his rights, why did he write a disclaimer, and why does the wife not say he removed himself from everything?
Abaye says a document is read narrowly, so the husband is assumed to relinquish only some of his rights.
Why not say the husband renounced only his rights to the produce, since a sale of land is a significant matter?
Abaye cites a proverb that a cucumber in hand is better than a gourd later, so present produce matters more to him.
Why not say he renounced only his rights to the inheritance?
Abaye says death is common while sale is not, and a person waives only uncommon matters; Rav Ashi gives wording-based reasons.
Rav Ashi explains the wording: 'your property' means during her life, so the disclaimer does not extend beyond her death.
Rabbi Yehuda holds the husband always eats the produce of the produce.
The Sages define produce and produce of produce, using land bought from sold produce as an example.
A dilemma about Rabbi Yehuda: is the phrase produce of produce alone effective, or must forever also be written?
If produce of produce alone were effective, writing forever would be unnecessary, so the word teaches it counts as forever.
If forever alone were required, the phrase produce of produce is needed, showing forever only covers produce of produce if both appear.
Both phrases are needed: each alone would leave a different category of produce unrelinquished.
If a husband disclaims 'your property or the produce of your produce', does that also cover the produce itself?
Obviously he has removed himself from everything, since otherwise there would be no produce of produce at all.
The same question arises in the mishnah, so the case must be one where he kept some produce to buy land.
The mishnah teaches that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds that even with a full disclaimer, the husband inherits.
Rav rules that the halakha follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's conclusion.
What does Rav mean by agreeing with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's conclusion but not his reasoning?
Rav holds the husband's inheritance is rabbinic, so a stipulation against it is void, and the Sages strengthened it beyond Torah law.

ranges.en: Does Rav really hold that a stipulation against Torah law is valid, given his own position on a fraud disclaimer?
Recalls the dispute between Rav and Shmuel on whether a buyer may waive a fraud claim against the seller.
Rav rules that the halakha follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's conclusion, though not his reasoning about inheritance.
If Rav's ruling follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's conclusion but not his reasoning, why not say the opposite?
Rav's restatement: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel voids only Torah-level stipulations, while Rav voids rabbinic ones too.
If Rav simply adds a detail to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's halakha, why does he need to state it separately?
Rav's final position: the husband's inheritance is rabbinic, yet a stipulation against it is void, since the Sages' enactments are binding.
Does Rav hold that inheritance is rabbinic, given a mishnah where Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Beroka requires a husband to return property in the Jubilee?
What does Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Beroka hold about inheritance, given the contradictions in his ruling?
Rav says Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Beroka holds inheritance is Torah law, and the case involves a wife bequeathing her family's graveyard.
What is the meaning of deducting the value of the property from the heirs?
It refers to the value of his wife's grave, since a husband must bury his wife, and a baraita on burial honor is cited.
Rav's statement does not show his own view; he was explaining Rabbi Yoḥanan ben Beroka's reasoning, which he does not share.
Mishnah: a man dies leaving a wife, creditors, and heirs, with a deposit or loan held by others, and the question is who receives it.
Rabbi Tarfon rules the deposit or loan goes to the weakest claimant, the one most in need.
Rabbi Akiva rules one is not merciful in judgment; the money goes to the heirs, who need no oath.
On detached produce, the first to seize it acquires it, and a dispute arises over any surplus.
Rabbi Tarfon holds the surplus goes to the weakest claimant.
Rabbi Akiva holds the surplus goes to the heirs, since heirs need no oath.
Why teach the halakha separately for a loan and a deposit, since either example would suffice?
Each case is needed: a loan could be taken as a special case of Rabbi Tarfon's view, and a deposit as one where Rabbi Akiva's applies.
Conversely, teaching only a deposit would leave the loan case open, so both examples are needed for the full ruling.
What is meant by 'to the weakest' in Rabbi Tarfon's ruling?
Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina says it means the weakest proof of debt; Rabbi Yoḥanan says it means the wife's marriage contract.
Rabbi Binyamin and Rabbi Elazar take the two views as a tannaitic dispute, one on proof, the other on the marriage contract.
The mishnah adds that detached produce left behind is subject to the same first-seizure rule.
Why does the mishnah specify the surplus for Rabbi Akiva, since he would give all the produce to the heirs?
Rabbi Akiva indeed holds the same for all detached produce; the mishnah specified the surplus because Rabbi Tarfon did.

ranges.en: Is a creditor's seizure of a debtor's assets wholly ineffective according to Rabbi Akiva, when others have a prior claim?
Rava reports Rav Naḥman: Rabbi Akiva accepts the seizure only if made while the debtor was alive, since after death the heirs take the assets.
Where was the produce placed according to Rabbi Tarfon, who holds the first to take possession acquires it?
Rav and Shmuel hold the rule applies only when the produce is in the public domain; Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish say an alley suffices.
Judges ruled like Rabbi Tarfon, and Reish Lakish reversed their decision, restoring the money to the heirs under Rabbi Akiva's view.
Rabbi Yoḥanan criticizes Reish Lakish for acting as if correcting a Torah-law ruling, since a court's error must be undone.
The Gemara proposes the dispute: whether an error on a matter found in the mishnah is revoked, which the Gemara then refutes.
The proposed explanation is refuted: all agree such an error is revoked, and the dispute concerns whether Rabbi Akiva's view follows against his teacher.
Alternatively, all agree Rabbi Akiva's view is followed against colleagues, and the dispute is whether Rabbi Tarfon was his teacher or colleague.
Alternatively, all agree Rabbi Tarfon was Rabbi Akiva's colleague, and the dispute is whether the halakha is settled or only leaned toward.
Rabbi Yoḥanan's relatives seized orphans' cow from an alley; Rabbi Yoḥanan approved, following Rabbi Tarfon.
Reish Lakish ordered the cow returned to the orphans, contrary to Rabbi Yoḥanan's ruling.
Rabbi Yoḥanan replies that he cannot dismiss the view of one whose stature matches his own.
A creditor seized an ox from an orphans' herdsman; Rav Naḥman rules the claimant may say he seized it while the debtor lived.
Did Reish Lakish not say that wandering livestock gives no presumption of ownership?
An ox is different, since it is handed to a shepherd and does not wander, so possessing it creates a presumption of ownership.
The prince's household seized an orphans' maidservant in an alley; Rabbi Abbahu says it was well done and the judges agree.
Rabbi Abba objects: they should not curry favor, since Reish Lakish reversed judges who followed Rabbi Tarfon.
Yeimar bar Ḥashu sent his agent to seize a dead debtor's boat, and the agent carried out the seizure.
Rav Pappa and Rav Huna object that seizing for one creditor harms others, citing Rabbi Yoḥanan's ruling against such seizure.
