ranges.en: The two Sages seized the boat together, each claiming all of it, though the seizure harms the other creditors.
Rav Pineḥas bar Ami objects that by Rav and Shmuel the seizure is valid only from a pile in the public domain, not a boat.
The Sages reply that they seized the boat from the middle of the river, which has the status of the public domain.
Rava rebukes them as unlawful from the start, and Rav Naḥman rules a seizure is valid only from a living debtor.
Avimi son of Rabbi Abbahu's agent paid his debts, and the creditors refused to return the document, claiming side debts.
Rabbi Abbahu says the creditors could have claimed side debts, so the agent cannot demand the money or the document.
What is the halakha on whether the agent must reimburse the one who appointed him for his loss?
Rav Ashi rules that if told to take the document first, the agent who paid first must reimburse; otherwise he does not.
The Gemara rejects Rav Ashi's ruling: in either instruction the agent must pay, since he was sent for the principal's benefit.
A woman holding a bag of documents was claimed by heirs, and she said the deceased owed her money during his lifetime.
Rav Naḥman rules that without witnesses of a claim during life, seizing after death is ineffective.
A woman was obliged to swear in Rava's court, and Rava reversed the oath onto the other party, since she was suspect.
Rav Pappa testifies he knows a document records a debt already paid, though he is the only witness.
Rava says one witness is nothing, even a master, since a judge needs certainty to rule.
Should Rav Pappa not be trusted like Rav Ḥisda's daughter, who is disqualified as a woman from testimony?
Rava replies he relied on Rav Ḥisda's daughter because he knows she is truthful, which he cannot say of Rav Pappa.
Rav Pappa says that if a judge is certain of a witness's word, the document may be torn on that basis.
How can a court tear a document on the word of one witness?
Rather, the document is weakened, so it cannot be used to claim payment without further proof.
A woman owed an oath in Rav Beivai bar Abaye's court asked for a document of rights before swearing, and he agreed.
Rav Pappi rebukes Rav Beivai, saying that someone from an unfortunate house speaks unfortunate things.
Rav Pappi says Rava held that judges' ratification written before witnesses verify signatures is invalid, so the document would appear false.
Rava's ruling is not accepted, because Rav Naḥman rules by a statement of Rabbi Meir.
Rav Naḥman reports Rabbi Meir's view that a divorce written with identical names is valid, while other documents need no such intent.
Rav Asi cites Rabbi Yoḥanan that a repaid document may not be reused for a new loan, since its lien is forgiven.

Rabbi Ami rules for the depositor: the household is not wealthy enough to own them, and the depositor gave a distinguishing mark.

Rav Naḥman rules for the depositor on the same grounds, with the same qualification about regular access to the place.
A man deposited silk with Rav Dimi, brother of Rav Safra, who died without instruction, and the case went before Rabbi Abba.

A verse teaches that a close neighbor is better than a distant brother, and if they are equal, the judges decide.
Rava reports Shmuel's rule that a creditor's forgiveness binds, and Rav Ḥiyya bar Avin's exception for a wife, since her husband shares her rights.

Rav Naḥman says no one can advise the daughter, so the claim stands.

ranges.en: The daughter forgave her father's debt on her mother's marriage contract, so she inherits it later and defeats the purchasers' claim.

At first he relied on a verse urging help to relatives; later he judged that an important person must avoid favoring family.

Ameimar holds that one liable for indirect damage must pay the note's full value, while others pay only the paper's value.
Rafram pressed Rav Ashi, who ruled as if he had damaged a beam, collecting the full debt value.
Ameimar reports Rav Ḥama on a debtor with land and money: creditors are paid in cash and the wife in land, by their respective laws.
If one plot can pay only one debt, it goes to the creditor, so creditors are not discouraged from lending.
Is it correct that Rav Ḥama reports Rava's ruling that a debtor with land must have the creditor sell the land himself?
The debtor tells the creditor to take payment from the land, and the court tells the creditor to sell it and collect.

The debtor had money but claimed it belonged to a gentile, and the court therefore forced him to sell land.

A baraita shows that compelled positive commandments, like the sukka, are enforced, so the debtor can be compelled to repay.

ranges.en: The court may strike a debtor repeatedly until he pays, since repaying a debt is a positive commandment.

Mishnah: a husband who makes his wife a storekeeper or steward may swear her at any time; Rabbi Eliezer extends it to household matters.

If the extension reading is right, a further oath adds little, so the Sages' objection suggests the ab initio reading.
The objection is refuted: a wife may say she cannot live with a husband who is so exacting, so no proof follows.

If the husband exempts her, her heirs, and those on her authority, he cannot swear them, but his heirs may swear her.

If the wife was exempted and left her husband's home or did not act as steward, heirs cannot swear her for past acts, only for future ones.
What is the purpose of the oath that prompts this condition in the marriage contract? Rav Yehuda, quoting Rav, begins to answer.

ranges.en: Rav Naḥman, citing Rabba bar Avuh, explains the mishna as dealing with a steward widow and with a widow who vitiates her ketubah

Rav Mattana disagrees: even between death and burial no oath may be imposed
The Neharde'a sages' rule on selling orphans' property for urgent needs supports Rav Mattana

A baraita version of Abba Shaul ben Imma Miriam's ruling is also transmitted, with the same strict conclusion
Rav Naḥman, citing Shmuel, rules that the halakha follows ben Imma Miriam

A dilemma: is a widow who says the ketubah is smaller than written treated like one who admits partial payment

Rava objects: saying I did not borrow is like saying I did not repay, so with proof of the loan full payment is due
The Gemara restates the ruling: where orphans say the father denied borrowing, collection is allowed even without oath
The mishna: one who collects her ketubah in the husband's absence can collect only by oath

Rav Sheshet objects: if this concerns an oath administered in a court matter, the mishna should say the court imposes it, not the heirs
Rav Sheshet reinterprets Rabbi Shimon as addressing a widow who did or did not become a steward after her husband died
Mishna on stewards: a steward appointed by the father swears on returning property, a court-appointed one does not; Abba Shaul reverses this

Abaye objects: on this reading Rabbi Shimon is the lenient one, so the phrase whenever she claims would be misplaced
Abaye's alternative: Rabbi Shimon's view concerns a different clause, about a husband who exempted her from vows and oaths
The mishna clause on wording that bars the husband and heirs from imposing vows or oaths is cited as the source for Abaye's reading
Rabbi Shimon's statement explained: the heirs may impose an oath on the widow whenever she claims her ketubah
Abaye explains: Rabbi Shimon follows Abba Shaul ben Imma Miriam, requiring an oath even after an exemption, while the Rabbis do not
Rav Pappa objects: this explains Rabbi Shimon's first clause but leaves his second clause about not claiming with nothing to teach
Rav Pappa's alternative: Rabbi Shimon is disputing Rabbi Eliezer and the Rabbis on oaths concerning her conduct as steward
Mishna opens a case: a woman produced a bill of divorce without the ketubah and demands payment of it

89a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The mishna's cases: a widow produces her ketubah without a get and both sides claim lost papers, and a creditor lacks a prosbol
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel: from the time of danger on, a widow collects without a get and a creditor without a prosbol, since such papers were destroyed
Inference from the mishna: a receipt must be written on repayment, since otherwise the widow could collect her ketubah twice
Rav rejects the inference: the mishna concerns a place where marriage contracts are not written, so double collection is impossible
Shmuel holds that the mishna applies even in a place where marriage contracts are written
According to Shmuel, does one write a receipt at all
Rav Anan reports Shmuel's explanation: the case depends on local custom, and whoever claims a document was or was not written must prove it
Rav retracts: with a bill of divorce she collects the principal, and any challenger may come forward to contest the ruling
The Gemara objects by quoting the mishna's lost-receipt cases, which seem to bar collection even on Shmuel's reading
Granted for Shmuel, the ruling is consistent, but on Rav's view why can the widow not still collect the surplus of the ketubah
Rav Yosef: the case is one where no witnesses to the divorce are present, so the husband can claim he never divorced her

89b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The husband can also claim that he divorced her and gave her the payment of her ketubah
From the mishna's last clause the Gemara asks whether witnesses to the divorce must be present, since otherwise she would have no proof
The whole mishna follows Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel with a missing phrase: when divorce witnesses are present she collects only the extra sum
From the time of danger on, even without producing a bill of divorce she collects the main sum, per Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
Rav Kahana and Rav Asi ask Rav: a widow from marriage collects with proof of death, so how do we rule out a prior divorce used to collect twice
Rav answers: she collects with witnesses to death only if she lived under her husband's authority throughout, showing no divorce
But perhaps he divorced her shortly before his death, unknown to anyone, so she could collect twice
That would be his own fault for failing to make the divorce known, so the concern need not be raised
The same question for a widow from betrothal: with witnesses to death, what prevents an earlier divorce from being used to collect twice
Where no other proof of earlier payment exists, a receipt must be written, since otherwise the widow could collect repeatedly
Mar the Elder asks Rav Ashi: where does a betrothed widow's ketubah come from, since the mishna may refer to a voluntarily written ketubah
The Gemara rejects that reading: the mishna's phrasing about the entire sum makes sense only for a written ketubah, so it proves nothing about betrothal
Rav Ḥiyya bar Avin's baraita, offered as proof: a betrothed husband does not mourn or defile himself for his wife, yet she collects her ketubah on his death
The Gemara refutes this proof: perhaps he wrote the ketubah voluntarily, so the rule need not be taught
Rav Naḥman challenges Rav: a bill of divorce yields the main sum, so repeated use is possible, and tearing it fails because she needs it
Rav Huna's solution: tear the bill of divorce and write on its back that it was torn only to prevent a second collection
Mishna: two divorces and two ketubot permit two collections; otherwise a remarried woman collects only the original ketubah, unless a new one was written
Which of two ketubot may she collect with when both exist, the larger sum or the earlier-dated one
The mishna seems to refute Rav Naḥman's rule, citing Shmuel, that a second document on the same deal voids the first
Rav Pappa defends Rav Naḥman: he concedes that a second document adding a new item shows intent to add, not to void
A baraita begins a case: she produces a bill of divorce, a ketubah, and witnesses to her husband's death

90a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Dating rule: an earlier-dated bill of divorce lets the wife collect both contracts; an earlier marriage contract means only one.
Mishnah: a minor's or convert's marriage contract stays valid after maturity or conversion, since he kept her as wife on those terms.
Rav Huna limits the wife's claim to the main sum; Rav Yehuda holds she also collects the additional sum written in the contract.
A baraita is cited against Rav Yehuda: additional sums are collected only if the minor or convert introduced them.
The Gemara argues the baraita refutes Rav Yehuda, since its continuation denies the additional sum, so his view is rejected.
Rav Yehuda was misled by the mishna's wording; it validates only the main sum set by the Sages, not the additional sum.
Chapter-closing formula, then the start of the next Mishnah.
Mishnah: when a husband with two wives dies, the first wife's claim, and her heirs', precedes the second's.
From the mishna's wording that the first wife precedes, one infers a second wife who seized property is not dispossessed.
The Gemara draws a rule: a later-dated creditor who collected first keeps what he collected.
Rejecting that rule: a later creditor who collected has not truly collected, so the property must be restored.
Asks what the mishna means by the first wife preceding, and whether it grants her complete priority.
Supports complete priority from a mishna on son and daughter inheritance, where the son fully precedes her.
Other scholars infer from the mishna's silence that a second wife who seized property can be dispossessed.
The Gemara states the opposite rule: a later creditor who collected has not collected, so it is taken back.
Rejecting that rule again: the later creditor keeps what he collected; the mishna's wording about heirs was incidental.

90b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Gemara notes the tanna also taught the first clause, then quotes the mishna case of a man marrying a first wife.
Three conclusions drawn from the mishna: the first wife's sons may claim her settlement, one settlement can be surplus, and it is not repossessed from liened property.
Asks the source for the first conclusion, and the Gemara responds that the wording of the mishna shows it.
Second conclusion: one marriage contract becomes surplus for the other, so the biblical inheritance shares are fulfilled.
Asks where the second conclusion comes from, answering from the mishna's omission of the surplus dinar.
Third conclusion: the marriage contract for male children cannot take property that was liened by a sale.
Reductio: if it could be repossessed from liened property, the first wife's sons could seize land the second's sons already hold.
Rav Ashi objects to two of the three conclusions and offers an alternative reading of the word precedes.
Objects to the alternative reading: the mishna would have no reason to mention the first wife's heirs unless it teaches something about them.
Rejects the second conclusion as well: one settlement need not be surplus for the other, and the case is one with an extra dinar.
The case of one wife dying in his life and one after is a dispute between tanna'im, as the Gemara states.
A baraita is cited, with ben Nanas holding the first wife's sons may claim their mother's settlement.
Rabbi Akiva holds the inheritance already passed to the second wife's sons, so the first wife's sons cannot claim.
Asks whether the two Sages actually disagree about whether the settlement counts as surplus from a debt-fulfilling estate.
Rabba reports that the Sages of Rav's school agreed on the basic case and disagreed only about surplus questions.
Lays out the two Sages' positions: ben Nanas says one contract is surplus for the other, Rabbi Akiva says it is not.
Rabba says everyone agrees a payment to a creditor counts as surplus, and the disagreement concerns marriage contracts.
Rav Yosef objects: if so, the baraita should have said surplus of a dinar, since that is the real point of dispute.
Rav Yosef explains that the Sages disagree on whether the marriage contract for male children applies when one wife died first.
Cites a parallel baraita of other tanna'im debating the same point, with Rabbi Shimon's view on surplus of a dinar.
Asks whether these tanna'im likewise disagree about whether the first wife's sons may collect when one wife died earlier.
Rejects that reading: all agree the sons of the first wife may collect their mother's marriage contract for male children.

91a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The first tanna holds a dinar surplus must be real estate, while Rabbi Shimon accepts movable property as surplus too.
Objects to that reading: the mishna has Rabbi Shimon requiring a dinar surplus in land, so he cannot accept movables.
Alternative reading: the dispute concerns a dinar of liened property, which the first tanna rejects and Rabbi Shimon accepts.
Objects that the baraita would have phrased Rabbi Shimon's view as since there is a surplus, not as if there is one.
Another reading: the dispute concerns a surplus under a dinar, which the first tanna rejects and Rabbi Shimon accepts.
Objects: Rabbi Shimon says a dinar surplus and not less, and reversing the first tanna would conflict with the mishna.
Resolves the matter: the dispute follows the first two readings, and the first tanna's view is reversed accordingly.
Mar Zutra, citing Rav Pappa, rules that the first wife's sons collect and that one marriage contract is surplus for the other.
Asks why Mar Zutra needed to state both halakhot, since each alone would imply a different condition.
Suggests that had he taught only the surplus point, the sons' claim would be understood from the same rule.
Explains that each teaching is needed: one applies to a daughter with no inheritance share, the other to a son who could cause quarrels.
Mishna: when two wives died and the husband followed, the estate divides equally unless a dinar surplus exists, then each collects.
The orphans cannot inflate the valuation of property by a dinar; the court appraises it, and only actual property counts.
Rabbi Shimon says movables count for nothing, and a surplus of land exceeding both contracts by a dinar is required.
A baraita cites a case with contracts of one thousand and five hundred dinars, showing the same surplus rule.
Asks what the halakha is when the estate depreciates after the death or appreciates after it, before the sons divide.
Brings a case from the house of bar Tzartzur, where the estate appreciated, as a possible answer to the question.
Rav Amram rules that the sons of the more valuable contract must appease the others, and threatens them when they refuse.
Rav Nahman rules that just as the halakha holds for abundant property that depreciated, the same holds for property that appreciated.

91b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Heirs acquire rights based on the estate's value at their father's death, and a mnemonic then lists the related halakhot.
Case: a creditor repossesses one of two mansions bought from a debtor, and the purchaser offers a thousand dinars to settle.
Rami bar Hama proposes the case matches the mishna about orphans inflating a property's value, and so the market value governs.
Rava objects: the orphans in the mishna would lose money by inflated valuation, but here the creditor loses nothing by accepting.
Asks what amount the document authorizing repossession of liened property should state, given the purchaser paid half.
Ravina says one thousand, Rav Avira says five hundred; the halakha follows Rav Avira, so the document states five hundred.
Second case: a creditor repossesses one of two small tracts bought for fifty each, and the purchaser offers one hundred dinars.
Rav Yosef proposes this case matches the mishna about orphans inflating a property's value, so the court would not accept it.
Abaye objects: the orphans in the mishna lose by inflation, whereas the creditor here loses nothing by taking the money.
Asks what amount the authorization document should state for the second case, given the purchaser's payment.
Ravina says one hundred, Rav Avira says fifty; the halakha follows Rav Avira, so the document states fifty dinars.
Third case: a debtor's orphans pay part of the debt on a land tract, and the creditor repossesses it again for the remainder.
Abaye rules that the orphans' payment was a mitzva but did not cancel the lien, so the creditor may repossess lawfully.
Qualifies the ruling: only where the orphans did not say the payment was for the tract, since such a statement removes the creditor's claim.
Fourth case: a man sells his right to his mother's marriage contract, promising not to object if she later contests the sale.
Rami bar Hama proposes that the son stands in his mother's place as her proxy and so may object to the sale.
Rava objects: though he did not guarantee against his mother's objection, he guaranteed against his own, so he cannot renege.
Rami bar Hama relates a similar case: a field sold without guarantee, then sold back with a guarantee against repossession.

92a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: When Reuven's creditor repossesses the field from the buyer, Shimon must compensate Reuven, since Shimon sold it with a guarantee.
Rava objects: Shimon guaranteed against general claims, but did he also guarantee against the buyer's own creditors?
Rava concedes to Rami bar Hama in a case where the field was inherited, sold without guarantee, and bought back with one.
Asks the reason for this ruling.
Ya'akov's creditor is like any creditor of a previous owner, unlike Reuven's own creditor, so Shimon bears the compensation.
Rami bar Hama's case: Shimon never paid for the field, set its value as a loan, and then appeased Reuven's creditor with money.
Ruling: Reuven's sons may demand payment from Shimon, since orphans' movable property cannot be liened to a creditor.
Rava says Shimon, if clever, should pay the orphans with real estate, which then lets him recover from them, per Rav Nachman.
Rav Nachman, citing Rabba bar Avuh, holds that a creditor of the father may seize land the orphans collected for the debt.
Rabba's case: Reuven sold all his fields, Shimon sold one to Levi, and Reuven's creditor may collect from either buyer.
Qualifies Rabba: this holds only if the land sold was intermediate quality, and only if no equivalent intermediate land was left.

92b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If Levi left similar intermediate land with Shimon, he can tell the creditor he left a place to collect, so the creditor goes to Shimon.
Abaye rules that with a guarantee, Reuven must help Shimon forestall the repossession, since whatever the creditor takes returns to Reuven.
Another view: even without a guarantee, Reuven joins in forestalling the repossession, to avoid Shimon's grievance against him.
Abaye's second case: Reuven sold without guarantee and it emerged that he had sold the field to someone else earlier.

93a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Before taking possession Shimon may renege on a no-guarantee purchase; after possession he cannot, since he accepted the risk.
Another view: even with a guarantee, Shimon cannot demand an immediate refund merely because of disputants.
Mishna: three wives with contracts of one, two and three hundred share the estate equally if it is only one hundred dinars.
Mishna continues with the amounts for estates of two and three hundred, and the same method for partners who pooled money.
Asks why the one-hundred wife takes fifty of two hundred, since her claim covers only the first hundred shared three ways.
Shmuel: the two-hundred wife writes that she has no dealings over the first hundred, leaving two claimants to share it equally.
Asks why the three-hundred wife does not take one hundred, since the two-hundred wife withdrew from the first hundred.
She withdrew only from litigation with the one-hundred wife, so she keeps her claim to the first hundred against the three-hundred wife.
Mishna case of three hundred dinars: fifty, one hundred and one hundred fifty, the three shares of the estate.
Asks why the two-hundred wife gets one hundred, not seventy-five, given her agreement not to litigate.
Shmuel: the three-hundred wife writes that she has no dealings over the first hundred, so the two-hundred wife gets a full hundred.
Rav Yaakov of Nehar Pekod, citing Ravina, says the mishna concerns estate income paid in installments, not a waiver.
Each clause describes two seizures of property, one installment at seventy-five and another at larger sums, shared accordingly.
A baraita gives Rabbi Natan's view on these women, and Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi disagrees, saying they divide the estate equally.
Shmuel's case of two partners who pooled one hundred and two hundred dinars, with the same division logic as the mishna.

93b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rabba: Shmuel's rule that earnings are split equally holds only when the ox was bought and used for plowing, not for slaughter.
Rav Hamnuna: even when the ox bought for plowing was used for slaughter, the earnings are still divided equally.
Objects from a tosefta that divides equally with unequal investments, which conclusively refutes Rabba unless it means plowing only.
Asks what the tosefta holds for an ox bought for plowing and used for slaughter, given its later clause on mixed oxen.
The tosefta should distinguish the cases; indeed it does, since slaughter-use ox partnerships are treated like mixed oxen, divided by investment.
Brings a proof from the mishna on three partners in a purse, dividing by investment after a loss or profit.
Poses a difficulty for Shmuel: the mishna's loss and profit mean actual loss and profit, divided proportionally, not equally.
Rav Nachman, citing Rabba bar Avuh, explains the mishna's gains and losses as changes in coin value, so Shmuel's view stands.
Mishna: four wives marry in sequence; each takes an oath to the next, except the last, and same-day contracts divide equally.
Asks on what point the first tanna and ben Nanas disagree; Shmuel's answer then follows.

94a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Case: a husband's field is found to be stolen, so repossession threatens an earlier wife, paralleling a later creditor who collected first.
The first tanna says what a creditor collected is not fully his, while ben Nanas says it is; this bears on the fourth wife's oath.
Rav Nachman, citing Rabba bar Avuh: all agree a later creditor's collection is reversible; they dispute whether to fear depletion of the field.
Ben Nanas holds we fear the fourth wife will deplete the field, so she takes an oath; the first tanna disagrees and sees no such risk.
Abaye the Elder rules that adult orphans are not aware of their parents' affairs, so anyone collecting from the estate must swear.
The first tanna rejects Abaye the Elder's ruling, so the fourth wife takes no oath; ben Nanas accepts it and requires one.
Rav Huna: when one of two brothers or partners loses a case, the other cannot disclaim it, since the one who appeared acted as agent.
Rav Nachman is asked about the halakha in Rav Huna's case, where only one of two brothers or partners attends court.
Rav Nachman cites the mishna's oaths: the second wife acts as agent for the third, which suggests the same agency for brothers or partners.
Objects that the analogy fails: an oath to one wife equals one to a hundred, but a second brother could say he would have argued better.
The doubt about the second partner counts only if he is out of town; if he is in town he should come to court to join.
Two deeds dated the same day: Rav says the item is divided between the claimants, while Shmuel says the judges decide at their discretion.
Asks whether Rav's ruling follows Rabbi Meir, who holds that signing witnesses effect the transaction, since no exact time was noted.

94b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Shmuel rules like Rabbi Elazar: delivery of the document effects the transaction, so the earlier recipient keeps the property.
Everyone follows Rabbi Elazar; Rav and Shmuel actually differ on whether to divide or leave the doubt to the judges' discretion.
Objects: Rav follows Rabbi Elazar on divorce documents, so the dispute is not so; a baraita divides equally, which refutes Shmuel.
Shmuel's view stands: the baraita follows Rabbi Meir, and the dispute with Rabbi Elazar concerns money of uncertain ownership.
Rami bar Hama's mother wrote two deeds on one day; Rav Sheshet awarded Rami, Rav Nachman awarded Mar Ukva.
Each asks the other why he ruled as he did.
Rav Nachman: hours aren't recorded locally, so timing doesn't matter; he ruled at judicial discretion, which Sheshet is not entitled to exercise.
Two deeds for the same field, one dated the fifth of Nisan and one just in Nisan; Rav Yosef awards it to the specifically dated one.
The other claimant objects that he should not lose, since his deed might have been written earlier.
Rav Yosef replies that his undated deed is at a disadvantage, since nothing shows it was from the twenty-ninth of Nisan.
The man asks Rav Yosef to write him a document, requesting that his own deed be recorded with a date.

95a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav Yosef: a purchaser can argue the earlier-dated deed is valid, so the field rightly belongs to the first buyer, not the other.
Asks what the remedy is; the answer is that deed holders authorize each other to repossess liened property.
Mishna: a husband's sale is liened to a first wife's claim; wives and the purchaser repossess in turn until they reach a compromise.
Objects with a baraita that a declaration of no involvement has no legal effect, and that a wife may later claim she acted only to please her husband.
Rabbi Zeira, citing Rav Chisda: the two mishnayot follow different tannaim, Rabbi Meir here and Rabbi Yehuda in Gittin.
A baraita: a wife who signed the second sale loses her settlement, per Rabbi Meir, while Rabbi Yehuda lets her claim she acted to please him.
Asks whether Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi would cite the same anonymous mishna as Rabbi Meir here and as Rabbi Yehuda there.
Rav Pappa and Rav Ashi answer: a divorcee's note binds her, and for Rabbi Meir the wife's claim fails only when there are two purchasers.
Mishna in Gittin: no repossession of liened property sold to a third party while unsold property remains, even if inferior.
Raises a dilemma: if the unsold property became blighted, may the creditor repossess liened property sold to a third party?
Resolves the dilemma with the baraita of the wife who signed the second sale, arguing that if repossession were allowed she could collect from the first buyer.
Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: Rabbi Meir means she lost only her claim against the second purchaser, not the first.
Rava rejects that: she lost her rights entirely, and a baraita shows a creditor's note to the second buyer leaves the first buyer unaffected.
The Gemara rejects using the case: the wife there caused her own loss by signing, so it does not decide a blighted field.
Rav Yeimar speaks to Rav Ashi; the passage here is only an opening remark that continues beyond this page.

95b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Objects that a court lets creditors collect from liened property when unsold property has spoiled, as with an aging orchard pledged for ten years.
The purchasers brought the loss on themselves, since they knew orchards age and could have expected the creditor to repossess.
The halakha: if unsold property becomes blighted, the creditor may repossess liened property sold to a third party.
Abaye's ruling: a husband who takes a bequest to a woman before marriage becomes a purchaser, and the later beneficiary gets nothing.
Asks in accordance with whose opinion Abaye ruled.
A baraita: a second beneficiary can reclaim only what the first left in hand, per Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, whom Abaye followed.
Objects that Abaye himself condemned advising a sale under Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's ruling to defeat the second beneficiary.
Abaye meant only that a woman who married by ordinary course should not be blamed for the property passing to her husband.
Abaye's further ruling: for a married woman, the husband repossesses from purchasers, and the chain of claims ends with the purchaser.
Asks how this case differs from the mishna's cycle of repossession ending in a compromise between the parties.
Rafram objects to Rav Ashi that Abaye's own earlier ruling makes the husband a purchaser, so the later purchaser cannot receive.
Rav Ashi: the difference is whether the bequest was made when she was unmarried or already married, so the husband gets nothing.
The mishna's phrase on creditors and female creditors is explained by a baraita on repeated repossession between two purchasers.
Chapter end and the next mishna: a widow is sustained from orphans' property, while her heirs must bury her from her marriage contract.
Raises a dilemma whether the mishna's wording a widow is sustained means all widows, or only those whose contracts provide sustenance.

96a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Brings a proof from Shmuel's ruling that a widow keeps found objects, which depends on whether the mishna says she is sustained by the heirs.
Asks what the reason is for Shmuel's ruling about a widow's found property.
The Sages gave the found property to the husband so the wife avoids his enmity; the heirs may bear enmity instead.
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina: a widow does all wifely tasks for the heirs except filling the cup, making the bed and washing his body.
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi: a student does for his teacher all tasks a slave does, except untying the teacher's shoe.
Rava and Rav Ashi qualify this: the student may untie the shoe only where he is known or wears phylacteries, so no slave is suspected.
Rabbi Yochanan and Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak: withholding service from a student withholds kindness and removes fear of Heaven.
Rabbi Elazar, supported by a baraita: a widow who seized movable property for her sustenance keeps what she seized.
Rav Dimi reports that the Sages could not remove a saddlebag of coins that Rabbi Shabbtai's daughter-in-law seized for sustenance.
Ravina: the seizure stands only for sustenance; a seizure as payment of her marriage contract is removed from her.
Mar bar Rav Ashi objects: why should marriage-contract seizures differ from sustenance ones, since both are paid from real estate only?
Rav Yitzchak bar Naftali cites Rava in agreement with Ravina: movable property seized as marriage payment is removed from her.
Rabbi Yochanan, citing Rabbi Yosei ben Zimra: a widow who waits two or three years without claiming sustenance forfeits it.
Asks why the statement needs both two years and three years if the first already implies forfeiture.
Reconciled by the wealth of the widow, or by whether she is shameless or modest about claiming from the heirs.
Rava: the forfeiture applies only to past years; from now on she may demand sustenance from the heirs.
Rabbi Yochanan raises a dilemma: if orphans say they paid the widow and she denies it, who must bring proof?

96b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether the property is presumed in the orphans' possession, so the widow must prove her claim, or in hers, so they must.
Brings a baraita of Levi and then a tanna dispute on whether a widow must specify if she sold property for sustenance or marriage payment.
Asks whether the baraita's dispute is really about who must bear the burden of proof, given Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei.
Rejects that inference: Rabbi Yehuda may simply give advice to avoid suspicion of excess spending, so no burden-of-proof rule follows.
If the rule were derived from it, Rabbi Yochanan's dilemma could be resolved from the mishna, so that mishna and baraita give only advice.
Alternatively, everyone agrees the property is in the orphans' possession, and that is the reasoning of Rabbi Yosei.
Abaye the Elder explains Rabbi Yosei by a deathbed gift parable: the word give lets the creditor choose debt or gift.

97a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If a creditor takes the gift instead of the debt, his position is not improved; the widow likewise may decide later why she sold.
Asks how a widow sells property to earn her support.
Rav Huna says she sells once every twelve months and Rav Yehuda says every six months, with the buyer paying monthly.
A baraita is cited in accordance with each view: Rav Huna's twelve months, and Rav Yehuda's six months.
Ameimar rules by Rav Yehuda: the widow sells every six months, and the buyer pays monthly.
Rav Ashi asks Ameimar what he says about Rav Huna's view.
Ameimar replies that he has not heard it, meaning he does not hold by Rav Huna's view.
Students ask Rav Sheshet whether a widow who sold property for sustenance may later seize it back for her marriage contract.
Background: the dilemma arose from Rav Yosef's ruling that the orphans bear the guarantee on a widow's sales.
Asks whether, since the orphans guarantee the sale, the widow may seize the property, or the buyers may object she guaranteed her own acts.
Rav Sheshet cites a baraita: a widow sells for sustenance until only her marriage contract's value remains, implying she cannot later seize.
Rejects that proof: the baraita may only give advice to avoid calling her a retractor; the word relies then shows the intended rule.
Raises a dilemma: if a seller needed money for a purpose that never arose, is the sale reversed as an error?
Brings a proof: Rav Pappa returned land to a seller who no longer needed money for oxen.
Rejects that proof: Rav Pappa acted beyond the letter of the law, so the case proves nothing.
Brings a second proof: during a Neharde'a drought, sellers of mansions who no longer needed wheat got them back, per Rav Nachman.
The sale was made in error, since the grain ship was already near the bays when the mansions were sold.
Rami bar Shmuel objects to Rav Nachman: restoring sales makes buyers fearful, and Rav Nachman limits this to drought, noting Neharde'a has them often.
The halakha: if one sold property for a purpose and then did not need the money, the sale is reversed.
Mishna: a widow, whether from betrothal or from marriage, sells her husband's property only in court.
Rabbi Shimon: a widow from marriage may sell outside court, but one from betrothal may sell only in court, since she has no sustenance.
The Gemara explains: a widow from marriage may sell outside court because her sustenance is pressing, so she need not wait for a court.

97b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks the reason a widow from betrothal may sell outside court.
Ulla: the Sages enacted measures for women's desirability; Rabbi Yochanan: a husband will not let his wife be shamed in court.
Asks what practical difference lies between these two reasons.
The difference shows in a divorcee: on the desirability reason she needs it too, but on the other reason no one cares about her shame.
Objects: if the reason is shame, why must a divorcee sell in court, since she is not protected from shame?
The continuation follows Rabbi Shimon, who requires court sale for a marriage-contract sale, since a divorcee lacks sustenance.
Objects: the first clause already covered the divorcee's lack of sustenance, so the mishna need not repeat it.

ranges.en: Legumes bought for a sela or for a peruta cost the same per unit even in bulk; learn from this the proper reading of the mishna.

Rav Sheisha son of Rav Idi repeats that the ruling concerns small tracts of land that do not form one unit, so it is no proof.

ranges.en: Rava reports Rav Naḥman: an agent is like the judges, who act without personal benefit, excluding a widow who sells for herself.

No, everyone agrees that an error in a mishna matter is revoked; they differ only on the details of what happened.
Rav Yosef rules: when a widow sells property for support or her contract, the guarantee falls on the orphans, including when the court sells.
Isn't this obvious, since a widow sells her husband's estate, so the guarantee clearly rests on the orphans' property?
Rav Yosef needed to mention the rule for the court, since the widow case is clear; lest one think the court's sale differs.

ranges.en: Buyers at a court sale may assume no claim exists, but Rav Yosef teaches that the property guarantee still rests on the orphans, not the court.

Rav Ashi objects to Ameimar using the mishna on one-sixth error; Ameimar replies that the mishna's case involved an announcement.

Rather, the first clause concerns sales without announcement; Ameimar refers to items requiring announcement, and the mishna to items not requiring it.
Items not announced include slaves, movable property and contracts.

Slaves might flee if they hear of the sale, and movables and contracts might be stolen; alternatively Ameimar speaks of a time when announcements are made.
The Sages of Neharde'a: for head tax, child support and burial, the court sells orphans' property without announcement, since these needs are pressing.

Some students infer that Neharde'a's sages were all expert appraisers, so no announcements were needed.
Rav Yosef bar Minyumi: Rav Naḥman explained that buyers were called consumers of announced property, so decent people stopped announcing sales.

Rav Ḥisda said that Avimi said movable property is sold on a market day, when many buyers gather and prices are fair.

Rav Kahana held beer belonging to an orphan past the Festival, which was a precedent for delaying a sale for higher money income.
Ravina held wine belonging to his orphaned nephew and brought it to Sikhra with his own wine, as a further precedent.
Ravina asked Rav Ashi whether he may bring the orphan's wine along with his own or must wait for a better time to sell.
Rav Ashi: take his wine along too, since his is no better than yours, and selling yours that way shows it is the proper method.
Mishna: a minor married by her mother or brother who refuses marriage, an ailonit, a secondary forbidden relative, or a widow of a High Priest has no marriage contract, except in some cases.
Rav taught: a minor divorced with a bill of divorce gets no marriage contract, and a woman who refuses marriage gets none either.
Shmuel taught: a woman who refuses marriage gets no contract, but one divorced with a bill of divorce is entitled to it.
Shmuel is consistent with his reasoning, stated in his own words: refusal means no contract, while a divorce entitles her to it.
Shmuel adds: refusal does not disqualify her from the husband's brothers or from the priesthood, unlike divorce; and she need not wait three months before remarrying.

What new point is Shmuel teaching by stating all of this?

It was needed to state the three-month wait for a divorced woman, since the mishna did not teach that halakha.
A baraita on a minor girl's marriage: Rabbi Eliezer says it has no legal effect, while Rabbi Yehoshua says it has full effect except for leaving by refusal.

ranges.en: A baraita taught before Rav Naḥman: a licentious woman loses her extant worn clothing, which is the basis for the discussion.

The mishna continues: if the daughter marries, her husband supports her, and sensible men wrote explicit conditions limiting their obligation to the marriage.

Let us say Rabbi Yoḥanan follows Rabbi Yishmael that a self-accepted obligation binds, and Reish Lakish follows Ben Nannas?
On Ben Nannas's view everyone agrees that a plain written promise of one hundred dinars does not bind, so there is no real dispute.

ranges.en: Rabbi Yoḥanan follows Rabbi Yishmael simply, while Reish Lakish limits him to a guarantor, whose obligation is by Torah law.
Rav Giddel's ruling is restated: parents' agreed gifts for children's betrothal are acquired by words alone.
Rava explains Rav's ruling: it holds for a minor daughter, since the father benefits, and even for a grown woman because fathers transfer rights to each other.

Rav Ashi: they may not be written down.

The wife's daughter was present at the transaction and so it is effective for her, while the husbands' daughters, born later, were not present.
Were the husbands' daughters present too, and what circumstances would make that possible?

Being included in the court's stipulation makes them worse off, rather than more powerful?
Rather, the reason is that fathers' support obligations lead to a concern they gave their daughters money in advance, so they cannot repossess liened property.
Mishna: the first husband must bring the wife's daughter her sustenance where her mother lives; Rav Ḥisda: this shows a daughter lives with her mother after divorce.

ranges.en: What is the purpose of stating that the daughter goes to the place where her mother lives?

The mishna: two men obligated to support the girl may not jointly say they will be partners in her support; each fulfills his own obligation.
A man rented a millstone to another for grinding; the owner later became rich and bought a new mill and donkey, no longer needing the grinding.
The owner asks for money now, since he no longer needs the service; the renter says he agreed only to grind, not to pay money.

Rav Avira objects: the cases differ, since the girl has one stomach while the renter can grind for others as well as for the owner.
The rule applies only when the renter has no other grinding to do; if he does, he is forced to pay money, to avoid the conduct of Sodom.
Mishna: a widow who wants to stay in her husband's house cannot be forced to move to her father's house; the heirs must maintain her there.
Mishna: if she wants to live in her father's house, the heirs may condition support on her living with them, unless she is young and they are too.
A baraita: a widow who stays in her husband's house uses the property as she did in his lifetime, as stated in the marriage contract.
Rav Yosef taught that the contract says she resides in my house, not in my hut, so a too-small house does not oblige the heirs.
Rav Naḥman: orphans who sell a widow's living quarters have accomplished nothing, so the sale is invalid.
How is this different from Rabbi Asi's report that Rabbi Yoḥanan upheld orphans' preemptive sales of their father's property?
Orphans' sales of property reserved for daughters are not mortgaged during the father's life, but the widow's quarters are mortgaged to her in her husband's lifetime.
Abaye: by tradition, if a widow's quarters collapsed, the heirs need not rebuild them, since they must maintain her only in the mortgaged residence.
A baraita: heirs need not rebuild a collapsed widow's quarters, and they may refuse even if she offers to rebuild at her own cost.
Abaye's dilemma: if she repaired the house, is it treated as collapsed and rebuilt, or does her right last while it stands? The dilemma is left unresolved.

Why, if she lived there, should they not support her as they would in her husband's house?
This supports Rav Huna, who held that a house's blessing lies in the number of residents, so sharing a home lowers each person's cost.
Should they then support her at her father's house according to the blessing of the house, as if she lived with them?
Rav Huna: the Sages' language teaches blessing, wealth and healing; blessing refers to the blessing of the house, and the rest follows.
Wealth: a mishna on sellers of produce shows acquisition by pulling or measuring, and that a buyer may rent the place to secure ownership.
Healing: a mishna forbids chewing wheat and placing it on a wound on Passover, since it would leaven, showing chewed wheat heals wounds.
At the death of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, he asked his sons to honor their mother, keep his lamp and table ready, and mentioned his two servants.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's instruction to his sons: be careful with the honor of your mother.
Why would he need to say this, since honoring one's parents is required by Torah law?
She was their father's wife, not their mother, so he had to warn them to honor her as their stepmother.
A baraita: the extra et in honor your father and mother includes the father's wife and the mother's husband, and the extra vav includes the older brother.
That obligation to honor a stepmother applies only during the father's lifetime, not after his death, which is why Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi warned them.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi repeats: keep his lamp lit, his table set and his bed arranged in their usual places.
What is the reason for these requests?
Every Shabbat eve, Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi would come to his house as before, so he wanted everything set up as usual.
On one Shabbat eve a neighbor knocked; the maidservant said Rabbi was sitting, and he never came again, so as not to cast aspersions on earlier righteous people.
Rabbi repeats that Yosef Ḥeifani and Shimon Efrati served him in life and will serve him in death.
They understood he meant this world, but when they died before him they concluded he meant the World to Come, so people would not blame them.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi asked the Sages of Israel to enter, and told them not to eulogize him in the small towns.

ranges.en: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi instructs: reconvene the yeshiva after thirty days, Shimon is a Sage, Ḥanina bar Ḥama presides, and do not eulogize him in the towns.
The Gemara explains: the towns instruction was to spare people travel, but seeing crowds came anyway, so it was meant to secure a large honorable gathering.
Rabbi's reason for the thirty-day study resumption: he is no greater than Moses.
The verse on the thirty days of weeping for Moses is cited, and practice then shows mourning alternating with study for a year.
A Divine Voice declared that all present at Rabbi's funeral merit the World-to-Come, and that a launderer who grieved and died also does.
Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi said: my son Shimon is a Sage, and my son Gamliel should be the Nasi.

He meant that although Shimon is the greater Sage, Gamliel should be the Nasi.
