The verse: the kingdom went to Jehoram because he was the firstborn, showing the firstborn inherits the father's appointment.
Jehoram filled his fathers' place in ability, but Gamliel did not, so Rabbi specifically commanded that Gamliel nevertheless be appointed Nasi.
If Gamliel was unfit, why did Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi choose him?
Gamliel lacked his father's Torah wisdom but matched him in fear of sin, which made him fit to be Nasi.
Ḥanina bar Ḥama declined to preside because Rabbi Afes was older, so Afes presided, Ḥanina sat outside, and Levi studied with him outside.
When Rabbi Afes died, Ḥanina presided and Levi had no one to study with, so he went to Babylonia, as Rav was told.
How did Rav know it was Afes who died rather than Ḥanina, since Levi could have left either way?
Levi was subordinate to Afes and sat outside only out of deference to Ḥanina; alternatively, Rabbi's appointment of Ḥanina proves it was Afes who died.
But was Rabbi Ḥiyya present, and why did Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi not appoint him as head of the yeshiva?
Objection: Rabbi Ḥiyya said he saw Rabbi's grave and wept, which seems to show Ḥiyya was not dead before Rabbi.
Reverse the names: it was Rabbi who saw Rabbi Ḥiyya's grave.
Objection: Rabbi Ḥiyya said that on the day Rabbi died sanctity ceased, which conflicts with the reversal.
Reverse the names: Rabbi made that statement about Rabbi Ḥiyya.
Objection via a baraita: Rabbi Ḥiyya found Rabbi crying during his illness, though the signs of death are good or bad depending on how one dies.
Rabbi replied he was crying for the Torah and mitzvot he could no longer fulfill, which shows Ḥiyya was present at his death.
Either reverse the names so Rabbi visited Ḥiyya, or Ḥiyya was busy with mitzvot, so Rabbi did not hold him back by appointing him.
Ḥanina and Ḥiyya argued, and Ḥanina said he could rediscover the Torah through analysis if it were ever forgotten.
Ḥiyya replies he preserves the Torah by making flax nets, trapping deer for scrolls, and teaching children the Five Books and the six orders of the Mishna.
Rabbi praised Ḥiyya's deeds; Shimon and Yishmael asked whether anyone was greater, and Rabbi said such comparisons are not to be made.
Rabbi transmitted wisdom to his younger son Shimon and the procedures of the Nasi's office to Gamliel, urging Gamliel to rule firmly.
Is it proper to rule firmly, when the verse honors those who fear the Lord and Jehoshaphat showed affection to scholars?
Affection is shown in private and sternness in public, to keep the teacher's authority.
A baraita says Rabbi lay ill in Tzippori with a burial place in Beit She'arim, while another suggests he resided in Beit She'arim.
Rabbi resided in Beit She'arim, but when he fell ill they moved him to Tzippori.

104a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The Sages decreed a fast and prayed that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi would not die; anyone who said he had died would be stabbed.
Rabbi's maidservant, seeing his suffering, asked that the upper worlds prevail; then she threw a jug to distract the Sages, and he died.
Bar Kappara went to check, found Rabbi dead, and reported it in coded terms, since no one was to say he had died.
At his death Rabbi raised his ten fingers in prayer for peace in his repose, and a Divine Voice quoted the verse on resting in beds.
Why does the verse say they rest in their beds in the plural, when the phrasing began in the singular?
This supports Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Gamda: Rabbi Yosei ben Shaul taught that angels greet a righteous person who departs, and the righteous receive him in peace.
Rabbi Elazar taught that three groups of angels greet a righteous person's departure, while three groups of destroying angels greet the wicked.
Mishna: a widow in her father's house may collect her contract always while supported by heirs, but in her husband's house only twenty-five years; Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis differ.
Abaye asked Rav Yosef whether a poor woman spends her contract's value only after twenty-five years, while the wealthy Marta bat Baitos spends it sooner.
Rav Yosef: according to the camel is the load, so a wealthy woman with a larger contract spends more in the same time.
Dilemma: if benefit depends on years passed, should she forfeit the proportionate share of her contract, and it remains unresolved?
The Rabbis say: while in her husband's house she always collects, and while in her father's house only within the twenty-five years.
Abaye asked: if she came before sunset at the end of the period, she collects, but if after, she does not; does a brief moment waive her right?
Rav Yosef: the Sages' measures are fixed, so exceeding a limit has no effect; a bath of forty se'a works, and one missing a kortov fails.
Rav Yehuda said Rav: Rabbi Yishmael testified in his father Rabbi Yosei's name that if she holds the contract, she collects forever, while Rabbi Elazar limits her to twenty-five years.
Rav Sheshet objects to Rabbi Yishmael from a Tosefta: a creditor may collect even after a long delay, and a widow with her contract should be likewise.
Rav Sheshet resolves it: in the Tosefta the creditor lacks the document, but the debtor admits the debt, so it proves nothing about widows.
Objection: Rabbi Ela's baraita says a divorcée is like a creditor and collects after a long time, which would show the rule for holders of contracts.
Here too the case is one where the debtor, the husband, admits the debt, even though she lacks the contract.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak reports Rav Yehuda bar Kaza's baraita from the school of bar Kaza: if the widow demanded her contract payment,

104b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: If she has the contract in hand, she is as at the start of her widowhood, and she collects her contract payment forever.
Rav Naḥman bar Rav Ḥisda asks Rav Naḥman bar Ya'akov whether Rabbi Meir's dispute applies when she holds the contract, and whose view is followed.
Rav Naḥman bar Ya'akov: the dispute applies only when she lacks the contract; with the contract in hand all agree she collects forever, and the Rabbis' view governs disputes.
Rav Dimi reports: Rabbi Shimon ben Pazi, citing Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi and bar Kappara, limits the waiver to the principal, not the additional sum.
Rabbi Abbahu cites Rabbi Yoḥanan, who extends the waiver to the additional sum, since stipulated additions count like the principal; Rav's view limits the waiver to the principal.
Rabbi Abba and Rav Huna exchange: Rabbi Abba admits he said Rav's view only to silence Rav Huna, showing he follows Rabbi Yoḥanan.
Rav Ḥiyya Arikha sustained his brother's widow in her father's house for twenty-five years, then she sued, and Rabba bar Sheila was asked to decide.
Rabba bar Sheila ruled that the embarrassment reason applies, so he must pay the contract; Rav Ḥiyya refused, and Rava upheld the faulty authorization to seize property.
The widow argues that even if the authorization yields no earlier produce, she should collect from the announcement period until now.
Rava: that applies only where no error was written; where the authorization contains an error, she has no right to the produce at all.
She objects: Rava himself said omitting a guarantee clause is a scribal error treated as if written, so the same should hold here.
Rava replies: here the omission was not a scribal error, since Rabba bar Sheila himself erred, and the authorization must name the husband's property to avoid losses.

Mishna: two judges, Admon and Ḥanan ben Avishalom, issued decrees in Jerusalem; Ḥanan states two disputed matters and Admon seven, such as a wife's claim for sustenance when her husband has gone overseas.

105a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: the widow takes an oath at the end, not at the outset, per Ḥanan; the sons of the High Priests say both times, and Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai agrees with Ḥanan.
Objection from a baraita: three judges in Jerusalem adjudicated theft cases, which conflicts with the mishna's two judges who issued decrees.
The count is no difficulty: the tanna mentions only judges relevant to the topic, not all of them.
But the difference between decrees and theft cases remains difficult.
Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak: the decrees concerned theft, as a baraita on a beast damaging a young plant shows, with set payments for plants of different ages.
Objection: another baraita lists three judges, Admon, Ḥanan, and Naḥum, which conflicts with the earlier baraita that omitted Naḥum.
Rav Pappa: the tanna is Rabbi Natan, who says Naḥum HaMadi also issued decrees, though the Sages did not agree with him.
Were there no more judges? Rabbi Oshaya said there were 394 courts in Jerusalem, with matching synagogues and study halls.
There were many judges, but the small number refers only to those who issued decrees.
Rav Yehuda said Rav Asi: those who issued decrees were paid ninety-nine maneh from the Temple chamber's collection.
What does 'if they did not wish' mean; does it imply the wicked took higher wages?
Rav Asi meant that if their wages were insufficient, they were supplemented even if they did not ask, so they could devote themselves to communal service.
The Sage Karna took an istera from each party before judging them.
How could he do so, since Exodus forbids a judge to take a bribe?
Objection: if the ban applies only where the judge might pervert justice, Karna's dual taking is fine; but a baraita says the verse forbids any bribe, even one that causes no perversion.
The ban concerns bribes; Karna took money as a salary, and a salary-taking judge's rulings are void, so he took compensation for lost work instead.
Is it permitted to take money for unemployment? A baraita calls a salary-taking judge ugly but says his rulings are valid; this seems to conflict with the mishna.
The ugliness applies when lost work is not evident; Karna's losses were evident, since he examined wine stores and was paid one dinar for leaving his work.
Rav Huna asked litigants to provide a water carrier so he could irrigate fields while judging; Rabbi Abbahu warned that bribes blind the eyes of the wise.
A baraita reasons a fortiori from the verse on bribes blinding the wise and perverting the righteous.
Are fools and the wicked fit to serve as judges, if a bribe blinds the wise and perverts the righteous?
Rather, even a very wise judge who takes a bribe will eventually lose his heart's clarity and turn foolish, and will pervert the words of the righteous.

105b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Even a completely righteous man who takes a bribe does not leave this world without losing his sound judgment.
Rav Naḥman bar Kohen reads Proverbs 29:4 homiletically: a judge who needs nothing establishes the land, while one who collects gifts like a priest overthrows it.
Rabba bar Rav Sheila: a judge who keeps borrowing without lending is disqualified, as if taking a salary; lending in return removes the problem.
But Rava borrowed from the house of bar Maryon even though they did not borrow from him, so is the rule not absolute?
Rava did so to raise their standing in the community, since he was wealthy and had no need to borrow.
Rava: a bribe draws the judge's thoughts toward the giver, and the word shoḥad reads as one mind; Rav Pappa says not to judge those one loves or hates.
Abaye: a Torah scholar is beloved in his town not for superiority but because he does not rebuke them in matters of heaven.
Rava: he once thought Meḥoza's residents loved him, but after judging he saw their feelings followed the outcome, so they must all love or all hate him.
A baraita on the verse 'you shall take no bribe' shows that even verbal favors, not just money, count as a bribe.
What are the circumstances of bribery by words?
Shmuel, helped across a river by a litigant, disqualified himself from hearing his case, since the favor created a bond.
Similar incidents: Ameimar disqualified himself after a litigant removed a feather from his head, and Mar Ukva after one covered spittle before him.
Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei refused his sharecropper's Thursday basket of fruit and disqualified himself from the case.
Rabbi Yishmael's reflection: even if he had received his own property, he would be biased; those who accept bribes are surely biased.
Rabbi Yishmael bar Elisha, a priest, refused a first shearing offered by a litigant and disqualified himself.
Rabbi Yishmael bar Elisha's reflection: even receiving his own priestly due would bias him, so bribed judges are all the more biased.
Rav Anan refused a basket of small fish from a litigant and disqualified himself due to the man's actions.
The man replied he did not need a judgment, but asked Rav Anan to accept the gift so he could fulfill the mitzva of first fruits.
A baraita on II Kings 4:42: bringing a gift to a Torah scholar is as though one brought first fruits, which is why the gift is permitted.
Rav Anan accepted the gift after the explanation, and sent the man to Rav Naḥman with a letter asking him to judge the case, since Anan was disqualified.

106a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Two positive mitzvot are weighed; honoring Torah takes precedence, so Rav Anan's bias in a case perverted justice.
Elijah visited Rav Anan and taught him, but left after the miscarriage of justice and later frightened him.
Rav Anan fasted, Elijah returned, and Rav Anan recorded all of Seder Eliyahu, explaining the Rabba and Zuta orders.
During a famine, Rav Yosef refuses to pray, reasoning that Elisha did not pray either when scholars were fed.
Asks from where we know that Elisha supported such a large number of scholars.
Brings the verse from II Kings: how should I set this before a hundred men.
Asks what the phrase before a hundred men means in the verse.
Rejects reading the food as all placed before one hundred men, since drought years made it ample.
Concludes that each loaf was set before a hundred men, reading the verse that way.
Reports how many scholars remained behind at each academy, and how Rav Huna lectured through thirteen speakers.
Dust from scholars leaving Rav Huna's lectures rose so high that Westerners said Babylonian scholars had just stood up.
Reports how many scholars remained at Rabba, Rav Yosef, Abaye, Rav Pappa and Rav Ashi, and that they called themselves orphans.
Rabbi Ami states that Jerusalem blemish inspectors took their wages from the Temple chamber's collection.
Rav Yehuda, quoting Shmuel, says teachers of slaughter laws to priests were paid from the chamber.
Rav Giddel, quoting Rav, says teachers of the handful-removal laws to priests were paid from the chamber.
Rabba bar bar Ḥana, quoting Rabbi Yoḥanan, says Jerusalem's Torah scroll proofreaders were paid from the chamber.
Rav Naḥman quotes Rav that curtain weavers get chamber wages, then holds they should be paid from building funds.
A baraita listing curtain weavers and the houses of Garmu and Avtinas paid from the chamber contradicts Rav Naḥman.
There, the baraita refers to the gate curtains, not the curtains of the Temple building.
Rabbi Zeira quotes Rav on the thirteen curtains of the Second Temple, supporting the gate-curtain distinction.
A baraita states that women raising children for the red heifer were paid from the chamber.
Abba Shaul disagrees: wealthy women of Jerusalem supported them instead of paying them from the chamber.
Rav Huna raises a dilemma and asks Rav a question.

106b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Whether Temple repair vessels count as altar needs or offering needs, and so whether they come from the chamber.
Rav replies that they are made only from the collection of the Temple treasury chamber.
Rav Huna objects with a verse from Chronicles saying vessels were made from the leftover money.
The verse quoted in the objection, describing vessels made from the rest of the money.
Rav replies that the objector studied the Writings and forgot the parallel verse in the Prophets.
Quotes the Kings verse saying the money went to workers, not to vessels, supporting Rav.
The Gemara objects that the two verses contradict each other.
No contradiction: one verse refers to surplus collected, the other to no surplus.
Asks what follows if surplus was collected, since those funds were consecrated for another purpose.
Rabbi Abbahu says the court stipulates that surplus goes to vessels if maintenance does not need it.
Baraita of Rabbi Yishmael's school derives vessel funding from the chamber via the phrase the rest of the money.
Objects that the remainder itself could fund vessels, so the verse does not prove the chamber source.
Rava's principle: the definite article marks the first money, so the verse means the first chamber collection.
A baraita says incense and communal offerings come from the chamber, while the golden altar and vessels come from libations.
The baraita continues, assigning altar upkeep to maintenance funds and city walls to chamber remainders.
Explains that the two sources are a tannaitic dispute.
Quotes the mishna on leftover funds, with the opinions of Rabbi Yishmael, Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Ḥanina.
States that these sages did not agree with each other about the leftover produce.
Asks what this leftover produce actually is.
A baraita explains: they bought produce cheaply, sold it dearly, and used the profit for the altar's repletion.
Asks why both Rabbi Akiva and Rabbi Ḥanina disagreed with Rabbi Yishmael about the leftover produce.
Mishna of leftover chamber funds: Rabbi Akiva forbids profiting from consecrated property or from the poor's funds.
Asks the reason one may not profit from consecrated property.
Because there is no poverty in a place of wealth, the Temple must be run lavishly.
Asks the reason one may not profit from funds set aside for the poor.
Because a poor person may arrive and nothing would be left to give, since the money was invested.
Describes the mishna case of a man who went overseas while his wife demands sustenance.
Notes that amoraim debated this issue, and begins Rav's position.

107a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Rav holds that the court provides maintenance for a married woman whose husband is abroad; Shmuel holds it does not.
Shmuel says Rav concedes that for three months nothing is withheld, and everyone agrees once the husband's death was reported.
Rav explains that the husband's estate is mortgaged to his wife; Shmuel rejects this.
Asks what Shmuel's reason is for denying maintenance.
Rav Zevid suggests the husband gave his wife a bundle of money before leaving.
Rav Pappa suggests the husband told her to support herself from her own earnings.
Asks what the practical difference is between the two explanations.
Differences appear with an adult wife who earns too little, or a minor wife who earns enough.
Quotes the mishna on a husband gone overseas, where Hanan and the priests dispute oaths about maintenance.
The dispute concerns only the oath; everyone agrees maintenance is given to the wife.
Shmuel interprets the mishna as referring to a case where the husband's death was reported.
A baraita says the court may give maintenance and the husband may claim he already provided, challenging Shmuel.
The baraita refers to a case where the death was reported, and the husband returned after a rumor.
A second baraita says the husband may tell his wife to earn her own keep, and the court's prior ruling stands.
This too refers to a case where the husband's death was reported.
A third baraita: the court seizes his property to feed his wife, but not his children, which challenges Shmuel.
Rav Sheshet says the case is where the husband supports his wife through a third party.
Asks why the children would not also be supported through a third party, and what the difference is.
Rav Pappa says the case is where the wife heard of his death from one witness, so maintenance is allowed to her but not to the children.
Asks what the baraita's phrase something else means.
Rav Ḥisda says it refers to the wife's ornaments, which she is entitled to beyond her sustenance.
Rav Yosef says it refers to money for charity, a different view of the phrase.
Concludes that whoever holds ornaments are not paid abroad a fortiori holds the same for charity.

107b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: The one who permits charity from the husband's property holds that jewelry is still given, since the husband would not want his wife degraded.
A baraita on a yevama: she is supported from the yavam's property if he fled, which seems to contradict Shmuel.
Shmuel could answer that the yavam would not leave her money, and her earnings are not yet owed to him.
A baraita where a wife claims her husband died abroad, challenging Shmuel's view that the court gives no maintenance.
Here too the death was reported, and she is limited to her marriage contract because she caused her own loss.
A baraita on a minor who refuses her husband implies a wife is supported from her husband's property abroad.
Shmuel could answer that a minor is not given money and her earnings do not suffice for her needs.
Asks what the final conclusion was about this dispute in practice.
Rav Dimi reports that Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and Rabbi Yishmael ruled differently on similar cases.
Rabbi Yoḥanan asks what Rabbi Yishmael saw that led him not to apportion sustenance.
Rav Shemen bar Abba says Shmuel already explained the case as one where the death was reported.
Rabbi Yoḥanan challenges whether the resolution has gone that far in its analysis.
Ravin reports the reverse version of the case, with Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi refusing and Rabbi Yishmael granting.
Rabbi Yoḥanan asks what Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi saw that led him not to apportion sustenance.
Rav Shemen bar Abba again says Shmuel explained the case as one where the death was reported.
Rabbi Yoḥanan again challenges the resolution as going too far.
The halakha follows Rav, so one apportions sustenance for a married woman whose husband went overseas.
The halakha follows Rav Huna's report of Rav: a wife may tell her husband she will not be sustained and will not work.
The halakha follows Rav Zevid on glazed vessels: white and black ones are permitted if washed, unless they have cracks.
The mishna on a man who supported the wife while the husband was abroad: Ḥanan says he lost his money, while others allow an oath.
Cites a mishna in Nedarim about one prohibited by a vow from benefiting from another, as a parallel source.

108a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: one prohibited by vow from benefit may contribute his shekel, repay a debt for him, or return a lost object.
Granted, contributing the shekel is a mitzva, and the one under the vow gains no direct benefit from it.
A baraita on collecting for lost, collected, and future funds shows communal offerings are made in his name regardless.
Returning a lost object is likewise a mitzva, so that clause raises no problem.
Repaying the debt is problematic because it gives the one under the vow a gain, as the debtor would otherwise pay himself.
Rav Oshaya says the mishna follows Ḥanan, who holds he lost his money, so the repayment is a favor to the creditor.
Rava says even the Rabbis could agree, if the borrower took a loan on condition that he need not repay it until he chooses.
Asks why Rav Oshaya did not adopt Rava's explanation about a loan with no repayment deadline.
Rav Oshaya could reply that although such a loan gives no benefit, the mishna still concerns a case with a benefit.

108b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Asks whether the one under the vow has no shame before his creditor, which should count as a benefit.
There too he has a benefit: the shame he feels before the creditor until the loan is repaid.
Mishna: Admon disagrees with the Rabbis in seven cases, including sons and daughters in a small estate; Rabban Gamliel agrees with Admon.
Asks what Admon means by saying he would lose out because he is a male.
Abaye says Admon means a male is fit for Torah study, so he should not lose out.
Rava objects that inheritance cannot depend on Torah study, since those who study would inherit and others would not.
Rava says Admon means a male has a greater right to inherit the large estate and should not lose out on a small one.
Mishna: a claim for jugs of oil admitted only in pitchers is a partial admission; Admon has the claimant swear, the Rabbis disagree.
Infers from the mishna that the Rabbis exempt a defendant who admits only one of wheat or barley.
Suggests this refutes Rav Naḥman's statement of Shmuel requiring an oath when one type of grain is admitted.
Rav Yehuda says in Rav's name the mishna concerns a claim for a measure of oil, not for jugs.
Asks: if so, what is Admon's reasoning, since the admission and claim do not refer to the same objects?
Rava says everyone agrees, depending on whether the claim is for oil alone, or for oil in full jugs.
The dispute arises only when the claimant says simply that ten jugs of oil are with the defendant.
Admon holds that the phrase includes jugs; the Rabbis hold it does not, and oath liability depends on that reading.
Objects that this refutes Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Abba, who exempted from an oath in the wheat and barley case.
Rav Shimi bar Ashi says the case is like a claim for a pomegranate in its peel, since jugs are needed for oil.
Ravina objects that the pomegranate comparison fails, because oil can be preserved without its jugs.
Rather, the case is one where the defendant admits some jugs but denies the oil, so the admission is not of the same kind.
Admon says the phrase includes jugs and the oath extends to oil; the Rabbis hold no oath is required in this case.
Mishna begins a new case: a man promised money as a dowry for his son-in-law and then went bankrupt.

109a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Admon says a betrothed woman may wait until her head turns white, or the groom must marry her or divorce; Rabban Gamliel agrees.
A Tosefta teaching of Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda: Admon and the Rabbis did not disagree when the father promised the dowry.
Asks what the dispute between Admon and the Rabbis was about, if not this case.
The dispute is when the woman herself promised the dowry; the Rabbis say she must wait until her head turns white.
Admon says she may argue she assumed her father would provide, and now that he does not, she may marry or be released.
Rabban Gamliel says he sees Admon's statement as correct, because she had no money and relied on her father.
A baraita: this applies to an adult woman, while for a minor the court compels payment.
Asks whom the court compels to pay, since if the father is compelled the baraita should say the reverse.
Rava says that for a minor, the court compels the groom to either divorce her or marry her.
Rabbi Yitzḥak ben Elazar in Ḥizkiyya's name: wherever Rabban Gamliel says he sees Admon's view, the halakha follows Admon.
Rava asks whether this principle also applies when the dispute is recorded in a baraita.
Rav Naḥman replies that the principle applies wherever Rabban Gamliel is recorded, including in a baraita.
Rabbi Zeira in Rabba bar Yirmeya's name: the halakha follows Ḥanan's two rulings, but not Admon's seven.
Asks what Rabbi Zeira means by this ruling.
Proposes that the halakha follows Ḥanan's two rulings and also Rabban Gamliel's, not Admon's seven.
Objects that Rabbi Yitzḥak ben Elazar in Ḥizkiyya's name says the halakha follows Admon wherever Rabban Gamliel agrees.
Rather, Rabbi Zeira means Ḥanan's rulings and Rabban Gamliel's agreed-with cases are followed, not Admon's seven.
Objects again to this reading: the Gemara infers that where Rabban Gamliel does not agree, Admon's view is not followed.
Rabbi Zeira means that among Admon's seven rulings, some follow him and some follow only the one who agreed with him.
Wherever Rabban Gamliel says he sees Admon's view, it is followed; in the other cases, Admon is not followed.
Mishna: a man who contests a field after signing as a witness on its sale; Admon allows the claim, the Rabbis do not.
Abaye limits the dispute to witnesses; a judge who certified the sale and contests it has not lost his right.
Rabbi Ḥiyya taught that witnesses sign only after reading the document, so they are presumed to know its full content.

109b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Judges sign a document even without reading it, since they only certify the signatures, not the content.
Abaye limits the lost-right rule to a marker set in a document for another person, not for oneself.
Abaye explains: the claimant would not have sold the other field without the marker, and public notice is impractical.
A man who set a field as a marker, later contested it, and died; Abaye rules he has lost his right to the field.
The steward argues that the father would have said he marked only one furrow, not the whole field.
Abaye accepts this, citing Rabbi Yoḥanan that such a claim is credible, and orders one furrow given to the buyer.
The palm row on that furrow: the steward argues the father sold and then bought the field back.
Abaye accepts this too, citing Rabbi Yoḥanan that a claim of repurchase is credible, and the steward wins.
Abaye concludes that one who appoints a steward should choose someone who protects the orphans' rights.
Mishna: a man abroad loses access to his field; Admon says he takes the shortest route, the Rabbis say he buys a path.
Asks what the reason is for the Rabbis' view, since Admon's position seems reasonable given the prior path.
Rav Yehuda in Rav's name: the field is surrounded on four sides by four owners, each denying the path.
Asks what the reason is for Admon's view, if the case is as Rav described.
Rava: if four owners come through four predecessors, all agree they may refuse; the dispute is one owner with four predecessors.
The dispute arises only where one current owner of four fields came through four previous owners.
Admon holds the claimant can say there is a path through the land; the Rabbis say the owner may refuse negotiation.
Anecdote: a father bequeathed a palm tree to his daughter, and the heirs did not give it; Rav Yosef compares it to the mishna.
Abaye objects that the cases differ: here the palm is in their joint possession, so the estate must be redivided.
A similar case: the father left two half-palm-trees, and the heirs want to give those halves to the daughter.
Rav Ashi asks whether people call two halves of a palm tree a whole palm tree.
Rav Mordekhai quotes Avimi of Hagronya in Rava's name: people do call two halves a palm tree, so the heirs may give them.

110a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: a lender who sold his debtor a field can be told he should have collected the debt then; Admon allows this, the Rabbis do not.
Asks the reason for the Rabbis' view, since Admon seems right in the case.
Where money is given before the bill of sale is written, everyone agrees the borrower may raise the objection.
The dispute is where the bill of sale comes first: Admon requires a preemptive declaration, the Rabbis do not.
Mishna: two people each hold a note against the other; Admon disputes the later note, the Rabbis let each collect.
Rav Naḥman says each collects his own debt; Rav Sheshet holds the same, but on different reasoning about shifting packs.
Rav Sheshet views exchanging the sums as shifting donkey packs, pointing out the dispute concerns mixed land qualities.
Rav Naḥman assesses land quality by the debtor's own fields, so each creditor takes different land.
Rav Sheshet assesses land quality by the standard of all people, so the exchange is pointless.
An example where the intermediate-quality creditor collects first and takes the inferior land.
Asks Rav Naḥman why the inferior-land creditor should collect first, since the same land would be traded back.
The case is needed only when the inferior-land creditor happens to claim first, or when one has mixed land and the other inferior.
The two positions: one assesses land by each borrower's own fields, the other by the standard for all people.
Cites the mishna's ruling that each creditor collects his own note.
Rav Naḥman reads the mishna in line with Rav Sheshet: one borrowed for ten years and the other for five.
Asks whether Admon would object if the first borrowed for ten years and the second for five.
Asks instead whether the first borrowed for five and the second for ten, and what the Rabbis' rationale would be.
It is needed on the day the five-year loan is due, where Admon holds a person does not borrow for one day.
Rami bar Ḥama: the case concerns orphans, who collect their father's debts, while others cannot collect from them.
Objects that the mishna says each collects, which does not fit Rami bar Ḥama's reading of only orphans collecting.
The mishna means one collects and the other has the right to collect but lacks land to seize.
Rava offers two objections to Rami: the mishna says each collects, and the creditor could return the land to the orphans.
Rav Naḥman's report of Rabba bar Avuh: a creditor may take back land orphans seized from their father's debt.
Notes that this poses a difficulty for Rami bar Ḥama's explanation.
Proposes that the orphans have inferior land while the other creditor has better land, so orphans pay only from inferior land.
Orphans pay only from inferior land only before seizure; once land has been seized, it stays seized.
Mishna: in Judea, Transjordan and the Galilee a husband may not move his wife between lands, only between towns within one land.

110b.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Mishna: a husband may move his wife from a bad place to a good one, not the reverse; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel forbids both.
Asks why the husband cannot move his wife from a town to a city, if the city is the harder place to live.
This supports Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina, who held that living in cities is difficult because of noise and bustle.
Quotes Nehemiah, where people blessed those who volunteered to live in Jerusalem, showing city living is hard.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view that a good residence also tests a person, abbreviated in the Gemara.
Asks what Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel means by a pleasant residence testing.
Shmuel: a change of diet or residence starts intestinal disease, so even an improvement harms the poor.
Quotes Ben Sira on the poor, whose roofs and vineyards suffer from runoff.
Mishna: one may force family to move to Eretz Yisrael or to Jerusalem, but not remove others from there.
Mishna: the currency for a marriage contract depends on where the wedding and divorce took place; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel disagrees.
Asks what case the inclusive phrase all may force family to ascend is meant to include.
It includes Hebrew slaves, who may be taken to Eretz Yisrael with their master's family.
Asks, on the version naming slaves explicitly, what case the phrase then includes.
It includes a move from a good residence abroad to a poorer one in Eretz Yisrael.
Asks what case the phrase but all may not remove others is meant to include.
It includes a runaway Canaanite slave who came to Eretz Yisrael: sell him there rather than take him abroad.
Mishna: all may force others to ascend to Jerusalem.
Asks what case the phrase all may force to Jerusalem is meant to include.
It includes a move from a good place elsewhere in Eretz Yisrael to a poor place in Jerusalem.
Mishna: but all may not remove them from Jerusalem.
Asks what case the phrase all may not remove them from Jerusalem includes.
It includes even a move from a poor residence to a pleasant one.
The second clause repeats the first clause's rule, which the first already implies, so the tanna taught it again.
Baraita on divorce and aliyah: a spouse who refuses to ascend to Eretz Yisrael is compelled, or else forfeits or pays the marriage contract.
Introduces a further mishna on a man who married a woman in Eretz Yisrael or Cappadocia.
Asks whether this ruling is itself difficult, since the mishna seems to contradict itself on which currency applies.
Presents the contrast: one married in Eretz Yisrael and divorced in Cappadocia pays in Eretz Yisrael currency, and the reverse also applies.
Rabba: the tanna holds the marriage contract is rabbinic, so the lenient currency is applied in both cases.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel holds the marriage contract is Torah law, so it is paid in the currency of where it arose.
Baraita on promissory notes: the currency follows what the note says about where it was written, and the principle does not apply to a marriage contract.
Asks which clause of the baraita this final statement, excluding marriage contracts, refers back to.
Rav Mesharshiyya: it refers to the first clause; the principle excludes Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's view that the marriage contract is Torah law.
Asks whether money in a note without specification could mean a silver ingot rather than coins.
Rabbi Elazar: the note must say coins, and the minted coin is the object meant.
Asks whether the debt could be paid in small perutot denominations instead.
Rav Pappa: people do not mint silver perutot, as silver is reserved for larger denominations.
Baraita: one should always live in Eretz Yisrael, even in a mostly gentile city, and never abroad, even in a mostly Jewish city.
Cites Leviticus 25:38, to give you the land of Canaan, to be your God, as the basis for that teaching.
Anyone who lives outside Eretz Yisrael is as if he serves idols, since he lacks a God there.
Cites David's words in I Samuel 26:19 about being driven out to serve other gods, supporting the claim.
Rabbi Zeira avoided his teacher Rav Yehuda, who held that ascending from Babylonia to Eretz Yisrael violates a positive mitzva.

111a.source: Machine-assisted draft of the Vilna text; awaiting editorial review

ranges.en: Jeremiah 27:22: they shall be taken to Babylonia until I recall them, said the Lord; Rav Yehuda relies on it.
Rabbi Zeira reads that verse as referring to the Temple vessels, while another verse is read differently by Rav Yehuda.
Song of Songs 2:7: I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the gazelles and hinds of the field.
Rabbi Zeira reads the oath as forbidding Israel to go up en masse like a wall, though individuals may go.
Rav Yehuda replies that the same oath wording appears in another verse, Song of Songs 3:5.
Asks how Rabbi Zeira explains the repetition of the oath in these verses.
Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Ḥanina: three oaths forbid going up as a wall, rebelling, and nations oppressing Israel excessively.
Rav Yehuda replies that the repeated wording in Song of Songs 2:7 amplifies the prohibition on immigration.
Asks how Rabbi Zeira explains the extra emphasis on the phrase, given Rabbi Levi's six oaths.
Rabbi Levi: three oaths are the earlier ones, and three more forbid revealing or postponing the end of days and revealing the secret to idolaters.
Quotes Song of Songs 2:7 again, the gazelles and hinds of the field, as the source for these oaths.
Rabbi Elazar: God tells Israel that if they keep the oath good, and if not, God will give their flesh to be devoured.
Rabbi Elazar: anyone dwelling in Eretz Yisrael lives without sin.
Proof from Isaiah 33:24: the inhabitant shall not say I am sick; the people dwelling there are forgiven their iniquity.
Rava objects to Rav Ashi: we learned that promise only regarding those who suffer from illness.
Rav Anan: anyone buried in Eretz Yisrael is as if buried beneath the altar.
Cites the altar of earth in Exodus 20:21 and the land of His people in Deuteronomy 32:43 as support.
Ulla used to go up to Eretz Yisrael, but died outside it.
Ulla's death is reported to Rabbi Elazar, who receives the news.
Rabbi Elazar cites Amos 7:17, you shall die in an unclean land, to mark Ulla's death abroad.
Told that Ulla's coffin is coming to Eretz Yisrael, Rabbi Elazar replies that being absorbed alive differs from after death.
A man's yevama case comes before Rabbi Ḥanina, from a woman living far away in Babylonia.
Asks whether he may descend to Babylonia to perform levirate marriage with the woman.
Rabbi Ḥanina says his brother married a Samaritan woman and died; he should stay in Eretz Yisrael.
Shmuel: just as leaving Eretz Yisrael for Babylonia is forbidden, so leaving Babylonia for other lands is forbidden.
Rabba and Rav Yosef forbid even leaving Pumbedita for Bei Kuvei; Rav Yosef excommunicated one who did, and another died in Astonia.
Abaye: had that Torah scholar stayed in Babylonia, he would still be alive.
Rabba and Rav Yosef: the worthy of Babylonia are absorbed by Eretz Yisrael, and the worthy of other lands by Babylonia.
Asks what matter the statement concerns, if it is about lineage.
Objects that lineage of all lands is muddled compared to Eretz Yisrael, and Eretz Yisrael's compared to Babylonia's.
Rather, the statement concerns burial, so that the worthy of Babylonia are buried in Eretz Yisrael.
Rav Yehuda: anyone living in Babylonia is as if living in Eretz Yisrael, citing Zechariah 2:11.
Abaye: Babylonia will not see the birth pangs of the Messiah; Hutzal deVinyamin was named the horn of salvation.
Rabbi Elazar: the dead outside Eretz Yisrael will not come alive, citing Ezekiel 26:20 on My desire in the land.
Rabbi Abba bar Memel objects with Isaiah 26:19 that the dead outside Eretz Yisrael will rise.
The verse about glory in the land refers to Nebuchadnezzar, a king swift as a deer, not the dead.
Rabbi Elazar says he reads Isaiah 42:5 instead, so resurrection is for those in Eretz Yisrael.
Asks: is it not written that My dead bodies shall arise, which seems to conflict with his reading?
That verse refers to stillborns, who also merit resurrection.
Asks what Rabbi Abba bar Memel does with the verse he is teaching, He gives breath to the people.
Rabbi Abbahu: even a Canaanite maidservant in Eretz Yisrael is assured a place in the World-to-Come.
Compares the phrase la'am with am in Genesis 22:5, a people like a donkey, to support Rabbi Abbahu.
Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba: anyone who walks four cubits in Eretz Yisrael is assured the World-to-Come; Rabbi Elazar differs.
Rabbi Ile'a: the righteous abroad will be resurrected by rolling to Eretz Yisrael.
Rabbi Abba Salla Rava objects that rolling is suffering for the righteous.
Abaye: tunnels are prepared for the dead underground, so they pass through to Eretz Yisrael.
Cites Genesis 47:30, bury me in their burial place, as Jacob's concern about the tunnels.
Karna: Jacob knew he was completely righteous, yet worried he might not merit the tunnels, so he had himself moved.
Cites Genesis 50:25 where Joseph makes his sons swear to carry his bones up.
Rabbi Ḥanina: Joseph too knew he was righteous, yet had his brothers carry his coffin four hundred parasangs out of concern.
Rabba's brothers write to him that Jacob knew he was completely righteous, as explained above.
Ilfa adds a story: a man suffering for love of a woman wanted to leave Eretz Yisrael, but stayed and died there.
Rabba's brothers: even a great sage learns better from a teacher, and Rabba has a teacher, Rabbi Yoḥanan.
Advice to balance sitting, standing, and walking, since each excess harms a different part of the body.
Asks whether standing can be better than sitting, since standing is hard on the heart; the letter then favors sitting.

ranges.en: Standing with a support is asserted to be better than standing without one
Yitzhak, Shimon and Oshaya agree the halakha follows Rabbi Yehuda about female mules
A baraita of Rabbi Yehuda forbids mating a female mule in heat with horse or donkey
Rav Naḥman identifies the named sages with well-known rabbis
Rabbi Elazar says common ignorant people will not be revived in the future
Isaiah 26:14 is cited for the claim that the dead do not live
A baraita reads the verse as referring only to those who weaken themselves from Torah
Rabbi Yoḥanan objects that Rabbi Elazar's reading is wrong and applies only to idolaters
Rabbi Elazar cites Isaiah 26:19 as his own scriptural basis
Rabbi Elazar explains that only those who use Torah light are revived by it
Rabbi Elazar, seeing the distress, offers a remedy found in the Torah
Deuteronomy 4:4 is cited to show the living cleave to God
Can a person really cleave to the Divine Presence, given that God is a consuming fire
Rather, one who helps Torah scholars is credited as cleaving to the Divine Presence
Deuteronomy 30:20 is cited as a parallel verse on cleaving to God
Is it actually possible for a person to cleave to the Divine Presence
Reply: the verse credits one who supports Torah scholars as if he cleaved to God
Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Yosef says the righteous will sprout up and rise in Jerusalem
Psalms 72:16 and II Kings 19:34 show that the city in the verse means Jerusalem
Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Yosef says the righteous will rise in the resurrection wearing their clothes
A fortiori argument from wheat, buried bare yet emerging clothed, to the righteous
Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Yosef says Eretz Yisrael will produce cakes and fine garments
Psalms 72:16 is cited as support for the claim about bread and garments
The Sages teach that in the future wheat will grow tall like a palm tree on mountaintops
Objection: would the harvesters then suffer hardship
Psalms 72:16 says the fruit will rustle like Lebanon, answering the objection
God will send a wind that loosens flour so a person gathers a palmful for his livelihood
Deuteronomy 32:14 kidney-fat of wheat is cited as the basis for the wheat claim
The Sages say future wheat kernels will be as large as the two kidneys of an ox
Example of a fox nesting in a turnip whose weight proves such growth is possible
Baraita anecdote of an enormous mustard plant, offered as evidence of exceptional growth
Rabbi Shimon ben Taḥlifa says a cabbage stalk was so tall they climbed it with a ladder
Deuteronomy 32:14 about drinking wine is cited regarding the grape claims
The World-to-Come is unlike this world: one grape yields thirty jugs of wine
Deuteronomy 32:14 is quoted as the verse behind the grape claim
The word read as ḥamer should be read as ḥomer, a measure of thirty se'a
Rav Dimi asks what Genesis 49:11 means as a prophecy about the future
Genesis 49:11 about binding the foal to the vine is cited
Every vine in Eretz Yisrael will need a foal to carry its harvest
Genesis 49:11 continues with the verse about the choice vine
Every barren tree in Eretz Yisrael will bear enough to load two donkeys
Objection: lest you say the trees contain no wine
Genesis 49:11 about washing garments in wine answers the objection
Objection: lest you say the wine is not red
Deuteronomy 32:14 about the blood of the grape answers the objection
Objection: lest you say the wine does not intoxicate
Genesis 49:11 about the wine inducing a state of drunkenness answers it
Objection: lest you say the wine has no flavor
Genesis 49:12 read homiletically: each palate tasting it says this is for me
Objection: lest you say the wine is good for the young but not the old
Genesis 49:12 read as teeth whitened by years, meaning an elderly person
What is the plain meaning of the verse, and to what context does it refer
Rav Dimi relates that the congregation of Israel speaks to God about love sweeter than wine
This supports Rabbi Yoḥanan's view that whitening teeth in a smile beats giving milk
Rav Ḥiyya bar Adda, Reish Lakish's teacher, was delayed three days and did not come
Reish Lakish asks why he was delayed
Rav Ḥiyya explains his father left a single vine yielding ever less wine; Reish Lakish adds his comment
Rami bar Yeḥezkel sees goats eating figs with honey and milk mixing, an anecdote about the land
Rami explains this is the meaning of a land flowing with milk and honey
Rabbi Ya'akov ben Dostai walks ankle-deep in fig honey between Lud and Ono
Reish Lakish reports seeing a region by Tzippori flowing with milk and honey
Rabba bar bar Ḥana reports seeing the milk-and-honey region of all Eretz Yisrael

ranges.en: The area of the land is measured as twenty-two by six parasangs
Anecdote of Sages receiving a huge peach, as large as a Kefar Hino stewpot, as evidence of fertility
How large was a stewpot of Kefar Hino
It held five se'a, and they ate one third, gave away one third, and fed one third to animals
Rabbi Elazar's next-year peach shrank; he cites Psalms 107:34 that sins cause the land to turn barren
Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi sees vine clusters as large as calves at Gavla
He remarks that calves stand between the grapevines
The locals reply that these are clusters, not calves
He addresses the earth, telling it to gather its fruit since it feeds gentiles who sin
Rabbi Ḥiyya's visit the next year: clusters as large as goats
Rabbi Ḥiyya says goats are standing between the grapevines
The locals tell him to leave, not to do what his colleague did
A baraita states that a beit se'a in Eretz Yisrael yields fifty thousand kor in blessed years
Rabbi Meir's baraita reports he saw a beit se'a in Beit She'an yield seventy kor
Genesis 13:10 cited: no land is better than Egypt, as the garden of the Lord
Zoan is the finest region in the land of Egypt
Isaiah 30:4 cited: kings were raised in Zoan, which explains its quality
Hebron is the rockiest land in Eretz Yisrael, yet it was developed sevenfold more than Zoan
Numbers 13:22 cited: Hebron was built seven years before Zoan
What is the meaning of the word nivneta, built, in this verse
If built literally, a man would not build a house for a younger son before an older one
Genesis 10:6 shows Mizraim, Egypt, was older than Canaan
The verse means Hebron was sevenfold more fertile; rocky land yields less than unrocky land, up to five hundred kor
Genesis 26:12 cited: Isaac reaped a hundredfold in a blessed year
A baraita of Rabbi Yosei says a se'a in Judea yields five se'a of various grades of flour
A Sadducee tells Rabbi Ḥanina that his own beit se'a of land yields oil, wine, produce, legumes and pasture
An Amorite asks a local how many kor of dates the palm tree on the Jordan yields
The local says sixty kor
The Amorite objects that the local has not even entered the land yet, and they once took 120 kor
The local replies that he too speaks only of one side of the tree, which he has not yet picked
Rav Ḥisda asks what Jeremiah 3:19 means and why the land is likened to a tzvi, a deer
Jeremiah 3:19 is cited as the verse under discussion
Like a deer's skin cannot contain its meat, the land cannot hold its fruit; it ripens swiftly
If so, like a deer's meat is lean, shouldn't the land's fruit also be lean
Exodus 3:8 teaches the fruit is fatter than milk and sweeter than honey
Rabbi Elazar says he escaped three curses: intercalation, ordination and the land
Ezekiel 13:9 cited: false prophets will not be in the council of My people
Ezekiel's verse refers to the calendar council, ordination, and entry into the land, read plainly
Rabbi Zeira crosses the Jordan by a rope bridge since no ferry was found
A Sadducee mocks him for hastiness, recalling that Israel said we will do before we will hear
Zeira replies that Moses and Aaron were denied this land, so he hurried in case he would not enter
Anecdote of Rabbi Abba kissing the rocks of Akko and Rabbi Ḥanina repairing its potholes

ranges.en: The sages of Eretz Yisrael would move between sun and shade so they never felt discomfort there
Rabbi Ḥiyya bar Gamda would roll in the dust of the land
Psalms 102:15 is cited to support rolling in the dust of the land
Rabbi Yirmeya bar Abba says before the Davidic messiah comes, there will be indictments against Torah scholars
Shmuel replies that the generation will be refined repeatedly, in several stages of cleansing
Isaiah 6:13 is cited: a tenth remains and is again consumed, supporting the refinement stages
Rav Yosef taught that in the messianic era despoilers and despoilers of despoilers will plunder the land
Rav says all barren trees in Eretz Yisrael will bear fruit in the future
Joel 2:22 is cited, read to show that every tree, not only fig and vine, will bear fruit
Closing formula marking the end of the second chapter and of tractate Ketubot
